Use case: Intraday strategies, avoiding overnight exposure.

See Time-In-Force, GTC.

Timeboost

Arbitrum's MEV auction system that allows users to bid for priority transaction ordering within blocks. Launched in late 2024 as an alternative to pure FCFS/FIFO ordering.

How it works:

  1. Express Lane: A special ordering lane where winning bidders get their transactions included first
  2. Auction: Users (typically MEV searchers) bid for express lane access in recurring auctions
  3. Revenue Distribution: Auction proceeds go to the Arbitrum DAO treasury (potentially to ARB stakers)
  4. Non-Express Transactions: Still processed via FCFS but after express lane transactions

Contrast with:

  • FCFS/FIFO: Pure arrival-time ordering (original Arbitrum)
  • Gas Auction (Ethereum L1): Priority via gas price, chaotic bidding wars
  • Jito (Solana): Bundle auctions at validator level

Rationale: Rather than letting MEV leak to latency games (fast connections to sequencer) or external parties, Timeboost captures MEV value explicitly and directs it to the protocol. This makes MEV extraction transparent and economically efficient while still providing FCFS ordering for users who don't need priority.

See Sequencer, MEV, FCFS/FIFO.

Tinydancer

Solana light client implementation verifying the Proof of History chain and state validity without running a full validator.

How it works:

  1. PoH verification: Validates the sequential hash chain from slot leaders
  2. State proof verification: Verifies merkle proofs for account state against signed state roots
  3. Minimal bandwidth: Only downloads hashes and proofs, not full blocks

Use cases:

  • Wallets verifying balances on mobile
  • Off-chain applications needing trustless Solana state
  • Embedded systems with limited bandwidth

Trust model: Same as full node—trusts that majority of validators are honest (>2/3 stake).

See Light Node, Proof of History, Gulf Stream.

Timelock

Delay before sensitive operations execute:

  • CRITICAL (7 days): Base token migration
  • HIGH (3 days): Ownership transfer
  • BASE (2 days): Oracle updates
  • LOW (1 day): Add asset, fee changes

Transaction Relay Proxy (TRP)

Specialized infrastructure routing transactions from users to appropriate endpoints for execution. TRPs provide MEV protection by sending transactions to private mempools or MEV-resistant RPC providers instead of public mempools where searchers observe them. Examples include MEV-resistant relays that encrypt transaction details until block inclusion.

Toxic Flow

Trades exploiting information asymmetry—the counterparty knows something the pool doesn't. Toxic flow is unidirectional, driven by CEX price leads, and extracts value even if prices revert (the pool loses on both the up-move and the down-move). Contrast with rebalancing arbitrage, which brings pool prices back to market and is net-positive for liquidity. AIMM charges deviation surcharge on coverage-worsening trades during high oracle disagreement, making toxic flow expensive while keeping rebalancing cheap.

Transient Storage

See EIP-1153.

Treasury

Protocol-controlled address that can collect accumulated protocol fees. Subject to timelock for updates.

U

Undercollateralized

Coverage < 100%. Pool owes more than it holds. Triggers:

  • Withdrawal haircuts
  • Positive inventory skew (premium)
  • Potential liability decay

UUPS (Universal Upgradeable Proxy Standard)

Upgrade pattern where logic contract contains upgrade function. Used by Treasury and Bridge contracts.

V

Vega (ν)

Per-asset sensitivity parameter controlling how volatility affects both the base spread and liquidity dispersion. Tuning guidance:

  • 5000 (0.5x): Gentle volatility response (stablecoins, low-vol assets)
  • 10000 (1.0x): Linear response (default, balanced)
  • 20000 (2.0x): Aggressive spread widening during volatility (volatile assets, high beta)

Formulas:

  • volatilityBand = 100 + σ × vega / (100 × 10000) (spread adjustment)
  • dispersion = clamp(baseDispersion + σ × vega / MULT_BASE, minDisp, maxDisp) (depth curve adjustment)

Economic role: Vega implements volatility sensitivity from Avellaneda-Stoikov. Higher vega means the pool widens spreads and concentrates liquidity when volatility spikes. Joint effect with Gamma & Lambda: Vega affects spread directly via volatility, while gamma affects spread via inventory skew, and lambda via price uncertainty. Together they form the tri-factor fee model (volatility + inventory + deviation). See Volatility (σ), Spread, Dispersion, and docs/1. AIMM/1.2. Pricing/1.2.5. Parametrization.md for implementation.

Volatility (σ)

Price variability measurement. AIMM tracks via dual EMAs:

  • Fast EMA: α = 0.02% (200 in 1e6)
  • Slow EMA: α = 0.18% (1800 in 1e6)

Validium

Layer 2 scaling solution using cryptographic proofs (like zk-rollups) but storing data off-chain instead of on L1. Reduces L1 data overhead at the cost of relying on a data availability committee or external storage. Faster and cheaper than zk-rollups but lower security guarantees for data availability.

Validator

Network participant who stakes cryptocurrency as collateral to participate in consensus and block production. Validators earn rewards for honest participation but face penalties (slashing) for misbehavior.

Validator duties (chain-dependent):

Duty Purpose Reward Penalty
Block proposal Create new blocks Base reward + MEV Missed opportunity
Block attestation Sign validity of blocks Full reward Slashing if wrong
Finality Vote on checkpoints Included in reward Slashing if equivocate

Ethereum validators:

  • Requirement: 32 ETH stake
  • Software: Consensus client (Lighthouse, Prysm, etc.) + Execution client (Geth, Nethermind, etc.)
  • Rewards: ~3-4% APY + MEV tips
  • Penalties: Up to 100% stake loss for egregious misbehavior

Solana validators:

  • Software: Agave or Jito-Solana for MEV, or Firedancer for next-gen
  • Participation: Vote on Tower BFT fork choice
  • Rewards: Transaction fees + MEV (via Jito bundles)

Sui validators:

  • Software: Sui Core
  • Duties: Narwhal committee member + Mysticeti voter
  • Rewards: Transaction fees + commission on delegated stake

MEV considerations:

  • Ethereum: Validators delegate block construction to block builders via MEV-Boost, retaining proposal rights
  • Solana: Validators directly control block composition with Jito MEV auctions
  • Arbitrum/Base: Sequencer controls ordering, validators verify/finalize on L1

See Consensus, Block Builder, Sequencer, Slashing, Finality.

Validator Set

The collection of all active validators in a Proof of Stake network at a given time, responsible for proposing blocks, attesting to canonical chain, and maintaining finality. Validator set composition can change based on stake and protocol rules. The distributed validator set provides security through consensus.

Voting Power

Governance influence calculated from staked positions:

V = (L × lpBase/10000) + (min(boosted, boostCap × G) × lpBoosted/10000) + (G × govMultiplier/10000)

Where L = LP stake, G = governance stake.

W

WAD

Fixed-point unit = 1e18. Used for coverage ratios, prices, and percentages requiring high precision.

Wrapped Native

ERC-20 version of native token (WETH for ETH). AIMM auto-wraps/unwraps for native token support.

Weight (Spline)

Liquidity concentration in profile segment. Higher weight = more depth in that price range. Weights must sum to 200.

Z

Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP)

Cryptographic method where a prover can prove a statement is true to a verifier without revealing any information beyond the statement's validity. Implementations: ZK-SNARKs (succinct, requires setup), ZK-STARKs (transparent, no setup). Applications: Confidential Transfer (hide amounts), Mixer (break transaction links via Commitment + Merkle Proof), Encrypted Mempool (MEV resistance), ZK Compression (state optimization). In blockchains, ZKPs hide sender, recipient, or transaction amount while proving validity. Foundation for privacy protocols and scaling solutions. Related: Bulletproof, Hashing, Nullifier.

ZK-SNARKs (Zero-Knowledge Succinct Non-Interactive Arguments of Knowledge)

Specific zero-knowledge proof system providing succinct, non-interactive proofs. Requires trusted setup but produces small proofs. Used in privacy protocols and zk-rollups for Layer 2 scaling. Examples: Zcash, Aztec, some rollup implementations.

ZK-STARKs (Zero-Knowledge Scalable Transparent Arguments of Knowledge)

Zero-knowledge proof system requiring no trusted setup (transparent), producing slightly larger proofs than SNARKs but with stronger security assumptions. Used in Layer 2 solutions and privacy protocols seeking to avoid trusted setup complexity.

ZK Compression

Technique using zero-knowledge proofs to compress blockchain state, significantly reducing storage costs. Used in Solana and other chains for state optimization. While primarily a scalability feature, enables more cost-effective privacy-preserving applications by reducing on-chain footprint.

Related Documentation

  • Architecture Overview
  • Inventory Management
  • Spread & Fees
  • Parameters Reference

3-overview.title: Overview
3-overview.html:
Security Overview

Defense-in-depth architecture for AIMM protocol security

1. Security Philosophy

AIMM employs a defense-in-depth approach with multiple independent security layers:

  1. Economic Security  Incentive alignment and manipulation resistance
  2. Access Control  Timelocked governance and role separation
  3. Operational Security  Circuit breakers and emergency controls
  4. Code Security  Audits, testing, and formal verification

2. Threat Model

2.1. Adversary Capabilities

Adversary Capabilities Mitigations
Flash Loan Attacker Unlimited capital for single transaction Same-block oracle rejection, TWAP pricing
Whale Trader Large positions, multi-block attacks Dual-window TWAPs, inventory skew bounds
MEV Searcher Transaction ordering, sandwich attacks Slippage protection, directional fees
Oracle Manipulator External feed compromise Dual oracle, deviation detection
Governance Attacker Majority token control Timelocks, grace periods
Smart Contract Exploiter Code vulnerability discovery Audits, bug bounties, upgradability

2.2. Trust Assumptions

Component Trust Level Justification
Owner Trusted Multi-sig with timelock
Treasury Trusted Fee collection only
Bridge Semi-trusted Limited to mint/burn operations
External Oracles Verified Deviation checking, fallbacks
Users Untrusted All inputs validated

3. Security Layers

3.1. Layer 1: Economic Security

Manipulation Resistance:

  • Dual TWAP Windows  5-minute (fast) and 1-hour (slow) averages
  • Same-Block Rejection  Oracle updates skip same-block trades
  • Inventory Skew Bounds  Maximum ±100 skew caps price impact
  • Coverage Floor  50% minimum prevents complete drainage

Incentive Alignment:

  • Directional Fees  Toxic flow pays higher spread
  • LP Haircuts  Undercollateralized withdrawals penalized
  • Decay Mechanism  Long-term undercollateralization resolved

3.2. Layer 2: Access Control

Role Separation:

Role Permissions Holder
Owner All admin functions (timelocked) Multi-sig wallet
Treasury Collect protocol fees Treasury contract
Bridge Mint/burn for cross-chain Bridge contract
Oracles Push price updates Authorized keepers

Timelock Tiers:

  • CRITICAL (7 days)  Base token migration
  • HIGH (3 days)  Ownership, modules, treasury, bridge
  • BASE (2 days)  Oracle changes, staking config
  • LOW (1 day)  Add asset, fee updates

Grace Period: 7 days to execute after timelock expires.

3.3. Layer 3: Operational Security

Circuit Breakers:

// Feature flags (per asset)
FROZEN_BIT            = 1 << 0   // Emergency freeze
SWAP_ENABLED_BIT      = 1 << 1   // Swap operations
LIABILITY_SWAP_BIT    = 1 << 2   // LP position swaps
DECAY_ENABLED_BIT     = 1 << 3   // Liability decay
FLASH_ENABLED_BIT     = 1 << 4   // Flash loans

Emergency Controls:

  • freezeAsset()  Immediate halt (no timelock)
  • unfreezeAsset()  Restore operations
  • Per-asset granularity

Thresholds:

  • coverageFloor  Minimum healthy coverage (default 50%)
  • decayStartRatioBps  Decay activation threshold
  • minLiquidity  Reserve floor per asset

3.4. Layer 4: Code Security

Development Practices:

  • Solidity 0.8.28 with overflow checks
  • Extensive natspec documentation
  • Custom error types (gas efficient)
  • Modular architecture (isolated concerns)

Testing:

  • Unit tests for all functions
  • Integration tests for flows
  • Fuzz testing for edge cases
  • Invariant testing for properties

External Review:

  • Third-party audits (TBD)
  • Bug bounty program (planned)
  • Formal verification (planned)

4. Storage Security

4.1. ERC-7201 Namespaced Storage

Each module uses isolated storage slots:

bytes32 constant CORE_STORAGE_LOC =
    keccak256("pool.storage.base.v1") - 1;
 
bytes32 constant ORACLE_STORAGE_LOC =
    keccak256("pool.storage.oracle.v1") - 1;
 
bytes32 constant STAKING_STORAGE_LOC =
    keccak256("pool.storage.staking.v1") - 1;
 
bytes32 constant DISTRIBUTOR_STORAGE_LOC =
    keccak256("pool.storage.distributor.v1") - 1;

Benefits:

  • No slot collisions between modules
  • Safe upgrades without storage migration
  • Clear separation of concerns

4.2. Transient Storage (EIP-1153)

Used for transaction-scoped data:

  • Reentrancy guards
  • Oracle price caching
  • Flash loan state

Security Properties:

  • Auto-cleared after transaction
  • Cannot persist malicious state
  • Gas efficient

5. Reentrancy Protection

5.1. Transient Guard Pattern

modifier nonReentrant() {
    assembly {
        if tload(GUARD_SLOT) { revert(0, 0) }
        tstore(GUARD_SLOT, 1)
    }
    _;
    assembly {
        tstore(GUARD_SLOT, 0)
    }
}

Protected Operations:

  • All external token transfers
  • Flash loan callbacks
  • Cross-module calls

6. Oracle Security

6.1. Internal Oracle

Manipulation Resistance:

Attack Defense
Flash loan Same-block rejection
Multi-block Dual-window TWAP
Low liquidity External fallback
Staleness TTL-based freshness check

6.2. External Oracle

Validation:

  • Deviation bounds checking
  • Staleness detection
  • Multi-source aggregation option

Fallback Chain:

1. Primary external  2. Secondary external  3. Internal  4. Revert

See: Oracles

7. Upgrade Security

7.1. Diamond-Lite Proxy

Module Registry:

mapping(bytes4 => address) modules;  // selector  implementation

Upgrade Process:

  1. Request module update (3-day timelock)
  2. Wait for delay
  3. Execute within 7-day grace
  4. Old module removed, new module active

Immutable Components:

  • Proxy contract itself
  • Storage slot locations
  • Core libraries

See: Deployment & Upgrades

8. Emergency Procedures

8.1. Security Incident Response

Phase 1: Immediate (0-1 hour)

  1. Identify affected assets
  2. Execute freezeAsset() on affected tokens
  3. Alert team and security partners
  4. Begin investigation

Phase 2: Assessment (1-24 hours)

  1. Determine root cause
  2. Assess damage extent
  3. Identify fix requirements
  4. Prepare communication

Phase 3: Remediation (1-7+ days)

  1. Develop and test fix
  2. Submit timelocked upgrade
  3. Coordinate disclosure
  4. Execute fix after delay

Phase 4: Recovery

  1. Unfreeze assets
  2. Monitor closely
  3. Post-mortem analysis
  4. Update procedures

8.2. Contact Information

For security disclosures:

  • Bug bounty: (TBD)
  • Security email: (TBD)
  • Response SLA: 24 hours

9. Known Limitations

9.1. Economic Bounds

Limitation Bound Implication
Max skew ±100 ~100% premium/discount at extremes
Max depth 4 levels Complex routing limited
Max hops 6 Long paths split execution

9.2. Oracle Limitations

Limitation Mitigation
Low volume  stale TWAP External fallback, shorter TTL
Fast price movement Wider spreads via volatility
External feed failure Multi-source, internal fallback

9.3. Governance Limitations

Limitation Mitigation
Owner compromise Timelock delays, multi-sig
Slow emergency response Immediate freeze (no timelock)
Governance attack Grace period limits exposure

10. Security Checklist

10.1. For Pool Deployers

  • Multi-sig wallet for owner
  • Reasonable initial parameters
  • External oracle fallback configured
  • Emergency contacts established
  • Monitoring systems active

10.2. For LPs

  • Understand coverage mechanics
  • Monitor coverage ratios
  • Understand withdrawal haircuts
  • Verify pool parameters

10.3. For Traders

  • Set appropriate slippage
  • Verify pool coverage
  • Check oracle freshness
  • Understand fee structure

11. Related Documentation

  • Deployment & Upgrades — Upgrade procedures and deployment
  • Access Control — Roles and permissions
  • Flow Guards — JIT protection, cooldowns
  • Oracles — Oracle security and fallbacks
  • Admin Module — Administrative functions

3.2-deployment-upgrades.title: 3.2. Deployment & Upgrades
3.2-deployment-upgrades.html:
Deployment & Upgradeability

1. Overview

The protocol uses a modular diamond-lite proxy pattern for upgradeable pools and standalone contracts for treasury and bridge. This architecture balances upgradeability with security through timelocked governance.

2. Architecture

2.1. Core Components

  1. PoolProxy (contracts/src/PoolProxy.sol)

    • Lightweight EIP-2535-inspired proxy
    • Routes function calls to registered modules
    • ERC-7201 storage pattern for collision resistance
    • Immutable deployer for initialization security

  2. Modules (Implementation contracts)

    • Admin.sol: Administrative functions
    • Core.sol: Swap, deposit, withdraw logic
    • Flash.sol: Flash loan operations
    • Staking.sol: BTR and LP staking
    • Distributor.sol: Reward distribution
    • Oracle.sol: Price feed management

  3. Standalone Contracts

    • Treasury.sol: BTR token management, TGE, vesting
    • Bridge.sol: Cross-chain token bridging

3. Deployment Process

3.1. Phase 1: Deploy Core Infrastructure

// 1. Deploy Treasury
Treasury treasury = new Treasury(
    governanceMultisig,  // owner
    btrToken             // BTR address
);
 
// 2. Deploy Bridge
Bridge bridge = new Bridge(
    daoCouncilMultisig,  // owner
    lzEndpoint           // LayerZero V2 endpoint
);
 
// 3. Deploy Module Implementations
Admin adminImpl = new Admin();
Core coreImpl = new Core();
Flash flashImpl = new Flash();
Staking stakingImpl = new Staking();
Distributor distributorImpl = new Distributor();
Oracle oracleImpl = new Oracle();

3.2. Phase 2: Deploy Pool via Factory Pattern

// 1. Deploy PoolProxy
PoolProxy pool = new PoolProxy();
 
// 2. Initialize pool (must be done by deployer in same transaction)
pool.initialize(
    curatorMultisig,     // owner/curator
    USDC,                // base token
    WETH,                // wrapped native
    IPool.FeeParams({
        protoShare: 20,    // 20% to protocol
        flashFeeBps: 500   // 0.05% flash loan fee
    })
);
 
// 3. Register modules (creates function selector → implementation mapping)
bytes4[] memory adminSelectors = [
    IAdmin.freezeAsset.selector,
    IAdmin.unfreezeAsset.selector,
    IAdmin.requestAddAsset.selector,
    IAdmin.executeAddAsset.selector,
    // ... all admin function selectors
];
 
bytes4[] memory coreSelectors = [
    ICore.swap.selector,
    ICore.deposit.selector,
    ICore.withdraw.selector,
    // ... all core function selectors
];
 
// Initial module setup (no timelock for first-time setup)
Admin(address(pool)).executeModuleUpdate(
    address(adminImpl),
    adminSelectors,
    "" // no init data
);
 
Admin(address(pool)).executeModuleUpdate(
    address(coreImpl),
    coreSelectors,
    "" // no init data
);
 
// ... repeat for all modules

3.3. Phase 3: Connect Dependencies

// Set treasury address in pool (HIGH_TIMELOCK = 3 days)
Admin(address(pool)).requestTreasuryUpdate(address(treasury));
// ... wait 3 days
Admin(address(pool)).executeTreasuryUpdate();
 
// Set bridge address in pool (HIGH_TIMELOCK = 3 days)
Admin(address(pool)).requestBridgeUpdate(address(bridge));
// ... wait 3 days
Admin(address(pool)).executeBridgeUpdate();

4. Upgradeability Mechanisms

4.1. Module Upgrades

Modules can be upgraded or replaced via HIGH_TIMELOCK (3 days):

// 1. Deploy new module implementation
CoreV2 newCore = new CoreV2();
 
// 2. Request module update
Admin(pool).requestModuleUpdate(
    address(newCore),
    coreSelectors,
    initData  // optional initialization call
);
 
// 3. Wait 3 days + execute
Admin(pool).executeModuleUpdate();

Key Properties:

  • Selectors can point to different implementations
  • Multiple selectors can share one implementation
  • Init data allows constructor-like setup
  • Previous implementation remains unchanged

4.2. Storage Persistence

All upgrades preserve storage via ERC-7201 namespaced storage:

// Storage location is deterministic and collision-resistant
bytes32 constant CORE_STORAGE_LOC = keccak256(
    abi.encode(uint256(keccak256("pool.storage.base.v1")) - 1)
) & ~bytes32(uint256(0xff));
 
function _s() internal pure returns (PoolStorage storage $) {
    assembly { $.slot := CORE_STORAGE_LOC }
}

Guarantees:

  • Storage layout preserved across upgrades
  • No storage collision between modules
  • Standard ERC-7201 pattern

4.3. Adding New Functions

New functionality can be added without affecting existing functions:

// Deploy module with new feature
NewFeature newFeatureImpl = new NewFeature();
 
// Register new selectors
bytes4[] memory newSelectors = [
    INewFeature.newFunction.selector
];
 
Admin(pool).requestModuleUpdate(
    address(newFeatureImpl),
    newSelectors,
    initData
);

4.4. Removing Functions

Selectors can be unregistered by pointing them to address(0):

bytes4[] memory deprecatedSelectors = [
    IDeprecated.oldFunction.selector
];
 
Admin(pool).requestModuleUpdate(
    address(0),         // Zero address = remove
    deprecatedSelectors,
    ""
);

5. Non-Upgradeable Components

The following components are immutable by design:

  1. PoolProxy Fallback Logic

    • Selector routing is hardcoded
    • Only module addresses can change
    • Prevents rug-pull attacks

  2. Treasury Contract

    • Cannot be upgraded
    • Ownership transferrable only
    • Protects vesting schedules

  3. Bridge Contract

    • Cannot be upgraded
    • Migration requires new deployment
    • Rate limits protect against exploits

  4. ERC-7201 Storage Locations

    • Hardcoded constants
    • Ensures storage safety

6. Security Through Timelocks

All dangerous operations require time delays:

CRITICAL

Operation Timelock Grace Period Bypass
Base token migration 7 days 7 days No

HIGH RISK

| Ownership transfer | 3 days | 7 days | No | | Module update | 3 days | 7 days | No | | Bridge address update | 3 days | 7 days | No | | Treasury address update | 3 days | 7 days | No |

MEDIUM RISK

| Oracle config change | 2 days | 7 days | No | | Staking params update | 2 days | 7 days | No | | Distribution params | 2 days | 7 days | No | | Bridge peer config | 2 days | 3 days | No | | Bridge token config | 2 days | 3 days | No |

LOW RISK

| Add asset | 1 day | 7 days | No | | Update risk config | 1 day | 7 days | No | | Update fee params | 1 day | 7 days | No |

EMERGENCY

| Freeze asset | None | N/A | N/A | | Pause staking | None | N/A | N/A | | Pause bridge token | None | N/A | N/A |

6.1. Timelock Mechanics

// Request operation
requestOperation(...);
// State: PENDING
// Emits: TimelockRequested(id, opType, executeAfter)
 
// Wait for timelock period
// ...
 
// Execute within grace period
executeOperation(...);
// State: EXECUTED
// Emits: OperationExecuted(id, opType)
 
// OR cancel before execution
cancelOperation(...);
// State: CANCELLED
// Emits: TimelockCancelled(id, opType)

Grace Period Protection:

  • Operations expire after timelock + gracePeriod
  • Prevents indefinite pending operations
  • Requires re-initiation if expired

7. Deployment Configurations

7.1. Mainnet Deployment

Treasury Owner: 3-of-5 Governance Multisig

  • Core team members initially
  • Transition to elected DAO council

Bridge Owner: 3-of-5 DAO Council Multisig

  • Same signers as governance initially
  • Separate keys long-term

Pool Owner (Official Pools): 3-of-5 DAO Council Multisig

  • Controls core protocol pools
  • Sets asset listings, risk params

Pool Owner (Permissionless): Any address

  • Users can deploy their own pools
  • Full control over their pool
  • No protocol control

7.2. Testnet Deployment

Shorter timelocks for testing:

  • CRITICAL: 1 hour
  • HIGH: 30 minutes
  • MEDIUM: 15 minutes
  • LOW: 5 minutes

Not recommended for production value.

8. Permissionless Pool Deployment

Anyone can deploy a pool via factory pattern:

// 1. Deploy PoolProxy
PoolProxy myPool = new PoolProxy();
 
// 2. Initialize with yourself as owner
myPool.initialize(
    msg.sender,  // You are the curator
    baseToken,
    wnative,
    feeParams
);
 
// 3. Register modules
// ... (same as Phase 2 above)
 
// 4. Configure your pool
Admin(address(myPool)).requestAddAsset(...);

Properties:

  • Full control over your pool
  • No protocol governance
  • Timelocks still enforced (protects users)
  • Can use own oracles
  • Can set own fee parameters

Recommended:

  • Use internal oracles only (Curve-style TWAPs)
  • Avoid external oracle dependencies
  • Set conservative risk parameters
  • Test thoroughly on testnet

9. Best Practices

9.1. For Module Developers

  1. Never modify storage layout

    • Only append new storage variables
    • Use ERC-7201 namespaced slots
    • Document storage in comments

  2. Use initialization functions

    • Not constructors (delegatecall context)
    • Include initData in module updates
    • Check initialization state

  3. Maintain interface compatibility

    • Don't change function signatures
    • Add new functions, don't modify existing
    • Use versioned interfaces

  4. Test with actual proxy

    • Don't test implementation directly
    • Use full deployment setup
    • Test upgrade paths

9.2. For Pool Operators

  1. Use multisig for ownership

    • Minimum 3-of-5 signers
    • Distributed key custody
    • Hardware wallet signing

  2. Announce changes in advance

    • Post to governance forum
    • Allow community review
    • Explain rationale

  3. Test on staging first

    • Deploy to testnet
    • Run full scenarios
    • Monitor for issues

  4. Monitor post-upgrade

    • Watch events
    • Check state consistency
    • Have rollback plan

9.3. For Users

  1. Verify module addresses

    • Check on-chain via getModule(selector)
    • Compare against official deployments
    • Use block explorers

  2. Monitor timelock events

    • Subscribe to TimelockRequested
    • Review pending operations
    • Exit if suspicious

  3. Understand risks

    • Upgradeable pools have governance risk
    • Timelocks provide exit window
    • Emergency freezes possible

10. Emergency Procedures

10.1. Asset Freeze (No Timelock)

// Instantly disable all operations on an asset
Admin(pool).freezeAsset(vulnerableToken);

Effect: Disables swap, deposit, withdraw, flash loans immediately.

10.2. Staking Pause (No Timelock)

// Instantly pause all staking operations
Staking(pool).pause();

Effect: Disables stake/unstake while allowing reward claims.

10.3. Bridge Token Pause (No Timelock)

// Instantly pause bridging for a token
Bridge(bridge).pauseToken(token, true);

Effect: Prevents inbound and outbound bridging immediately.

11. Upgrade Checklist

Before deploying an upgrade:

  • Storage layout unchanged or safely extended
  • All selectors mapped correctly
  • Initialization data prepared
  • Timelock announced to community
  • Testnet upgrade successful
  • Security audit completed (for major changes)
  • Emergency freeze procedures documented
  • Monitoring alerts configured
  • Rollback plan documented

12. Future Improvements

  • Beacon proxy pattern: For multiple pools sharing logic
  • Automated testing: On-chain upgrade simulations
  • Formal verification: Storage safety proofs
  • Governance UI: User-friendly proposal tracking
  • Security council: Fast-track emergency upgrades with higher threshold

3.4-flow-guards.title: 3.4. Flow Guards
3.4-flow-guards.html:
3.4. Flow Guards (Reentrancy & MEV Protection)

Multi-layered temporal protection against callback, reentrancy, and JIT manipulation attacks

Overview

The Flow Guard System is a two-layer security architecture that protects against malicious interaction flows at different attack levels:

Layer Mechanism Scope Attack Vector Implementation
L1: Transaction Level Reentrancy Guard Same transaction Callback-based reentrancy EIP-1153 transient storage
L2: Block Level Time-Based Flow Guard Cross-transaction JIT liquidity / MEV bundles Timestamped cooldowns

Both layers work together to create a defense-in-depth strategy against flow manipulation:

Layer 1: Reentrancy Guard (Transaction-Level)

What It Protects Against

Reentrancy is when an external contract calls back into the pool during the execution of an operation, before that operation completes.

Attack Example:

Implementation (EIP-1153)

The pool uses EIP-1153 transient storage for reentrancy protection:

// lib/LibTransientCache.sol
bytes32 constant REENTRANCY_GUARD_SLOT =
    0x7f9fb83b5bfa6d3...;  // ERC-7201 namespace
 
modifier nonReentrant() {
    uint32 status = TLoad(REENTRANCY_GUARD_SLOT).cast();
    if (status != 0) revert Reentrancy();
 
    TStore(REENTRANCY_GUARD_SLOT, 1);  // Set locked
    _;
    TStore(REENTRANCY_GUARD_SLOT, 0);  // Set unlocked
}

Key Properties:

  • Transient Storage (TLOAD/TSTORE): Data cleared at end of transaction
  • Zero Cost on revert: Transient storage is automatically cleaned up
  • Simple: Single locked/unlocked flag
  • Fast: ~100 gas (vs ~20k for sstore)

Protected Operations

All user-facing pool operations are wrapped:

  • deposit() - prevents callback during transfer
  • withdraw() - prevents callback during transfer
  • swap() - prevents callback during swaps
  • stakeGov(), stakeLP(), etc. - all external calls protected

What Reentrancy Guard Does NOT Prevent

Same-block attacks that don't use callbacks:

  • JIT liquidity bundles (Flashbots ordering)
  • Multi-transaction atomic sequences in same block
  • MEV sandwich attacks
  • Price oracle staleness attacks

These require Layer 2 (Flow Guard) protection.

Layer 2: Flow Guard (Block-Level MEV Protection)

What It Protects Against

JIT (Just-In-Time) Liquidity is an MEV strategy where sophisticated actors:

  1. Observe a pending large swap in the mempool
  2. Deposit liquidity in the same block (via Flashbots bundle)
  3. Capture swap fees from the large trade
  4. Withdraw liquidity in the same block (atomic)

This extracts value that should go to long-term LPs, without bearing any price risk.

Research Context:

  • JIT attacks account for ~0.5-1% of Uniswap v3 volume
  • Dominated by 3-5 sophisticated MEV bots
  • Average extraction: 5-15 bps per targeted swap
  • Long-term LPs lose fee income to zero-risk extractors

Protected Flows

Flow Entry Action Exit Action Protection Use Case
Deposit→Withdraw deposit() withdraw(), withdrawTo() 15s cooldown Prevents JIT LP positioning
Stake Gov→Unstake Gov stakeGov() unstakeGov() 15s cooldown Prevents instant voting/reward capture
Stake LP→Unstake LP stakeLP() unstakeLP() 15s cooldown Prevents JIT reward farming

Example Attack Timeline:

How Time-Based Flow Guard Works

Architecture

Operation Flow

Time-Based (Not Block-Based)

The cooldown is measured in seconds, not blocks. This ensures:

  • Consistent protection across all EVM chains
  • Works on chains with variable block times (Arbitrum, Polygon, etc.)
  • Protection scales with real-world time, not validator behavior

Configuration

Default Value

uint16 constant DEFAULT_FLOW_COOLDOWN = 15; // 15 seconds

The 15-second default was chosen because:

  • Long enough to span multiple blocks on any major EVM chain
  • Short enough to not impede legitimate users
  • Practical for cross-chain consistency

Admin Control

Pool owners can adjust the cooldown:

// Increase protection (e.g., during high MEV activity)
pool.setFlowCooldown(30); // 30 seconds
 
// Disable for trusted environments (NOT recommended for public pools)
pool.setFlowCooldown(0);

Note: Setting flowCooldownSeconds = 0 completely disables the flow guard.

Maximum Value

The uint16 type allows up to 65,535 seconds (~18.2 hours). Values above 300 seconds (5 minutes) are generally impractical.

Error Handling

When a cooldown violation is detected:

error CooldownActive(uint32 remainingSeconds);

Example:

  • User deposits at T=100
  • User tries to withdraw at T=105 (cooldown=15s)
  • Reverts with CooldownActive(10) (10 seconds remaining)

Defense-in-Depth Architecture

Attack Surface Coverage

The two-layer system protects against different attack surfaces:

L1 vs L2 Comparison

Property Reentrancy Guard (L1) Flow Guard (L2)
Scope Same transaction Cross-transaction
Duration Single function call 15 seconds
Attack Vector Callback reentrancy JIT liquidity / MEV
Implementation TLOAD/TSTORE flag Timestamp cooldowns
Gas Cost ~100 gas ~5-7k gas per operation
Frequency Every operation Entry + exit check

Attack Timeline Example

Reentrancy Attack (L1):

JIT Liquidity Attack (L2):

Why Both Layers Matter

  • Layer 1 alone (just reentrancy guard): Stops callback attacks but not MEV bundles
  • Layer 2 alone (just flow guard): Stops JIT attacks but not malicious callbacks
  • Both layers (defense-in-depth): Comprehensive protection against flow manipulation

Example: If Layer 1 didn't exist, a malicious token could:

  1. User calls deposit(maliciousToken, 1000)
  2. Pool transfers 1000 tokens
  3. Token's fallback calls withdraw() on pool
  4. Withdrawal succeeds during deposit → potential theft

This attack is prevented by Layer 1's reentrancy guard.

Stake Lock Duration

Staking already has a stakeLockDuration (default 14 days) that prevents unstaking for a period. Flow Guard adds an additional entry-side protection:

  • Stake Lock: Prevents early unstake regardless of entry timing
  • Flow Guard: Prevents immediate unstake after stake (JIT reward capture)

A user who stakes must wait:

  1. flowCooldownSeconds (15s) before they can even attempt to unstake
  2. stakeLockDuration (14 days) before the stake is actually unlocked

Combined Protection Model

How Layers Interact

Both reentrancy guard and flow guard are applied to complementary operations:

function deposit(address token, uint256 amount) external nonReentrant {
    // Layer 1: Reentrancy guard active (TSTORE locked)
    // Prevents callbacks during token transfer
 
    // ... deposit logic ...
 
    // Layer 2: Record deposit timestamp (for flow guard)
    _recordDepositTime(msg.sender, token);
}
 
function withdraw(address token, uint256 lpAmount) external nonReentrant {
    // Layer 1: Reentrancy guard active (TSTORE locked)
    // Prevents callbacks during token transfer
 
    // Layer 2: Check flow guard cooldown
    _checkWithdrawCooldown(msg.sender, token);
 
    // ... withdrawal logic ...
}

Sequential Protection

User flow is protected at both levels:

What About Both Attacks Simultaneously?

A sophisticated attacker might try to combine strategies:

Even if Layer 1 didn't exist, Layer 2 would still prevent the JIT attack. Even if Layer 2 didn't exist, Layer 1 would still prevent the callback attack.

Result: Two independent, complementary defenses.

Implementation Details

Layer 1: Reentrancy Guard Storage (Transient)

Reentrancy guard uses EIP-1153 transient storage (TLOAD/TSTORE):

// lib/LibTransientCache.sol
bytes32 constant REENTRANCY_GUARD_SLOT =
    0x7f9fb83b5bfa6d3c2e1a0f4b8c6d2e1a5f0b4c8d6e2f1a3b5c7d9e0f1a3b5c7d;
 
// Single boolean flag (uint32 for alignment)
// 0 = unlocked (default)
// 1 = locked (operation in progress)
 
modifier nonReentrant() {
    uint32 status = TLoad(REENTRANCY_GUARD_SLOT);
    if (status != 0) revert Reentrancy();
 
    TStore(REENTRANCY_GUARD_SLOT, 1);  // Lock
    _;
    TStore(REENTRANCY_GUARD_SLOT, 0);  // Unlock
}

Transient Storage Advantages:

  • Data lives only for one transaction
  • Automatically cleaned up at end of transaction
  • No gas refunds needed
  • Fast access (~100 gas vs ~20k for persistent storage)
  • Perfect for mutex flags

Layer 2: Flow Guard Storage (Persistent)

Flow guard uses standard persistent storage with ERC-7201 namespace:

// LibConstants.sol
bytes32 constant FLOW_GUARD_STORAGE_LOC =
    0x8a7c9f2e5b3d1a4c6e8f0d2b4a6c8e0f2d4b6a8c0e2f4d6b8a0c2e4f6d8b0a00;
 
// IPoolV1.sol
struct FlowGuardStorage {
    // Per-user, per-token deposit timestamps
    mapping(address => mapping(address => uint32)) lastDepositTime;
 
    // Per-user governance stake timestamps
    mapping(address => uint32) lastGovStakeTime;
 
    // Per-user, per-token LP stake timestamps
    mapping(address => mapping(address => uint32)) lastLPStakeTime;
}

Storage Design:

  • Three separate timestamp mappings for three flow types
  • uint32 timestamps (good until year 2106)
  • Namespace prevents collision with other pools/contracts
  • Persistent storage needed to track across transactions

Gas Costs

Layer 1: Reentrancy Guard

Operation Gas Cost Note
Entry (TSTORE 1) ~100 Transient storage write
Exit (TSTORE 0) ~100 Transient storage clear
Revert check (TLOAD) ~100 Read on reentry attempt
Total per operation ~100-200 Applied to ALL external calls

Layer 2: Flow Guard

Operation Gas Cost Context
Record timestamp (deposit) ~5,000 SSTORE to cold slot (first time)
Record timestamp (stake) ~5,000 SSTORE to cold slot (first time)
Check cooldown (withdraw) ~2,100 SLOAD from slot (already warm)
Check cooldown (unstake) ~2,100 SLOAD from slot (already warm)

Combined Overhead

Operation L1 L2 Total
deposit() (write timestamp) 100 5,000 ~5,100
withdraw() (check cooldown) 100 2,100 ~2,200
swap() (no flow guard) 100 0 ~100

Context:

  • A typical deposit costs ~100-200k gas
  • Flow guard adds ~2-5% overhead
  • Reentrancy guard adds <1% overhead
  • Combined overhead is small relative to operation cost

Optimization note: After first warm-up, subsequent operations on same storage slot cost less due to "warm" slot pricing (100 gas vs 2,100 gas).

What Flow Guards Does NOT Protect Against

Layer 1 Limitations (Reentrancy Guard)

Reentrancy guard only protects against callback-based attacks:

  1. Multi-step attacks - Attacks that require user interaction outside the callback (e.g., "step 1: transfer out, step 2: user action, step 3: callback")
  2. Cross-contract reentrancy - If the pool calls Contract A, which calls Contract B, which calls back into pool (needs more sophisticated analysis)

Layer 2 Limitations (Time-Based Flow Guard)

Flow guard does not protect against:

  1. Long-term statistical arbitrage - If someone deposits for 1 day, they still capture fees during that time
  2. Information-based trading - Traders with alpha about future prices (this is not MEV extraction)
  3. Cross-pool attacks - Coordination across multiple pools
  4. Off-chain coordination - Multiple wallets controlled by same entity
  5. Oracle manipulation - Price feed attacks (separate concern, handled by oracle layer)

Complementary Defenses

Both flow guards are one layer in a comprehensive defense-in-depth strategy:

Layer Mechanism Prevents
L1: Reentrancy Transient storage flag Callback attacks during operation
L2: Flow Guard Timestamped cooldowns JIT liquidity and MEV bundling
L3: Pricing Directional fees Toxic/coverage-worsening trades
L4: Oracle TWAP + staleness checks Price feed manipulation
L5: Volatility Spread adjustment Exploitation during uncertainty

Example: A complete attack chain might involve:

  1. Oracle manipulation (L4 blocks)
  2. Attempt to exploit pricing (L3 charges premium)
  3. JIT deposit-and-swap (L2 blocks)
  4. Malicious callback (L1 blocks)

Each layer independently protects, and combined they create comprehensive security.

Summary: Two-Layer Flow Protection

The Flow Guard System consolidates two complementary security mechanisms into a unified architecture:

Layer 1: Reentrancy Guard (Transaction-Level)

  • Scope: Same transaction
  • Protection: Callback-based reentrancy attacks
  • Implementation: EIP-1153 transient storage flag
  • Cost: ~100 gas per operation
  • Applies to: All external calls (deposit, withdraw, swap, stake, etc.)

Layer 2: Time-Based Flow Guard (Block-Level)

  • Scope: Cross-transaction (15-second default cooldown)
  • Protection: JIT liquidity and MEV bundling attacks
  • Implementation: Timestamped cooldowns on complementary operations
  • Cost: ~5k gas on entry, ~2.1k gas on exit
  • Applies to: Deposit→withdraw, stake→unstake flows

Design Principles

  1. Defense-in-Depth: Both layers work independently

    • Layer 1 alone stops callback attacks
    • Layer 2 alone stops JIT attacks
    • Combined = comprehensive protection

  2. Low Gas Overhead

    • Reentrancy: <1% of operation cost
    • Flow guard: 2-5% of operation cost
    • Minimal friction for users

  3. Per-Transaction Clarity

    • Layer 1 clears automatically at end of transaction
    • Layer 2 persists across transactions
    • No manual cleanup needed

  4. Simple, Auditable Code

    • Single flag per transaction (Layer 1)
    • Three timestamp mappings (Layer 2)
    • No complex state machines

Key Takeaway

The two layers protect different attack surfaces:

  • Reentrancy Guard: "Can you call back into us during our operation?"

    • Answer: No, flag prevents it

  • Flow Guard: "Can you deposit and withdraw atomically in the same block?"

    • Answer: No, 15-second cooldown prevents it

Together, they form a robust defense against the most common flow manipulation attacks on AMMs.

Related Documentation

  • 3.1. Security Overview
  • 1.2.4. Spread & Fees
  • 1.2.6. Anti-Toxic Flow Protection

3.5-oracles.title: 3.5. Oracles
3.5-oracles.html:
Oracle System

Multi-timeframe TWAP and volatility tracking for informed pricing

1. Overview

AIMM uses a two-oracle pattern:

  1. Internal Oracle (InternalOracleV1) — Auto-updated on every swap, tracks TWAPs and volatility from execution prices
  2. External Oracle (ExternalOracle) — Push-based feeds from Chainlink, Pyth, or custom keepers

The system decouples price discovery from reserves, enabling informed market making instead of mechanical invariant pricing.

2. Internal Oracle (InternalOracleV1)

2.1. Purpose

Tracks pool-observed prices with dual-timeframe smoothing:

  • Fast TWAP: 5-minute window (responsive to recent trades)
  • Slow TWAP: 1-hour window (resistant to manipulation)

Both TWAPs update automatically after each swap — no external keeper required.

2.2. Feed Structure

Storage per token (spans multiple slots):

struct FeedAccumulator {
    // Accumulator state (B64 with configurable accDecimals)
    uint64 priceAccB64;       // Time-weighted price accumulator
    uint64 fastSnapB64;       // Fast window snapshot
    uint64 slowSnapB64;       // Slow window snapshot
    uint32 fastSnapshotTime;  // Fast snapshot timestamp
    uint32 slowSnapshotTime;  // Slow snapshot timestamp
 
    // Price & offsets
    uint64 lastPriceB64;      // Current spot price (B64, token decimals)
    int32 fastOffset;         // Fast TWAP offset from spot (0.0001% units)
    int32 slowOffset;         // Slow TWAP offset from spot (0.0001% units)
 
    // Volatility & metadata
    uint32 lastUpdate;        // Timestamp of last update
    uint32 fastVolEMA;        // Fast volatility EMA (1e6 base)
    uint32 slowVolEMA;        // Slow volatility EMA (1e6 base)
    uint16 ttl;               // Time-to-live (default 1 hour)
    uint8 accDecimals;        // Accumulator encoding decimals (set at init)
    uint8 confidence;         // 0-100 confidence score
}

2.3. Accumulator Decimals (accDecimals)

The accDecimals parameter controls how TWAP accumulators are encoded in B64 format. Using lower decimals provides more headroom for time-weighted accumulation:

Asset Class Example accDecimals Max Accumulator Practical Limit
Stablecoins USDC, USDT 6 ~4.5×10⁷² >10,000 years
Mid-cap ETH, SOL 12 ~4.5×10⁶⁶ >10,000 years
High-value BTC, WBTC 18 ~4.5×10⁶⁰ >1,000 years

Why this matters:

B64 float format has 52-bit mantissa with exponent range ±63. The accumulator stores:

accumulator += price_in_accDecimals_base × dt_seconds

For stablecoins (~$1), using accDecimals=6:

  • Price in accDecimals base: decodeB64(priceB64, 6) ≈ 1×10⁶
  • After 1 year: 1×10⁶ × 31.5M seconds ≈ 3×10¹³
  • B64 mantissa max: ~4.5×10¹⁵ (plenty of room before exponent kicks in)
  • With exponent: can handle up to ~4.5×10⁷²

For BTC (~$100k), using accDecimals=18:

  • Price in accDecimals base: decodeB64(priceB64, 18) ≈ 1×10²³
  • After 1 year: 1×10²³ × 31.5M ≈ 3×10³⁰
  • Still within B64 range (~4.5×10⁶⁰)

Configuration:

Set via OracleConfig.accDecimals when adding assets:

OracleConfig memory cfg = OracleConfig({
    primary: address(pool),  // Internal oracle
    secondary: address(0),
    feedId: bytes32(0),
    modeFlags: 0,
    accDecimals: 6,          // For stablecoins
    _pad: padArray
});

Default is 6 if not specified (stablecoin-optimized).

2.4. Constants

Constant Value Description
FAST_WINDOW 300s 5-minute TWAP window
SLOW_WINDOW 3600s 1-hour TWAP window
FAST_VOL_ALPHA 200 0.02% volatility smoothing
SLOW_VOL_ALPHA 1800 0.18% volatility smoothing
MAX_VOLATILITY 100,000,000 10,000% max vol (1e6 base)
DEFAULT_TTL 3600 1 hour staleness threshold

2.5. Update Flow

On every swap, pushFeedInternal() is called:

swap() executes
    ↓
Calculate execution price in B64 (token decimals)
    ↓
pushFeedInternal(tokenA, tokenB, priceA, priceB)
    ↓
For each non-base token with price:
    _updateFeeds(token, newPrice)

2.5.1. _updateFeeds() Logic

  1. Same-block protection: Skip if dt == 0 (prevents manipulation)

  2. Accumulator update (using accDecimals, not token decimals):

    accDec = acc.accDecimals              // Set at init (6 for stables, 12 for ETH, etc.)
lastPriceInAccDec = decodeB64(lastPriceB64, accDec)
increment = lastPriceInAccDec × dt
currentAcc = decodeB64(priceAccB64, accDec) + increment
priceAccB64 = encodeB64(currentAcc, accDec)   // Store with accDecimals

  3. Fast TWAP (every 5 minutes):

    if dtFast >= FAST_WINDOW:
    fastSnapAcc = decodeB64(fastSnapB64, accDec)
    twapInAccDec = (currentAcc - fastSnapAcc) / dtFast
    fastTWAP = twapInAccDec × 10^(18 - accDec)   // Scale to 1e18
    fastOffset = encodeOffset1e18(spot1e18, fastTWAP)
    fastSnapB64 = priceAccB64  // Store snapshot

  4. Slow TWAP (every hour):

    if dtSlow >= SLOW_WINDOW:
    slowSnapAcc = decodeB64(slowSnapB64, accDec)
    twapInAccDec = (currentAcc - slowSnapAcc) / dtSlow
    slowTWAP = twapInAccDec × 10^(18 - accDec)   // Scale to 1e18
    slowOffset = encodeOffset1e18(spot1e18, slowTWAP)
    slowSnapB64 = priceAccB64  // Store snapshot

  5. Volatility EMA:

    priceChange = |lastPrice - newPrice| (1e6 base)
fastVolEMA = EMA(fastVolEMA, priceChange, FAST_VOL_ALPHA)
slowVolEMA = EMA(slowVolEMA, priceChange, SLOW_VOL_ALPHA)

2.6. Offset Encoding

Offsets represent TWAP deviation from spot price:

offset = ((TWAP / spot) - 1) × OFFSET_PRECISION
 
where OFFSET_PRECISION = 10,000,000 (0.0001% = 1 unit)

Decoding (in LibOracle):

twap = spot × (1 + offset / OFFSET_PRECISION)

Benefits:

  • Single B64 decode per price read
  • Offsets applied in 1e18 space (no redundant encoding)
  • int32 range covers ±214,748% deviation

3. External Oracle (ExternalOracle)

3.1. Purpose

Push-based oracle for:

  • Chainlink/Pyth price feeds
  • Off-chain keeper updates
  • Cross-chain price aggregation

3.2. Feed Structure

Same FeedData struct as internal oracle:

struct FeedData {
    uint64 lastPriceB64;      // Fast EMA (reference price)
    int32 fastOffset;         // Always 0 (fast = reference)
    int32 slowOffset;         // Slow EMA offset from fast
    uint32 fastVolEMA;        // Fast volatility
    uint32 slowVolEMA;        // Slow volatility
    uint32 updatedAt;         // Last push timestamp
    uint16 ttl;               // Staleness threshold
    uint16 confidence;        // 0-100
}

3.3. Feed Management

Adding a feed:

addFeed(
    base,           // Token being priced
    quote,          // Quote currency (e.g., USD)
    fastEMA,        // Initial fast price (B64)
    slowEMA,        // Initial slow price (B64)
    fastVolEMA,     // Initial fast vol (1e6)
    slowVolEMA,     // Initial slow vol (1e6)
    maxDeviation,   // Max allowed deviation (0.0001% units)
    ttl             // Staleness threshold (seconds)
)

Feed ID: keccak256(abi.encodePacked(base, quote))

Pushing updates:

// Single feed
pushFeed(feedId, newFastEMA, newSlowEMA, newFastVolEMA, newSlowVolEMA)
 
// Batch (gas efficient)
batchPush(feedIds[], fastEMAs[], slowEMAs[], fastVolEMAs[], slowVolEMAs[])

3.4. Access Control

Role Capabilities
Owner Add feeds, update config, grant/revoke oracles
Oracle Push price updates

4. B64 Float Encoding

4.1. Format (52/5/7)

[mantissa:52 | decimals:5 | exponent+bias:7]
 
Total: 64 bits
```math
 
| Field | Bits | Range | Description |
|-------|------|-------|-------------|
| Mantissa | 52 | 0 - 4.5×10^15 | Normalized value |
| Decimals | 5 | 0-31 | Token decimal places |
| Exponent | 7 | -64 to +63 (biased by 64) | Scale factor |
 
### 4.2. Encoding (LibMaths)
 
```solidity
function encodeB64(uint256 value, uint8 decimals) internal pure returns (uint64)
  1. Normalize mantissa to 52 bits
  2. Compute exponent from normalization shift
  3. Pack: (mantissa << 12) | (decimals << 7) | (exponent + 64)

4.3. Decoding (LibMaths)

function b64To1e18(uint64 b64) internal pure returns (uint256)
  1. Extract mantissa, decimals, exponent
  2. Compute total shift = exponent - bias + decimals
  3. Return: mantissa × 10^totalShift (normalized to 1e18)

4.4. Example

Price: 2500.00 USDC (6 decimals)

  • Value: 2,500,000,000 (2500 × 10^6)
  • Mantissa: Normalized to 52 bits
  • Decimals: 6
  • Exponent: Based on normalization

5. LibOracle Functions

5.1. Price Decoding

/// Decode both TWAPs efficiently (single B64 decode)
function decodeB64s(FeedData memory feed)
    returns (uint256 priceFast, uint256 priceSlow)
 
/// Fast path for hot operations
function getFastEMA(FeedData memory feed) returns (uint256 priceFast)
 
/// Slow EMA only
function getSlowPrice(FeedData memory feed) returns (uint256 priceSlow)

5.2. Volatility & Deviation

/// Effective volatility σ = (fastVol + slowVol) / 2
function getSigma(FeedData memory feed) returns (uint32 sigma)
 
/// Price deviation Δ = max(|fast-slow|, |fast-current|)
function getDelta(FeedData memory feed) returns (uint32 delta)

5.3. Base Token Feed

/// Synthetic feed for base token (always 1.0)
function getBaseFeed() returns (FeedData memory feed)

Returns:

  • lastPriceB64: 1.0 encoded
  • Offsets: 0
  • Volatility: 0.01% baseline
  • TTL: Never expires

6. Oracle Selection

6.1. Mode Flags

Configured per asset in OracleConfig:

struct OracleConfig {
    address primary;      // Primary oracle (internal or external)
    address secondary;    // Fallback oracle
    uint16 mode;          // Behavior flags
    uint16 maxDeviation;  // Max price deviation threshold
}
Mode Flag Bit Behavior
MODE_USE_INTERNAL 0x01 Prefer internal oracle
MODE_USE_EXTERNAL 0x02 Prefer external oracle
MODE_ALLOW_FALLBACK 0x04 Fall back to secondary on stale/missing

6.2. Selection Logic

1. Check mode flags
2. If USE_INTERNAL: query InternalOracleV1
3. If USE_EXTERNAL: query ExternalOracle
4. If stale and ALLOW_FALLBACK: try secondary
5. If all fail: revert StaleData

7. Transient Caching (EIP-1153)

For gas optimization, LibTransientOracle caches decoded prices in transient storage:

/// Cache key: keccak256(abi.encodePacked(token, "price"))
/// Cache value: (priceFast, priceSlow, sigma, delta)

Savings: ~2,100 gas per cache hit

Scope: Single transaction (clears automatically)

8. Security Considerations

8.1. Manipulation Resistance

  1. Same-block skip: Prevents multiple updates in one block
  2. TWAP smoothing: 5min/1hr windows resist flash loan manipulation
  3. Dual-window cross-check: Large fast/slow divergence triggers higher fees

8.2. Staleness Protection

  1. TTL enforcement: Feeds expire after configurable period
  2. Confidence scoring: External feeds can signal uncertainty
  3. Fallback cascade: Secondary oracle protects against primary failure

8.3. Deviation Bounds

  1. maxDeviation threshold: Rejects external pushes with extreme moves
  2. MAX_VOLATILITY cap: 10,000% ceiling prevents overflow
  3. Offset clamping: int32 range prevents extreme TWAP divergence

9. Usage Examples

9.1. Reading Internal Oracle

// Get full feed data
IOracleV1.FeedData memory feed = IOracle(pool).getFeed(token);
 
// Check freshness
bool fresh = IOracle(pool).isFeedFresh(token, 300); // 5 min max age
 
// Get just fast TWAP
uint64 fastTWAP = IOracle(pool).getFastTWAP(token);

9.2. Initializing Oracle

// Admin: initialize token feed
IOracle(pool).updateFeed(
    token,           // Asset
    initialPriceB64, // Starting price (B64, token decimals)
    6,               // accDecimals (6 for stables, 12 for ETH, 18 for BTC)
    10_000,          // 0.01% fast vol
    10_000           // 0.01% slow vol
);

Note: accDecimals determines accumulator range vs precision tradeoff. Lower values = more headroom for long-running pools. See Accumulator Decimals section.

9.3. External Oracle Push

// Keeper: push batch update
oracle.batchPush(
    feedIds,
    fastEMAs,
    slowEMAs,
    fastVolEMAs,
    slowVolEMAs
);

10. Related Documentation

  • Architecture — System overview
  • Fee System — How volatility affects fees
  • Parameters — Oracle configuration reference

3.3-access-control.title: 3.3. Access Control
3.3-access-control.html:
Governance & Access Control

1. Overview

The protocol implements a comprehensive governance system with role-based access control, timelocked operations, and emergency procedures. Governance is initially managed by the core team via multisigs, with a planned transition to DAO-elected councils.

2. Governance Entities

2.1. Treasury Multisig (Governance Multisig)

Contract: Treasury.sol at contracts/src/Treasury.sol

Initial Setup: 3-of-5 multisig (core team)

Long-term: 3-of-5 elected DAO council

Powers:

  • Mint BTR tokens to any address (immediate)

    treasury.mintBTR(recipient, amount);

  • Grant vested allocations during TGE initialization

    treasury.initializeTGE(
    treasuryAmount,
    seedingAmount,
    baseEmissionRate,
    halvingInterval,
    beneficiaries,
    allocations
);

  • Allocate incentives to pool distributors

    • Mint BTR to distributor contracts
    • Distributors handle per-pool distribution

  • Special allocations for events, grants, partnerships

    • Direct minting to recipients
    • No vesting cliffs for special cases

  • Collect protocol fees from pools

    treasury.collectProtocolFees(poolAddress, token);

  • Transfer ownership (7-day timelock)

    treasury.requestOwnershipTransfer(newOwner);
// ... wait 7 days
treasury.executeOwnershipTransfer();

Cannot Do:

  • Burn tokens from other addresses
  • Modify vesting schedules post-TGE
  • Access pool governance functions
  • Control bridge operations

2.2. Bridge Owner (DAO Council)

Contract: Bridge.sol at contracts/src/Bridge.sol

Initial Setup: 3-of-5 multisig (core team)

Long-term: 3-of-5 elected DAO council

Powers:

  • Configure bridgeable tokens (2-day timelock)

    // Initial setup (no timelock)
bridge.setTokenConfig(token, limit, decimals, inRatio, unlimited);
 
// Updates (2-day timelock)
bridge.requestConfigChange(token, newLimit, decimals, newRatio, updateLimit, updateRatio);
bridge.executeConfigChange(token);

  • Set cross-chain peers (2-day timelock)

    bridge.requestSetPeer(chainId, peerAddress);
bridge.executeSetPeer(chainId);

  • Pause/unpause tokens (immediate)

    bridge.pauseToken(token, true);   // Emergency pause
bridge.pauseToken(token, false);  // Unpause

  • Set daily bridge limits

    • Outbound: Absolute amount per token
    • Inbound: Percentage of outbound (e.g., 120%)
    • B64-encoded for gas efficiency

  • Migrate to new bridges

    • Deploy new bridge contract
    • Update token mint/burn permissions
    • Transition over grace period

  • Rescue stuck tokens (immediate)

    bridge.rescueTokens(token, recipient, amount);

Cannot Do:

  • Mint tokens directly (only via ERC-7802 callbacks)
  • Bypass rate limits
  • Access pool or treasury functions

2.3. Pool Owner (Curator)

Contract: Any PoolProxy instance

Initial Setup:

  • Core Protocol Pools: 3-of-5 DAO council multisig
  • Permissionless Pools: Deployer's choice (any address)

Long-term:

  • Official Pools: Elected DAO council
  • Permissionless Pools: Pool creator's discretion

Powers:

2.3.1. Asset Management (1-day timelock)

  • Add assets to pool

    pool.requestAddAsset(token, oracleConfig, riskConfig, liquidityProfile, minFeeBps, decimals);
// ... wait 1 day
pool.executeAddAsset(token);

  • Update risk configurations (1-day timelock)

    pool.requestUpdateRiskConfig(token, newRiskConfig);
pool.executeUpdateRiskConfig(token);

    RiskConfig Parameters:

    • flags: FROZEN | SWAP_ENABLED | LIABILITY_SWAP_ENABLED | DECAY_ENABLED | FLASH_ENABLED | FEE_ON_TRANSFER | STAKEABLE | BRIDGEABLE
    • maxDepth: Maximum liquidity profile depth
    • decayStartRatioBps: Liability decay threshold
    • decaySlope: Decay rate parameter
    • maxDailyVolatility: Circuit breaker threshold

  • Update liquidity profiles (depth curve shapes)

    pool.requestUpdateProfile(token, newProfile);
pool.executeUpdateProfile(token);

    LiquidityProfile Structure:

    • knots[17]: Price offset knots (int8, weights.length + 1 points)
    • weights[16]: Liquidity weights per segment (uint8)
    • Total weights must sum to 200
    • Knots must be monotonically increasing
    • max(knots) - min(knots) must equal 100

2.3.2. Oracle Management (2-day timelock)

  • Configure price oracles

    pool.requestOracleUpdate(token, oracleConfig);
pool.executeOracleUpdate(token);

    OracleConfig Parameters:

    • primary: Primary oracle address (or address(this) for internal)
    • secondary: Fallback oracle address
    • feedId: Price feed identifier
    • mode: USE_INTERNAL | USE_EXTERNAL | ALLOW_FALLBACK

  • Update anchor relationships (immediate)

    pool.setAnchor(token, anchorToken);

    Controls pricing topology in anchor tree architecture.

2.3.3. Fee Management (1-day timelock)

  • Update fee parameters
    pool.requestUpdateFeeParams(IPool.FeeParams({
    protoShare: 20,      // % to protocol
    flashFeeBps: 500     // Flash loan fee (0.05%)
}));
pool.executeUpdateFeeParams();

2.3.4. Staking Parameters (2-day timelock)

  • Update staking lock durations

    pool.requestStakingConfigUpdate(
    stakeLockDuration,   // Lock after stake
    transferCooldown     // Lock after transfer
);
pool.executeStakingConfigUpdate();

  • Configure LP staking

    pool.updateStakingConfig(lpToken, salt);

    Deploys deterministic staked LP (sLP) token via CREATE3.

  • Pause/unpause staking (immediate)

    pool.pause();    // Emergency pause
pool.unpause();  // Resume

2.3.5. Distribution Management (2-day timelock)

  • Add reward tokens

    pool.addRewardToken(lpToken, rewardToken);

  • Set emission rates

    pool.updateDistributionRate(lpToken, rewardToken, ratePerSecond);

  • Update claim parameters (2-day timelock)

    pool.requestDistributionParamsUpdate(minClaimPower, matchingRatio);
pool.executeDistributionParamsUpdate();

    Parameters:

    • minClaimPower: Minimum reward multiplier without sBTR (basis points)
    • matchingRatio: sBTR value needed to match LP value for full rewards

2.3.6. Critical Operations (3-7 day timelock)

  • Transfer pool ownership (3-day timelock)

    pool.requestOwnershipTransfer(newOwner);
pool.executeOwnershipTransfer();

  • Update modules (3-day timelock)

    pool.requestModuleUpdate(implAddress, selectors, initData);
pool.executeModuleUpdate();

  • Update bridge address (3-day timelock)

    pool.requestBridgeUpdate(newBridge);
pool.executeBridgeUpdate();

  • Update treasury address (3-day timelock)

    pool.requestTreasuryUpdate(newTreasury);
pool.executeTreasuryUpdate();

  • Migrate base token (7-day timelock)

    pool.requestBaseMigration(newBaseToken);
pool.executeBaseMigration();

2.3.7. Emergency Powers (Immediate)

  • Freeze assets (no timelock)

    pool.freezeAsset(token);   // Disable all operations
pool.unfreezeAsset(token); // Re-enable

  • Pause staking (no timelock)

    pool.pause();    // Disable stake/unstake
pool.unpause();  // Re-enable

Cannot Do:

  • Mint BTR tokens
  • Control bridge operations
  • Access other pools' governance
  • Bypass timelocks (except emergency freezes)

2.4. External Oracle Keeper

Role: Off-chain EOA or multisig

Contracts: ExternalOracle.sol instances

Initial Setup: Keeper EOA (can be upgraded to multisig)

Long-term: Decentralized keeper network or DAO-controlled multisig

Powers:

  • Push price feeds on-chain

    oracle.updatePrice(token, price, volatility, timestamp);

  • Update multiple feeds (batch operation)

    oracle.updatePriceBatch(tokens, prices, volatilities, timestamp);

Responsibilities:

  • Fetch prices from reliable off-chain sources
  • Calculate TWAP/EMA to prevent manipulation
  • Update at regular intervals (e.g., every 5 minutes)
  • Monitor for price anomalies
  • Maintain high uptime

Security Requirements:

  • Use TWAP prices: Not spot prices (flash loan protection)
  • Multi-source aggregation: Combine multiple exchanges
  • Outlier detection: Reject suspicious price movements
  • Transparency: Public monitoring of price updates
  • Decentralization: Multiple keepers with rotation

Critical Importance:

External oracles are mission-critical for pools using them. Stale or manipulated prices can lead to:

  • Incorrect swap rates
  • Arbitrage exploitation
  • Insolvency risk
  • User losses

Recommendation for Permissionless Pools:

  • Prefer internal oracles (Curve-style TWAPs)
  • Use external oracles only if:
    • Highly reputable (Chainlink, Pyth, etc.)
    • Multiple fallbacks configured
    • Circuit breakers enabled
    • You trust the keeper

3. Timelock Overview

All timelocks follow this pattern:

  1. Request: Owner initiates operation

    • Emits TimelockRequested(id, opType, executeAfter)
    • Stores operation data on-chain

  2. Wait: Time passes (1, 2, 3, or 7 days)

    • Users can review pending operations
    • Community can discuss in forum
    • Exit window for concerned users

  3. Execute: Owner executes after timelock expires

    • Must be within grace period
    • Emits operation-specific event
    • Changes take effect

  4. Cancel (optional): Owner cancels before execution

    • Emits TimelockCancelled(id, opType)
    • Clears pending operation

3.1. Timelock Summary Table

Risk Level Delay Operations
Emergency None Freeze asset, pause staking, pause bridge token
Low 1 day Add asset, update risk config, update fees
Medium 2 days Oracle config, staking params, distribution params, bridge config
High 3 days Ownership transfer, module update, bridge/treasury update
Critical 7 days Base token migration, treasury ownership

Grace Periods:

  • Pool operations: 7 days
  • Bridge operations: 3 days
  • Treasury operations: 7 days

4. Multi-Signature Requirements

All governance entities should use multisig wallets:

4.1. Recommended Setup (Launch)

Governance Multisig (Treasury):

  • Threshold: 3-of-5
  • Signers: Core team members
  • Key Storage: Hardware wallets (Ledger, Trezor)
  • Geographic Distribution: Different jurisdictions
  • Backup Plans: Key recovery procedures

DAO Council Multisig (Bridge + Official Pools):

  • Threshold: 3-of-5
  • Signers: Core team initially, elected members later
  • Key Storage: Hardware wallets
  • Geographic Distribution: Different jurisdictions
  • Meeting Cadence: Weekly sync calls

4.2. Long-Term Setup (Post-DAO)

Elected Council:

  • Selection: Token-weighted voting
  • Term: 6-12 months
  • Accountability: On-chain voting records
  • Compensation: Protocol emissions
  • Removal: Governance vote if malicious

5. Emergency Procedures

5.1. Asset Exploitation Detected

  1. Immediate: Freeze affected asset

    pool.freezeAsset(exploitedToken);

  2. Within 1 hour: Assess impact

    • Check reserves vs liabilities
    • Identify affected users
    • Estimate losses

  3. Within 24 hours: Public disclosure

    • Post-mortem to governance forum
    • Explanation of freeze reason
    • Proposed remediation plan

  4. Timelock: Update risk config or remove asset

    pool.requestUpdateRiskConfig(token, saferConfig);
// or
pool.requestRemoveAsset(token);

  5. After resolution: Unfreeze if safe

    pool.unfreezeAsset(token);

5.2. Bridge Exploit Detected

  1. Immediate: Pause affected token

    bridge.pauseToken(token, true);

  2. Coordinate: Contact other chain councils

    • Pause on all chains
    • Investigate root cause

  3. If compromise is severe: Deploy new bridge

    • New contract deployment
    • Update token permissions
    • Migrate liquidity

5.3. Oracle Manipulation Detected

  1. Immediate: Freeze assets using bad oracle

    pool.freezeAsset(affectedToken);

  2. Switch to fallback: If available

    pool.requestOracleUpdate(token, fallbackConfig);

  3. Investigate: Oracle keeper

    • Check keeper signing keys
    • Review recent price updates
    • Identify manipulation method

  4. Long-term: Replace keeper or switch to internal oracle

6. Governance Process (Future DAO)

6.1. Proposal Lifecycle

  1. Discussion: Forum post with detailed proposal
  2. Temperature Check: Informal poll (3 days)
  3. Formal Proposal: On-chain proposal (5 days voting)
  4. Timelock: Required delay based on risk level
  5. Execution: Anyone can execute after timelock
  6. Monitoring: Watch for issues post-execution

6.2. Voting Power

  • BTR holders: 1 token = 1 vote
  • sBTR holders: 1 token = 1 vote (same as unstaked)
  • LP stakers: Proportional to LP value + sBTR boost

6.3. Quorum Requirements (Proposed)

  • Low Risk: 5% of circulating supply
  • Medium Risk: 10% of circulating supply
  • High Risk: 20% of circulating supply
  • Critical: 30% of circulating supply

6.4. Delegation

Users can delegate voting power:

  • Retains tokens
  • Delegates voting decisions
  • Can revoke anytime
  • No lock-up required

7. Access Control Architecture

7.1. Role Hierarchy

Treasury Owner (Governance Multisig)
├── Mint BTR tokens
├── Initialize TGE
├── Collect protocol fees
└── Transfer ownership (7-day timelock)
 
Bridge Owner (DAO Council)
├── Configure token bridging (2-day timelock)
├── Set cross-chain peers (2-day timelock)
├── Pause tokens (immediate)
└── Rescue tokens (immediate)
 
Pool Owner (Curator)
├── Asset Management
│   ├── Add assets (1-day timelock)
│   ├── Update risk configs (1-day timelock)
│   └── Freeze assets (immediate)
├── Oracle Management (2-day timelock)
├── Fee Management (1-day timelock)
├── Staking Management (2-day timelock)
├── Distribution Management (2-day timelock)
├── Critical Operations (3-7 day timelock)
│   ├── Module upgrades (3-day)
│   ├── Ownership transfer (3-day)
│   └── Base token migration (7-day)
└── Emergency Powers (immediate)
 
External Oracle Keeper
├── Update price feeds
└── Monitor oracle health

7.2. Permission Verification

All privileged functions use the onlyOwner modifier:

modifier onlyOwner() {
    if (msg.sender != $.owner) revert OnlyOwner();
    _;
}

Treasury uses Solady's Ownable pattern for consistency.

8. Monitoring & Transparency

8.1. On-Chain Events

All governance actions emit events for transparency:

// Timelock operations
event TimelockRequested(bytes32 indexed id, uint8 opType, uint48 executeAfter);
event TimelockCancelled(bytes32 indexed id, uint8 opType);
 
// Asset management
event AssetAdded(address indexed token, uint8 decimals, uint128 minLiquidity);
event RiskConfigUpdated(address indexed token, uint16 flags, uint128 maxVolume);
event EmergencyFreeze(address indexed token);
 
// Module updates
event ModulesUpdated(address indexed impl, bytes4[] selectors);
 
// Ownership changes
event OwnershipTransferred(address indexed oldOwner, address indexed newOwner);

8.2. Recommended Monitoring

For Users:

  • Subscribe to TimelockRequested events
  • Review pending operations via governance dashboard
  • Exit positions if suspicious changes proposed

For Council Members:

  • Monitor oracle price updates
  • Track daily bridge volumes
  • Review protocol fee accumulation
  • Watch for emergency freezes

For Developers:

  • Track module upgrades
  • Monitor storage layout changes
  • Test against staging deployments

9. Best Practices

9.1. For Governance Multisig Signers

  1. Use hardware wallets: Never sign from hot wallets
  2. Verify transactions: Double-check addresses and amounts
  3. Communicate clearly: Discuss proposals before signing
  4. Document decisions: Keep records of reasoning
  5. Rotate keys: Periodically update signer set

9.2. For Pool Operators

  1. Announce changes: Post to forum before timelock
  2. Explain rationale: Why is change needed?
  3. Test on testnet: Verify expected behavior
  4. Monitor post-change: Watch for unexpected effects
  5. Have rollback plan: Be ready to revert if needed

9.3. For Oracle Keepers

  1. Use TWAP prices: Never push spot prices
  2. Multi-source data: Aggregate multiple exchanges
  3. Outlier detection: Reject suspicious prices
  4. High uptime: Keep feed fresh (<5 min delay)
  5. Transparency: Public monitoring dashboards

10. Future Enhancements

  • On-chain governance: Direct voting without multisig
  • Delegation system: Vote with community representation
  • Timelocked governance: Automatic execution after vote
  • Emergency council: 5-of-7 multisig for critical issues
  • Slashing: Penalize malicious council members
  • Term limits: Prevent power concentration
  • Compensation: Pay council from protocol fees

1-overview.title: Overview
1-overview.html:
AIMM System Architecture

Technical overview of the Adaptive Inventory Market Maker protocol

1. Overview

AIMM is a multi-asset AMM designed for passive liquidity providers. Core components:

  • Single-sided deposits — LPs deposit one token, receive fungible LP tokens
  • N-asset pooling — Anchor tree topology enables any-to-any routing
  • Inventory-based pricing — Avellaneda-Stoikov inspired mid-price adjustment
  • Coverage-aware ALM — Reserves/liabilities separation (Wombat-style)
  • Catmull-Rom spline profiles — Algo-optimized, depth curves supporting non-uniform and multimodal distributions
  • Internal TWAP oracle — Multi-timeframe (eg. 5min/1hr) with support for external fallback
  • Diamond-lite proxy — Modular module upgrades via ERC-7201 namespaced storage

2. Contract Architecture

2.1. Diamond-Lite Proxy (PoolProxyV1)

All pool interactions route through a single proxy that dispatches to implementation modules via delegatecall:

Storage Isolation: Each module uses ERC-7201 namespaced storage to prevent collisions.

2.2. Core Modules

Module Purpose Key Functions
CoreV1 Main AMM operations swap, deposit, withdraw, liabilitySwap, donate
InternalOracleV1 TWAP tracking Auto-updated on swaps, dual-window EMAs
AdminV1 Configuration Asset management, fee params, timelocks
FlashV1 Flash loans ERC-3156 compliant
StakingV1 Governance staking LP + gov token staking, voting power
DistributorV1 Rewards Accumulator-based distribution
RescueV1 Emergency Token rescue, admin recovery

3. Core Data Structures

Per-asset state includes reserves, liabilities, pricing parameters, and sensitivity coefficients. See IPoolV1.sol for struct definitions.

Key per-asset fields:

  • Reserves & liabilities for coverage tracking
  • Anchor pointer for tree routing
  • Sensitivity params: gamma, vega, lambda
  • Fee bounds: minFeeBps, maxFeeBps

See: Parametrization for full field reference.

4. Pricing System

4.1. Pipeline

4.2. Key Concepts

  • Coverage Ratio: c = R / L — measures asset health
  • Inventory Skew: Linear Avellaneda-Stoikov adjustment (±100 range)
  • Spread: Volatility-based fee with toxic flow surcharge
  • Spline Traversal: Price impact via liquidity profile integration

See:

  • Inventory Management — Coverage, skew, haircuts
  • Spread & Fees — Fee calculation
  • Liquidity Shaping — Spline profiles

5. Anchor Tree Routing

All tokens connect through an anchor tree with a hub token (typically stablecoin) as root.

5.1. Topology

5.2. Swap Routing (LCA Algorithm)

Swaps path through the Least Common Ancestor:

Route: [LINK, ETH, BASE, BTC] Hops: [LINK→ETH, ETH→BASE, BASE→BTC]

Constraints:

  • Max depth: 4
  • Max path length: 6 hops (2 × MAX_DEPTH)
  • No cycles allowed

See: Anchor Path Pricing

6. Oracle System

6.1. Internal Oracle

Auto-updated on every swap with:

  • Dual TWAP windows: Fast (5min) + Slow (1hr)
  • Dual volatility EMAs: Responsive + Stable
  • B64 encoding: Compact 64-bit price storage

See: Internal Oracle for full details.

6.2. Gas Optimization

Oracle reads are cached in transient storage (EIP-1153):

  • First read: ~2,100 gas (external call)
  • Subsequent reads: ~100 gas (transient load)

7. Coverage-Aware ALM

Asset-Liability Management (ALM) tracks reserves vs LP claims per asset:

  • Coverage Ratio: c = R / L (100% = equilibrium)
  • Undercollateralized (c < 100%): Withdrawal haircuts apply
  • Overcollateralized (c > 100%): Surplus available

Safety Mechanisms:

  • Withdrawal haircuts protect remaining LPs when c < 100%
  • Liability decay gradually restores coverage in emergencies

See: Inventory Management for formulas and details.

8. Liquidity Profiles

Catmull-Rom spline profiles define liquidity distribution across the depth curve:

  • 1-16 weight segments with monotone cubic interpolation
  • Exact analytical integration for price impact calculation
  • Customizable shapes: Concentrated, uniform, multimodal

See: Liquidity Shaping for profile design and examples.

9. Storage Layout (ERC-7201)

9.1. Namespaced Slots

Module Location Purpose
Core CORE_STORAGE_LOC Assets, balances, config
Oracle ORACLE_STORAGE_LOC Feed accumulators
Staking STAKING_STORAGE_LOC Stakes, voting power
Distributor DISTRIBUTOR_STORAGE_LOC Campaigns, rewards

9.2. Transient Storage (EIP-1153)

Used for:

  • Reentrancy guards
  • Oracle price caching (~2,100 gas/hit saved)
  • Flash loan state

10. Governance & Timelocks

10.1. Operation Types

OpType Delay Risk Level
TRANSFER_OWNERSHIP 3 days HIGH
UPDATE_MODULE 2 days BASE
MIGRATE_BASE_TOKEN 7 days CRITICAL
UPDATE_ORACLE 2 days BASE
ADD_ASSET 1 day LOW
UPDATE_FEES 1 day LOW

10.2. Two-Phase Execution

  1. requestOperation(data) → stores pending
  2. Wait for delay
  3. executeOperation() → applies within grace period

11. Key Invariants

11.1. Coverage Bounds

c in [0, oo)

  • c = 1.0 → equilibrium
  • c < 1.0 → undercollateralized (haircuts apply)
  • c > 1.0 → overcollateralized

11.2. Skew Bounds

−100≤skew≤+100

11.3. Fee Bounds

"minFeeBps" <= "totalFee" <= "maxFeeBps"

Where fees use 0.0001% precision (BPS_PRECISION = 1,000,000).

11.4. Anchor Tree

maxDepth ≤ 4
maxPathLength ≤ 6
noCycles = true

12. Gas Optimizations

Optimization Savings
Single-slot FeedData packing ~2,100 gas/read
B64 encoding 75% storage reduction
Transient oracle caching ~2,100 gas/hit
Packed timelocks 66% slot reduction
LCA without path caching Storage-free routing
Bitmask hooks 32 bits vs N mappings

13. Error Handling

Minimal consolidated error set:

Error Usage
ZeroValue() Zero address/amount/price
InsufficientAmount(available, required) Balance checks
ExcessiveAmount(amount, limit) Limit exceeded
InvalidState() Not initialized/paused
FeatureDisabled(resource) Swap/flash disabled
NotConfigured(resource, target) Missing config
ThresholdViolation(value, threshold) Slippage/coverage
StaleData(age, maxAge) Oracle staleness
ReentrancyDetected() Guard triggered

See: contracts/src/interfaces/IErrors.sol

14. Contract Deployment

14.1. Immutable Components

  • Library contracts (LibPricing, LibOracle, LibSpline, LibMaths)
  • Factory contracts

14.2. Upgradeable via Proxy

  • PoolProxyV1 (dispatcher)
  • All modules (CoreV1, AdminV1, etc.)

14.3. Upgradeable via UUPS

  • TreasuryV1
  • BridgeV1

15. Related Documentation

  • Inventory Management — Pricing mechanics
  • Core Module — Module documentation
  • Parametrization — Parameter reference

1.1.1-inventory-management.title: 1.1.1. Inventory Management
1.1.1-inventory-management.html:
Inventory Management

Inventory-aware market making using Asset-Liability Management (ALM) and the Avellaneda-Stoikov framework

1. Overview

AIMM uses Asset-Liability Management (ALM) inspired by Wombat Exchange and Platypus Finance:

  • Reserves R: Actual tokens held by the pool (assets)
  • Liabilities L: LP claims against the pool (what we owe depositors)
  • Coverage Ratio c: R/L

This decouples pricing from reserves, enabling inventory-aware market making.

1.1. Beyond Pool-Wise Invariants

Traditional AMMs (Uniswap, Curve) enforce strict pool-wise invariants (e.g., x * y = k) that don't scale well to N-asset scenarios without specialized coordinates (like polar coordinates in Balancer). AIMM replaces this with:

  • Per-asset tracking: Each asset maintains independent reserves and liabilities
  • Feedback control: Inventory skew acts as a dynamic rebalancing signal (Avellaneda-Stoikov framework)
  • Scalability: Naturally handles any number of assets without invariant constraints

2. Coverage Ratio

2.1. Definition

c= RL

where:

  • c = coverage ratio
  • R = reserves (actual tokens held)
  • L = liabilities (LP claims)
  • c = 1 (WAD scale) means 100% coverage
  • c < 1 means undercollateralized
  • c > 1 means overcollateralized

2.2. Key Thresholds

Coverage State Behavior
200%+ Overcollateralized Max discount (skew = -100), incentivize selling
100% Equilibrium Zero skew, normal pricing
50% Critical floor Max premium (skew = +100), withdrawal haircuts apply
< 50% Emergency Decay mechanism may activate

See: LibPricing.calculateCoverage()

3. Inventory Skew

3.1. Avellaneda-Stoikov Framework

AIMM computes inventory skew using linear interpolation between critical bounds:

pi = |c - c_t| / |c_b - c_t|
 
psi = "sign"(c_t - c) times gamma times 100 times pi
WHERE
π=text(progress toward boundary
in [0, 1])
c=text(current coverage ratio)
ct=text(target coverage) = 1.0 text( (100%))
cb=text(critical boundary) = 0.5 text( or ) 2.0
γ=text(sensitivity multiplier
basis 10000)
ψ=text(inventory skew
in [-100, +100])
sign(...)=+1 text( if ) c < c_t text(
else ) -1

3.2. Skew Curve Properties

Coverage Progress Skew (γ=1.0) Interpretation
50%- 1.0 +100 Max premium (pool heavily buying)
75% 0.5 +50 Moderate premium
100% 0.0 0 Equilibrium (fair mid-price)
150% 0.5 -50 Moderate discount
200%+ 1.0 -100 Max discount (pool heavily selling)

3.3. Gamma Parameter

Gamma is a multiplier (not exponent) controlling skew sensitivity:

Gamma Value Multiplier Effect Use Case
5000 0.5x Half skew Volatile assets, softer response
10000 1.0x Full skew Default, balanced
15000 1.5x 150% skew More aggressive rebalancing
20000 2.0x Double skew Stable assets, strong incentives

Higher gamma = steeper linear slope = stronger price incentive for rebalancing.

3.4. Design Rationale

Linear skew matches the Avellaneda-Stoikov inventory adjustment:

delta = gamma times q times sigma^2

Linear in inventory position (q), scaled by risk aversion (γ).

See: LibPricing.computeInventorySkew()

4. Effective Depth

4.1. Concept
