Effective depth D determines how much volume the pool can absorb at the current coverage level. It's used in price impact calculations via spline traversal.

4.2. Formula

When undercollateralized (c<1):

D=R+k times(L−R) timesπe

where:

  • D = effective depth
  • R = reserves
  • L = liabilities
  • k = normalized depth amplifier (raw value / 10^6)
  • π = (c - c_f) / (1 - c_f) (progress from floor to target)
  • c = coverage ratio
  • c_f = critical floor (e.g., 0.5)
  • e = 1 / (1 + 2k) (exponent, concave curve)

4.3. Properties

  • At critical floor (c=cf): D=R (no virtual depth)
  • Concave monotonically increasing from critical to target
  • At equilibrium (c≥1): D=R (full depth = reserves)

4.4. Depth Amplifier

The depth amplifier k controls virtual depth addition:

Value k Effect
0 0 No amplification (D=R always)
500000 0.5 50% max virtual addition
1000000 1.0 100% max virtual addition

Higher amplification = tighter spreads at low coverage, but increased risk if coverage continues dropping.

5. Withdrawal Haircut

5.1. Purpose

When c<1, withdrawals take a haircut to prevent bank runs and protect remaining LPs.

5.2. Power-Law Formula

h(c)=(1−c)p

where:

  • h = haircut ratio
  • c = coverage ratio
  • p = 1 + η / M (haircut exponent)
  • η = suppressor parameter
  • M = MULT_BASE (10000)

5.3. Properties

  • h(0)=1 (100% haircut—no reserves → no withdrawal)
  • h(1)=0 (0% haircut—fully covered → full withdrawal)
  • η controls curve convexity (higher = gentler)

5.4. Suppressor Parameter

η Exponent p Curve Shape
0 1 Linear (harsh)
10000 2 Quadratic (moderate)
30000 4 Convex (gentle mid-range)
40000 5 Very gentle

5.5. Examples

At 80% coverage with p=2:

h=(1−0.8)2=0.04=4%

At 50% coverage with p=2:

h=(1−0.5)2=0.25=25%

See: LibPricing.applyWithdrawalHaircut()

6. Liability Decay

6.1. Purpose

Emergency mechanism to restore coverage when undercollateralized for extended periods. Decays LP claims at a controlled rate.

6.2. Activation

Decay activates when c<cd where cd = decay start ratio (e.g., decayStartRatioBps = 980000 means cd=0.98).

6.3. Formula

ΔL=L timesρ times(ΔtW)

where:

  • ΔL = liability decay amount
  • L = current liabilities
  • ρ = decay slope
  • Δt = time elapsed
  • W = WAD (10^18)

6.4. Constraints

  • Never decays below reserves: Caps at $L - R$
  • Stopped at equilibrium: Decay halts when c≥1

6.5. Parameters

Parameter Unit Example
decayStartRatioBps 0.0001% 980000 (98%)
decaySlope WAD/second 3.17e10 (1%/year)

See: LibPricing.calculateDecay()

7. Net Coverage Impact

7.1. Purpose

Determines if a swap improves or worsens pool balance. Used to apply directional fee asymmetry.

7.2. Formula

ΔI=I1−I0

where:

  • ΔI = net coverage impact
  • I = ∑_j p_j × |R_j - L_j| (sum of imbalances across assets)
  • p_j = price of asset j
  • R_j, L_j = reserves and liabilities of asset j
  • Subscripts 0, 1 = before and after trade

7.3. Interpretation

ΔI Meaning Fee Treatment
<0 Improves coverage Lower spread (arbitrage-friendly)
>0 Worsens coverage Higher spread (toxic flow penalty)
=0 Neutral Base spread only

See: LibPricing.netCoverageImpact()

8. Coverage Classification

8.1. Single Asset

Coverage State
c > 200% OVER
200% >= c > 100% ADEQUATE
100% >= c > 50% UNDER
c <= 50% CRITICAL

8.2. Pool Level

Aggregate coverage across all assets:

C=  ∑jRj timespj ∑jLj timespj

where:

  • C = pool-level coverage ratio
  • R_j = reserves of asset j
  • L_j = liabilities of asset j
  • p_j = price of asset j

9. ALM Flow: Deposit

  1. User deposits token A
  2. RA←RA+x (add to reserves)
  3. LA←LA+x (1:1 LP minting)
  4. Coverage remains unchanged
  5. User receives LP tokens

9.1. Single-Sided Deposits

ALM enables single-sided deposits — no forced pairing required. Each token's coverage ratio tracks independently.

10. ALM Flow: Withdrawal

  1. User requests withdrawal of x LP tokens
  2. Calculate c=RL
  3. If c<1:
    • Calculate h=(1−c)p
    • y=x⋅(1−h) (apply haircut)
  4. $R larr R - y$
  5. $L larr L - x$ (full LP burn)
  6. User receives y tokens

10.1. Cross-Asset Withdrawal

User can withdraw into a different asset:

  1. Burn LP tokens for token A
  2. Swap internal value to token B
  3. Apply haircut on token B
  4. User receives token B

11. ALM Flow: Swap

  1. User swaps x of token A for token B
  2. Calculate ψA=f(cA,γ)
  3. Calculate ψB=f(cB,γ)
  4. Price via spline traversal with skew offsets
  5. RA←RA+x
  6. RB←RB−y
  7. Liabilities unchanged (no LP mint/burn)
  8. Coverage shifts: cA↑, cB↓

12. Parameter Summary

12.1. Per-Asset RiskConfig

Field Type Unit Purpose
coverageFloor uint16 0.0001% Critical coverage threshold (e.g., 500000 = 50%)
decayStartRatioBps uint16 0.0001% Decay activation threshold
decaySlope uint32 WAD/second Decay rate
depthAmplifier uint16 raw (scaled by 10^6) Virtual depth at low coverage

12.2. Per-Asset Sensitivity

Field Type Unit Purpose
gamma uint16 basis 10000 Inventory skew multiplier (10000 = 1.0x)
haircutSuppressor uint16 basis 10000 Withdrawal haircut gentleness

13. Comparison: Traditional AMM vs AIMM ALM

Aspect Traditional AMM AIMM ALM
Price source Reserves ratio Oracle + inventory skew
LP tracking Shares of pool Specific asset liabilities
Deposit Both tokens required Single-sided
Withdrawal Pro-rata pool share Specific asset with haircut
Rebalancing Arbitrageurs only Inventory skew incentives
Under-collateral Implicit (IL) Explicit (c < 100%)

14. Security Considerations

14.1. Bank Run Protection

  1. Haircut curve penalizes late withdrawers progressively
  2. Min liquidity prevents complete drainage
  3. Decay mechanism gradually restores coverage

14.2. Manipulation Resistance

  1. TWAP-based pricing resists flash loan attacks
  2. Skew bounds (±100) cap maximum impact
  3. Coverage floor provides hard safety boundary

14.3. Circuit Breakers

  • FROZEN_BIT flag halts all operations
  • Critical coverage triggers max premium
  • Min liquidity requirement per asset

15. Related Documentation

  • Liquidity Shaping — Spline-based depth curves
  • Spread & Fees — Fee calculation using coverage
  • Internal Oracle — Price feeds for coverage valuation
  • Parametrization — Full parameter reference

1.1.3-anchor-path-pricing.title: 1.1.3. Anchor Path Pricing
1.1.3-anchor-path-pricing.html:
Anchor Path Pricing

Assets priced through anchor paths (lowest common ancestor routing) while accounted in base denomination (O(N) complexity, natural asset relationships)

Problem: Hub-and-Spoke Limitations

Issue 1: Volatility Misrepresentation

  • Trading correlated assets (wstETH→WETH) used √(σ_WETH/USDC × σ_wstETH/USDC) ≈ 49%
  • Actual correlation only ~2% volatility

Issue 2: Liquidity Profile Mismatch

  • Assets priced against USDC even when naturally trading against other assets
  • wstETH liquidity should concentrate against WETH, not USDC

Core Innovation: Tree-Based Routing

Assets form a tree where:

  • Root: Base token (USDC, no anchor)
  • Each asset: Has one anchor (parent node) defining pricing relationship
  • Swaps route: Through anchor paths via lowest common ancestor (LCA)

Result: O(N) complexity + economically accurate pricing

Graph Topology

Constraints:

  • Maximum depth: 4 (root at 0, leaves at ≤4)
  • Single root guarantees acyclicity
  • Each asset: exactly one anchor
  • Every asset: path to root

Anchor Path Examples

Route Path LCA Hops
USDT→DAI USDT → USDC → DAI USDC 2
wstETH→WETH wstETH → WETH WETH 1
wstETH→rETH wstETH → WETH → rETH WETH 2
USDT→wstETH USDT → USDC → WETH → wstETH USDC 3

Max path: 2×depth = 8 hops for depth-4 tree (capped at 6)

Hop Semantics

Each hop has distinct behavior based on position in anchor path:

Hop Type Reserves Pricing Oracle Purpose
Edge (1st/last) ✓ Change Full impact Required Consume liquidity
Intermediate (middle) ✗ Fixed Mid-price only Price only Numeraire transform

Example (USDT→wstETH via USDC→WETH):

  1. USDT→USDC (edge): Price impact on both, reserve changes
  2. USDC→WETH (intermediate): Mid-price only, no reserve change
  3. WETH→wstETH (edge): Price impact on both, reserve changes

Risk Aggregation

Per-Hop Signals

Volatility (blend recent + baseline):

σ_i = (σ_fast,i + σ_slow,i) / 2

Deviation (multi-timeframe disagreement):

d_fs = |fastOffset - slowOffset|
d_fc = |fastOffset|
Δ_i = max(d_fs, d_fc)

Path-Level Risk

Conservative max across all hops:

σ_pair = max_i(σ_i)
Δ_pair = max_i(Δ_i)

Rationale: Path risk dominated by noisiest hop. If WETH (intermediate node) moves 10% during swap, trader bears that risk.

Spread Calculation

Only endpoint parameters (where reserves change):

vega_spread   = max(vega_in, vega_out)
lambda_spread = max(lambda_in, lambda_out)

Volatility band (symmetric):

S_vol = 100 + (σ_pair × vega_spread) / (100 × 10,000)

Deviation surcharge (toxic side only):

U = (Δ_pair × lambda_spread) / 10,000

Final spread:

spreadBps = improvesCoverage ? S_vol : S_vol + U

Creates asymmetric spreads: coverage-improving trades pay volatility band (arb-friendly), coverage-worsening trades pay extra (toxic penalty).

See spread.md for full model.

Key Advantages

Aspect Hub-and-Spoke Anchor Tree Benefit
Correlated pair spreads √(50% × 48%) ≈ 49% 2% (actual) Accurate pricing
Oracles N N O(N) scaling
Governance O(N) O(N) Simple management
LP concentration Suboptimal Natural Market-aligned

Multiple peg support: USD stablecoins (USDC anchor), ETH LSTs (WETH anchor), BTC wraps (WBTC anchor)

Trade-offs

Downside Mitigation
Routing complexity LCA caching, precomputed paths
Higher gas (long paths) Direct anchors preferred, depth limit
Anchor concentration risk Circuit breakers, monitoring
Configuration complexity Clear governance, phased rollout

Implementation Notes

Oracle Requirements

Each non-root asset needs oracle in terms of its anchor:

  • wstETH/WETH oracle
  • USDT/USDC oracle
  • WETH/USDC oracle

Internal TWAP oracles preferred (no external dependencies).

State Updates

Only edge assets change balances:

  • Input asset reserves: +volume
  • Output asset reserves: -volume
  • Intermediate anchors: unchanged

Migration Path

  1. Phase 1: All assets→USDC (hub-and-spoke, backward compatible)
  2. Phase 2: Stablecoins→USDC anchor
  3. Phase 3: LSTs→WETH anchor
  4. Phase 4: Wrapped assets→native anchors

Security

  • Oracle resistance: Leaf manipulation affects only that asset; anchor manipulation affects subtree
  • Arbitrage: Direct wstETH/WETH arbitrage without USDC friction
  • Capital efficiency: LPs concentrate where naturally deep (stablecoins near parity, LSTs near staking ratio)

Summary

Tree-based routing elegantly balances O(N) complexity with accurate market pricing:

  • ✓ Correct spreads for correlated assets
  • ✓ Multiple simultaneous peg groups
  • ✓ Natural liquidity concentration
  • ✓ Unified risk management in base denomination

Trade-offs manageable with caching, monitoring, and phased deployment.

1.1.2-liquidity-shaping.title: 1.1.2. Liquidity Shaping
1.1.2-liquidity-shaping.html:
Liquidity Shaping

Catmull-Rom spline-based liquidity profiles for customizable price impact curves

1. Overview

Traditional AMMs use fixed mathematical invariants (x * y = k, StableSwap) that determine price impact. AIMM uses Catmull-Rom spline interpolation with user-defined control points, allowing precise control over depth at any price point.

Key Benefits:

  • Concentrate liquidity around expected price ranges
  • Create asymmetric depth for directional markets
  • Match depth curves to asset volatility characteristics
  • Update profiles without redeploying contracts

2. Profile Structure

2.1. Storage Layout

struct LiquidityProfile {
    uint8[16] weights;      // Segment weights (0.5% resolution)
    int8[17] knots;         // Price offset knots (weights.length + 1 points)
}

Knot Semantics: Knots represent price offsets as percentage of dispersion range around TWAP:

  • Dispersion defines the liquidity breadth around TWAP (e.g., 1% = 10000 bps means ±1% range)
  • Knots are offsets within this range as percentage of dispersion
  • Formula: price = TWAP × (1 + dispersion × knot / 100 / BPS_PRECISION)
  • Example: TWAP = $1.00, dispersion = 1% (10000 bps), knot = -50:
    • Offset = -50% of 1% dispersion = -0.5% from TWAP
    • Calculation = -50 × 10000 / 100 = -5000 bps = -0.5%
    • Price = 1.00×(1−0.005)=0.995
  • Range: knots span from -100 to +100 (full dispersion range coverage)
  • Constraint: max(knots) - min(knots) = 100 ensures complete dispersion range

2.2. Constraints

Property Requirement
Segments 1-16 active (first zero weight marks end)
Weight sum Must equal 200 (represents 100% depth)
Knots Must be monotonically non-decreasing (N weights → N+1 knots)
Knot range max(knots) - min(knots) = 100 (100% of dispersion coverage)
Weight resolution 0.5% per weight unit (1 unit = 0.5% of domain)
Knot resolution 1% per knot unit (1 unit = 1% of dispersion)

2.3. Domain Mapping

Profile weights define control points on a cumulative depth axis:

x= wc times10000200

where:

  • x = control point position (depth axis)
  • w_c = cumulative weight
  • Maps weight domain [0, 200] to [0, 10000] (0% to 100% of depth)

2.4. Example: Concentrated Stablecoin Profile

Segment   Weight   Cumulative   X-position   End Offset
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
0         80       80           4000         0
1         60       140          7000         +5
2         30       170          8500         +20
3         20       190          9500         +50
4         10       200          10000        +100
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Total     200

Interpretation: 40% of liquidity depth available at ≤0 offset, 70% within +5 offset.

3. Catmull-Rom Spline Mathematics

3.1. Why Catmull-Rom?

AIMM uses Catmull-Rom splines (a variant of monotone cubic Hermite interpolation) for efficiency:

  1. C¹ continuity: Smooth price curve without discontinuities
  2. Local control: Each segment depends only on adjacent points
  3. Gas efficient: Simple tangent calculation vs full cubic solve
  4. Monotonic: Guaranteed non-decreasing price with depth

3.2. Knot Point Construction

From profile storage, we build spline control points:

points[0] = (x: 0,     y: -dispersion)        // Start: max discount
points[i] = (x: x_i,   y: offset_i × disp/100)  // User-defined
points[n] = (x: 10000, y: +dispersion)        // End: max premium

Where disp = dispersion parameter (in 0.0001% units).

3.3. Tangent Calculation

At interior knot i, the tangent is the average of adjacent secants:

mi= si−1+si2
si= yi+1−yixi+1−xi

where:

  • m_i = tangent at knot i
  • s_i = secant slope between knots
  • y, x = price offset and depth position coordinates

If adjacent secants have opposite signs, m_i = 0 (preserves monotonicity).

3.4. Cubic Hermite Interpolation

For $t in [0, 1]$ within segment [pi,p(i+1)]:

y(t)=(2t3−3t2+1)yi+(t3−2t2+t)mih+(−2t3+3t2)yi+1+(t3−t2)mi+1h

where:

  • t = parameter in [0, 1] within segment [p_i, p_{i+1}]
  • h = x_{i+1} - x_i (segment width)
  • m_i, m_{i+1} = tangents at endpoints
  • y_i, y_{i+1} = values at endpoints

3.5. Implementation

function eval(uint256 x, Point[] memory pts) internal pure returns (int256)

See: contracts/src/libraries/LibSpline.sol:15-49

4. Spline Integration (Area)

4.1. Purpose

For VWAP (volume-weighted average price) calculations, we need the integral of the price curve over a traversed range.

4.2. Exact Analytical Integration

The integral of a cubic Hermite polynomial has closed form:

 ∫01y(t) ,dt= yi+yi+12+ (mi−mi+1)h12

where:

  • h = segment width (x_{i+1} - x_i)
  • m_i, m_{i+1} = tangents at endpoints
  • y_i, y_{i+1} = values at endpoints

For arbitrary bounds [a, b], we sum contributions across segments.

4.3. Average Execution Price

Given traversal from x0 to x1:

 p¯=pT times left(1+ A(x0,x1)(x1−x0) timesB right)

where:

  •  p¯ = average execution price
  • p_T = TWAP (oracle price)
  • A = integrated area over depth range [x_0, x_1]
  • B = BPS_PRECISION (1,000,000)

4.4. Implementation

function area(Point[] memory pts, uint256 x1, uint256 x2)
    internal pure returns (int256 res)

See: contracts/src/libraries/LibSpline.sol:51-132

5. Inventory Skew Mapping (Skew → Depth)

For how skew is computed from coverage ratio, see Inventory Management §3.

5.1. Skew to Depth Position

Once computed, inventory skew ψ∈[−100,+100] maps to cumulative depth $d in [0, 10000]$:

d=5000+ψ times50

where:

  • d = cumulative depth position (∈ [0, 10000])
  • ψ = inventory skew (∈ [-100, +100])
ψ d Meaning
-100 0 Maximum discount (full sell pressure)
0 5000 Mid-price (equilibrium)
+100 10000 Maximum premium (full buy pressure)

See: LibPricing._skewToDepth()

6. Dispersion Dynamics

6.1. Purpose

Dispersion kappa scales the profile's price range based on volatility. Higher dispersion = wider price curve = steeper impact.

6.2. Formula

κ= clamp left(κ0+ σ timesν1000 timesM,κ min,κ max right)

where:

  • κ = dispersion (basis points, clamped)
  • κ₀ = base dispersion (1000 = 0.1%)
  • σ = volatility (VOL_BASE = 10^6, so 1% = 1,000,000)
  • ν = vega sensitivity (basis M = 10000)
  • κ_min, κ_max = dispersion bounds (0.0001% units)

6.3. Parameters

Parameter Type Unit Purpose
vega uint16 basis 10000 Volatility sensitivity
minDispersion uint32 0.0001% Floor (prevents free options)
maxDispersion uint32 0.0001% Ceiling (prevents illiquidity)

6.4. Volatility Effect

σ (1e6) $nu$ Δκ
1,000,000 (1%) 10000 +100
5,000,000 (5%) 10000 +500
1,000,000 (1%) 20000 +200

6.5. Implementation

function _calculateDispersion(
    uint32 volatility,
    uint16 vega,
    uint32 minDispersion,
    uint32 maxDispersion
) internal pure returns (uint32 dispersion)

See: contracts/src/libraries/LibPricing.sol:254-271

7. Depth Calculation

7.1. Effective Depth

When undercollateralized, virtual depth is added based on coverage:

D=R+k times(L−R) timesπe

where:

  • D = effective depth
  • R = reserves
  • L = liabilities
  • k = normalized depth amplifier (raw / 10^6)
  • π = (c - c_f) / (1 - c_f) (progress from floor to target)
  • c = coverage ratio
  • c_f = critical floor
  • e = 1 / (1 + 2k) (exponent, concave curve)

7.2. Properties

Coverage Effective Depth
c≥1 D=R (full reserves)
c=cf D=R (no virtual depth)
Between Interpolated (concave curve)

7.3. Implementation

function calculateDepth(
    uint128 reserves,
    uint128 liabilities,
    uint16 depthAmplifier
) internal pure returns (uint256 depth)

See: contracts/src/libraries/LibPricing.sol:951-1020

8. Profile Design Patterns

8.1. Concentrated (Stablecoins)

Maximize depth near peg, wide wings for black swan events:

weights:  [80, 60, 30, 20, 10, 0, ...]
offsets:  [0,  5,  20, 50, 100, ...]

Use case: USDC/USDT pools where 99% of trades occur within 10 bps.

8.2. Uniform (Volatile Assets)

Even distribution across price range:

weights:  [25, 25, 25, 25, 25, 25, 25, 25, 0, ...]
offsets:  [0,  25, 50, 75, 100, 125, 150, 200, ...]

Use case: ETH/BTC pairs with unpredictable price movements.

8.3. Asymmetric (Directional)

More depth on expected direction:

weights:  [30, 40, 50, 40, 30, 10, 0, ...]
offsets:  [-20, 0, 20, 60, 120, 200, ...]

Use case: Pools expecting persistent buy/sell pressure.

8.4. Deep Core (Institutional)

Very high concentration for large trades:

weights:  [120, 40, 20, 10, 10, 0, ...]
offsets:  [0,   2,  5,  10, 20, ...]

Use case: Institutional stablecoin pools with tight spread requirements.

9. Traversal Flow

9.1. Complete Pricing Pipeline

1. Load oracle data → get TWAP, σ
2. Compute dispersion: κ = f(σ, vega, min, max)
3. Compute inventory skew: s = f(coverage, gamma)
4. Compute effective depth: D = f(reserves, liabilities, amplifier)
5. Map skew to start position: x₀ = 5000 + s × 50
6. Compute volume fraction: Δx = amountIn × 10000 / D
7. Compute end position: x₁ = x₀ ± Δx (buy/sell)
8. Build spline points from profile + dispersion
9. Integrate: Area(x₀, x₁)
10. Average price: TWAP × (1 + Area / Δx / BPS_PRECISION)

9.2. Implementation

function _traverseSplineByVolume(
    uint256 twap,
    uint32 dispersion,
    IPoolV1.LiquidityProfile storage profile,
    int8 inventorySkew,
    uint256 amountIn,
    uint256 depth,
    bool selling
) internal view returns (uint256 avgPrice)

See: contracts/src/libraries/LibPricing.sol:325-399

10. Profile Validation

10.1. Rules

  1. First weight must be non-zero
  2. Weights must sum to exactly 200
  3. Offsets must be monotonically non-decreasing
  4. Zero weight terminates the profile

See: AdminV1._validateProfileMemory()

11. Gas Optimization

11.1. Efficient Storage

  • Profiles fit in 2 storage slots (32 bytes each)
  • Weights as uint8 (0-255 range)
  • Offsets as int8 (-128 to +127 range)

11.2. Traversal Cost

Operation Gas Cost
Load profile ~2,100 (cold) / 100 (warm)
Binary search O(log n) comparisons
Cubic interpolation ~500 gas
Total (typical) ~3,000-5,000 gas

Comparable to Uniswap v3 tick traversal for small swaps.

12. Comparison: AIMM vs Uniswap v3

Aspect Uniswap v3 AIMM Profiles
Granularity Per-tick (0.01% spacing) Per-segment (0.5% resolution)
Management Individual LP ranges Pool-level curator
Updates LP rebalancing Timelocked governance
Gas per swap O(ticks crossed) O(log segments)
Customization Any LP can position Curator-designed
Complexity High (active management) Low (passive)

13. Best Practices

13.1. For Stablecoins

  1. Heavy concentration (60%+) within 5 bps offset
  2. Moderate wings to 50-100 bps
  3. Low dispersion bounds (1000-5000 in 0.0001% units)
  4. High depth amplifier (500,000+)

13.2. For Volatile Assets

  1. More uniform distribution
  2. Wider max offsets (200+ bps)
  3. Higher dispersion bounds
  4. Lower depth amplifier

13.3. For New Assets

  1. Start with conservative (uniform) profile
  2. Monitor trade distribution
  3. Adjust based on observed depth utilization
  4. Consider volatility regime changes

14. Related Documentation

  • Inventory Management — Coverage ratio mechanics
  • Spread & Fees — How profiles affect pricing
  • Parametrization — Tuning guide

1.1.7-parametrization.title: 1.1.7. Parametrization
1.1.7-parametrization.html:
Configuration Parameters

Complete reference for all configuration parameters in the AIMM pool system.

1. Table of Contents

  • Asset Configuration
  • Risk Configuration
  • Oracle Configuration
  • Fee Parameters
  • Liquidity Profile
  • Admin Functions
  • Units Reference

2. Asset Configuration

Contract: IPoolV1.Asset (struct) Admin Function: AdminV1.addAsset()

Per-asset parameters stored in PoolStorage.assets[token].

Field Type Units Description Typical Values
reserves uint128 Token wei Total reserves held by pool Dynamic
liabilities uint128 Token wei Total liability (LP deposits) Dynamic
minLiquidity uint128 Token wei Minimum reserves floor (swaps revert below) Asset-specific
liquidityIndex uint64 WAD Cumulative interest index for lenders 1e18 initially
lastUpdate uint32 Unix timestamp Last update timestamp Auto-updated
minFeeBps uint16 0.0001% Minimum asset fee (lower bound) 100-1000 (0.01%-0.1%)
maxFeeBps uint16 0.0001% Maximum asset fee (upper bound) 5000-50000 (0.5%-5%)
decimals uint8 - Token decimals (6, 8, 18, etc.) 18 for most ERC20
minDispersion uint32 0.0001% Minimum liquidity dispersion bound 1000 (0.1%)
maxDispersion uint32 0.0001% Maximum liquidity dispersion bound 10000 (1.0%)
gamma uint16 Basis 10000 Inventory sensitivity multiplier 10000 (1.0x)
vega uint16 Basis 10000 Volatility sensitivity multiplier 10000 (1.0x)
lambda uint16 Basis 10000 Momentum sensitivity multiplier 10000 (1.0x)
haircutSuppressor uint16 Basis 10000 Withdrawal haircut exponent modifier 10000 → p=2
reservationPrice uint64 B64 Price floor vs anchor (swaps revert below) 0 (disabled)

2.1. Sensitivity Parameters

2.1.1. Gamma (γ) - Inventory Sensitivity

  • Default: 10000 (1.0x)
  • Purpose: Multiplier controlling inventory skew strength
  • Effect: Higher gamma → steeper linear slope → stronger price incentive for rebalancing

Formula (linear with bounded progress):

pi = |c - c_t| / |c_b - c_t|
 
psi = "sign"(c_t - c) times gamma times 100 times pi
WHERE
π=text(progress toward boundary
in [0, 1])
c=text(current coverage ratio)
ct=text(target coverage) = 1.0
cb=text(critical boundary) = 0.5 text( or ) 2.0
γ=text(multiplier
basis 10000)
ψ=text(inventory skew
in [-100, +100])

Key Properties:

  • At criticalMin (c=0.5): ψ=+γ×100 (max premium, pool buying)
  • At target (c=1): ψ=0 (equilibrium)
  • At criticalMax (c=2): ψ=−γ×100 (max discount, pool selling)
  • Linear interpolation — predictable, matches Avellaneda-Stoikov theory
Gamma Multiplier Effect Use Case
5000 0.5x Half skew Volatile assets, softer response
10000 1.0x Full skew Default/balanced
15000 1.5x 150% skew More aggressive rebalancing
20000 2.0x Double skew Stablecoins, strong incentives

2.1.2. Vega (ν) - Volatility Sensitivity

  • Default: 10000 (1.0x)
  • Purpose: Controls how volatility affects both liquidity dispersion and base spread
  • Effect: Higher vega → wider spreads during volatile markets

Dispersion Formula:

κ=clamp(1000+(σ⋅ν)(1000⋅10000),κ(min),κ(max))

Spread Formula:

Sv=100+(σp⋅ν)(100⋅10000)

Tuning:

  • Increase vega (e.g., 20000 = 2.0x) to widen spreads more aggressively with volatility
  • Decrease vega (e.g., 5000 = 0.5x) to dampen volatility impact

2.1.3. Lambda (λ) - Momentum Sensitivity

  • Default: 10000 (1.0x)
  • Purpose: Controls how price deviation (fast vs slow TWAP divergence) affects spread surcharge
  • Effect: Higher lambda → larger penalty when fast/slow EMAs diverge (toxic flow detection)

Formula:

U=(Δp⋅λ)10000

Tuning:

  • Increase lambda (e.g., 15000 = 1.5x) to penalize trending/uncertain price action heavily
  • Decrease lambda (e.g., 5000 = 0.5x) for smoother response to price uncertainty

2.1.4. Haircut Suppressor (η) - Withdrawal Penalty Modifier

  • Default: 10000 → exponent p=2
  • Purpose: Controls withdrawal haircut curve when c<1
  • Effect: Higher suppressor → gentler haircut curve

Power-Law Formula:

h(c)=(1−c)p quad with quad p=1+η10000
η Exponent p Curve Shape
0 1 Linear (harsh)
10000 2 Quadratic (moderate)
30000 4 Gentle
40000 5 Very gentle

Example: At 80% coverage with η=10000 (p=2):

h=(1−0.8)2=0.04=4%

2.2. Dispersion Bounds

Dispersion defines the price range over which liquidity is distributed (in 0.0001% units).

  • minDispersion: Lower bound (e.g., 1000 = 0.1% range)
  • maxDispersion: Upper bound (e.g., 10000 = 1.0% range)

Effect: Tighter bounds create denser liquidity (better execution), wider bounds spread liquidity (more slippage).

2.3. Liquidity Floor (minLiquidity)

Type: uint128 (raw token units) Default: 0 (no floor)

Minimum reserves that must remain in the pool. Swaps and flash loans that would reduce reserves below this threshold revert.

Use Cases:

  • Prevent complete liquidity drain attacks
  • Ensure minimum depth for price discovery
  • Protect against dust/griefing attacks
  • Maintain market functionality during extreme events

Example: For WETH (18 decimals), set minLiquidity = 1e18 to ensure at least 1 WETH remains.

Implementation:

if (assetOut.reserves < assetOut.minLiquidity) {
    revert IErrors.InsufficientAmount(assetOut.reserves, assetOut.minLiquidity);
}

2.4. Price Floor (reservationPrice)

Type: uint64 (B64 format) Default: 0 (disabled)

Minimum price vs anchor asset. Swaps that would push the price below this floor revert.

Use Cases:

  • Prevent flash crash attacks
  • Protect against oracle manipulation
  • Circuit breaker for extreme market conditions
  • Protect LST peg (e.g., wstETH vs WETH floor at 0.95)

Configuration:

// Example: Set wstETH reservation at 95% of WETH
// B64 encode price 0.95 with 18 decimals
uint64 reservationPrice = LibMaths.encodeB64(0.95e18, 18);

Implementation:

if (feed.lastPriceB64 < reservationPrice) {
    revert IErrors.PriceBelowReservation(feed.lastPriceB64, reservationPrice);
}

2.5. Fee Bounds

Fees use 0.0001% precision (BPS_PRECISION = 1,000,000):

Parameter Type Max Value Max Fee
minFeeBps uint16 65,535 ~6.5%
maxFeeBps uint16 65,535 ~6.5%

Examples:

  • 100 = 0.01% (1 standard bps)
  • 1000 = 0.1%
  • 10000 = 1%
  • 50000 = 5%

3. Risk Configuration

Contract: IPoolV1.RiskConfig (struct) Admin Function: AdminV1.updateRiskConfig()

Field Type Units Description Typical Values
decayStartRatioBps uint16 0.0001% Coverage threshold for liability decay 980000 (98%)
coverageFloor uint16 0.0001% Critical coverage floor 500000 (50%)
decaySlope uint32 WAD/second Linear decay rate for liabilities ~3.17e10 (1%/year)
depthAmplifier uint16 Raw Depth curve amplifier (scaled by 1e6 in formula) 0 or 500000
flags uint16 Bitfield Feature flags See flags table

3.1. Risk Flags (Bitfield)

Bit Flag Description
0 SWAP_ENABLED_BIT Enable/disable swaps for this asset
1 FLASH_ENABLED_BIT Enable/disable flash loans
2 LIABILITY_SWAP_ENABLED_BIT Enable/disable liability swaps
3 DECAY_ENABLED_BIT Enable/disable liability time decay
4 FROZEN_BIT Freeze all operations (emergency)

3.2. Coverage Thresholds

Threshold Default Purpose
coverageFloor 50% (500000) Maximum premium boundary
target 100% (hardcoded) Equilibrium point (zero skew)
critMax 200% (hardcoded) Maximum discount boundary

3.3. Depth Amplifier

Formula:

D=R+(k⋅(L−R)⋅π(1(1+2k)))106
WHERE
kis the depth amplifier (raw value)
π=(c−cf)(1−cf)is the progress from floor to target

Key Properties:

  • At critical floor (c=cf): D=R (no virtual depth)
  • At target (c≥1): D=R (full reserves)
  • Between: concave interpolation adds virtual depth
Value Effect
0 No amplification (D=R always)
500000 50% max virtual addition
1000000 100% max virtual addition

3.4. Liability Decay

When coverage falls below cd (decay start ratio):

ΔL=L⋅ρ⋅(ΔtW)

where ρ = decay slope, W = WAD.

Constraints:

  • Never decays below reserves
  • Stops when c≥1

4. Oracle Configuration

Contract: IPoolV1.OracleConfig (struct) Admin Function: AdminV1.requestOracleUpdate() (timelocked)

Field Type Description
primary address Primary oracle address
secondary address Secondary oracle (fallback)
feedId bytes32 Pyth/Redstone feed ID
modeFlags uint16 Oracle mode flags
accDecimals uint8 Accumulator decimal precision

Oracle Modes:

  • USE_INTERNAL: Pool's internal TWAP oracle
  • USE_EXTERNAL: External oracle (Chainlink, Pyth, etc.)
  • ALLOW_FALLBACK: Try secondary if primary fails

5. Fee Parameters

Contract: IPoolV1.FeeParams (struct)

Field Type Units Description Typical Values
protoShare uint8 Percentage (base 100) Protocol's share of total fees 25 (25%)
flashFeeBps uint16 0.0001% Flash loan fee rate 90 (0.009%)

5.1. Fee Calculation

Spread Model:

Sv=100+(σp⋅ν)(100⋅10000)
U=(Δp⋅λ)10000
S={Svif improves coverageSv+Uotherwise
S(final)=clamp(S,f(min),f(max))

50/50 Split:

ϕ(in)=(x⋅S)(2B)
ϕ(out)=(y⋅S)(2B)

Protocol Split:

ϕ(proto)=ϕ⋅r100

where r = protocol share percentage.

6. Liquidity Profile

Contract: IPoolV1.LiquidityProfile (struct)

Field Type Description Constraints
weights uint8[16] Segment weights (each unit = 0.5% of depth) Must sum to 200
knots int8[17] Price offset knots as % of dispersion range around TWAP. Dispersion defines liquidity breadth (e.g., dispersion=1% → ±1% around TWAP), knots are % of this (knot=-50 → -0.5% from TWAP) Monotone increasing, max - min == 100

6.1. Profile Structure

  • X-axis: Cumulative depth [0, 10000] = 0-100%
  • Y-axis: Price offset from TWAP (scaled by dispersion)
  • Interpolation: Catmull-Rom spline with exact analytical integration

6.2. Validation Rules

  1. First weight must be non-zero
  2. Weights must sum to exactly 200
  3. Offsets must be monotonically non-decreasing
  4. First zero weight marks profile end

6.3. Example Profiles

Concentrated (Stablecoins):

weights:  [80, 60, 30, 20, 10, 0, ...]
offsets:  [0,  5,  20, 50, 100, ...]

Uniform (Volatile Assets):

weights:  [25, 25, 25, 25, 25, 25, 25, 25, 0, ...]
offsets:  [0,  25, 50, 75, 100, 125, 150, 200, ...]

7. Admin Functions

All admin functions require onlyOwner. Critical operations are timelocked.

7.1. Immediate Functions

Function Purpose
addAsset() Add new asset with all config
setAssetParams() Update asset pricing/risk parameters
updateRiskConfig() Update risk parameters
updateRiskFlags() Update feature flags only
updateLiquidityProfile() Update liquidity distribution
updateFeeParams() Update protocol share and flash fee

7.1.1. setAssetParams()

Updates asset-level pricing and risk parameters including minLiquidity and reservationPrice:

function setAssetParams(
    address token,
    uint128 minLiquidity,     // Reserves floor (raw token units)
    uint16 minFeeBps,         // Min fee (0.0001% units)
    uint16 maxFeeBps,         // Max fee (0.0001% units)
    uint16 gamma,             // Inventory sensitivity
    uint16 vega,              // Volatility sensitivity
    uint16 lambda,            // Deviation sensitivity
    uint16 haircutSuppressor, // Haircut curve modifier
    uint64 reservationPrice   // Price floor (B64, 0=disabled)
) external onlyOwner;

7.2. Timelocked Functions

Function Delay Purpose
requestOwnershipTransfer() 3 days Transfer pool ownership
requestModuleUpdate() 2 days Upgrade module implementation
requestBaseMigration() 7 days Migrate base token
requestOracleUpdate() 2 days Update oracle configuration

8. Units Reference

Unit Type Basis Precision Example
Fees (minFeeBps, maxFeeBps, flashFeeBps) 1,000,000 0.0001% 100 = 0.01%, 10000 = 1%
Volatility (slowVolEMA, fastVolEMA) 1,000,000 0.0001% 1,000,000 = 1%
Coverage (decayStartRatioBps, coverageFloor) 1,000,000 0.0001% 980000 = 98%, 500000 = 50%
Dispersion (minDispersion, maxDispersion) 1,000,000 0.0001% 1000 = 0.1%, 10000 = 1.0%
Protocol Share (protoShare) 100 1% 25 = 25%
Multipliers (gamma, vega, lambda, suppressor) 10,000 0.01x 10000 = 1.0x
Prices (WAD) 1e18 18 decimals 1e18 = 1.0
Depth Amplifier (depthAmplifier) Raw Scaled by 1e6 500000 = 0.5 in formula
Decay Slope (decaySlope) WAD/second 18 decimals ~3.17e10 = 1%/year

9. Parameter Tuning Guide

9.1. Conservative Pool (Stablecoins)

Asset {
    minFeeBps: 10,        // 0.001%
    maxFeeBps: 500,       // 0.05%
    minDispersion: 100,   // 0.01%
    maxDispersion: 1000,  // 0.1%
    gamma: 10000,         // 1.0x multiplier
    vega: 5000,           // 0.5x volatility sensitivity
    lambda: 10000,        // 1.0x deviation sensitivity
    haircutSuppressor: 10000  // p=2 haircut curve
}
 
RiskConfig {
    coverageFloor: 900000,       // 90% floor
    decayStartRatioBps: 980000,  // 98% decay trigger
    depthAmplifier: 0,           // No amplification
    flags: 0x07                  // Swap + Flash + Liability Swap
}

9.2. Aggressive Pool (Volatile Assets)

Asset {
    minFeeBps: 500,       // 0.05%
    maxFeeBps: 50000,     // 5%
    minDispersion: 5000,  // 0.5%
    maxDispersion: 50000, // 5%
    gamma: 15000,         // 1.5x multiplier (steeper skew)
    vega: 20000,          // 2.0x volatility sensitivity
    lambda: 15000,        // 1.5x deviation sensitivity
    haircutSuppressor: 20000  // p=3 haircut curve
}
 
RiskConfig {
    coverageFloor: 500000,       // 50% floor
    decayStartRatioBps: 950000,  // 95% decay trigger
    depthAmplifier: 500000,      // 50% virtual depth amplification
    flags: 0x07                  // Swap + Flash + Liability Swap
}

1.1.5-slippage-price-impact.title: 1.1.5. Slippage & Price Impact
1.1.5-slippage-price-impact.html:
1.2.4.5. Slippage & Price Impact

Understanding execution costs and how to protect against unexpected price deviations

Overview

When executing a swap, traders face two distinct types of execution costs:

  1. Price Impact: The deterministic cost of trade size against available liquidity
  2. Slippage: The unexpected deviation between quoted and actual execution price

Understanding the difference is crucial for setting appropriate trade parameters and choosing execution strategies.

Price Impact (Deterministic)

Price impact is the predictable price movement caused by your trade consuming liquidity. It's known before execution and depends on:

  • Trade size relative to available liquidity
  • Liquidity depth at current price levels
  • AMM curve shape (invariant-based vs. spline-based)

Calculation

For a constant-product AMM (x·y=k):

priceImpact ≈ tradeSize / (poolReserve + tradeSize)
Trade Size (% of Pool) Approximate Impact
0.1% ~0.1%
1% ~1%
5% ~4.8%
10% ~9.1%

AIMM's Approach

AIMM uses spline-based liquidity profiles rather than fixed invariant curves. This allows:

  • Shaped depth: Pool operators can concentrate liquidity where trading occurs most
  • Dynamic adjustment: Depth scales with coverage ratio and volatility
  • Retail-friendly: Tighter impact for small trades, wider for large

The dispersion parameter controls price impact curvature:

dispersion = baseDispersion + σ × vega / MULT_BASE

Higher volatility → wider dispersion → greater price impact protection for LPs.

Slippage (Stochastic)

Slippage is the unexpected difference between quoted price and execution price. Unlike price impact, slippage is unpredictable and can be positive or negative.

Causes of Slippage

Source Description Direction
Market movement Price changes between quote and execution Either
Front-running MEV searcher trades ahead of you Negative
Sandwich attacks MEV bot manipulates price before and after Negative
Network latency Delayed transaction confirmation Either
Oracle updates Price feed changes during execution Either

Positive Slippage

Slippage can be positive (favorable) if the market moves in your favor between quote and execution. However, this is rare on public mempools because:

  1. MEV searchers monitor pending transactions
  2. Favorable price movements are captured by backrunners
  3. Only unfavorable movements pass through to the original trader

This asymmetry is why MEV protection matters—without it, traders experience systematically negative slippage.

Protection Mechanisms

1. minAmountOut Parameter

AIMM's swap() function enforces slippage protection via minAmountOut:

function swap(
    address tokenIn,
    address tokenOut,
    uint256 amountIn,
    uint256 minAmountOut,  // ← Slippage protection
    address recipient
) external returns (uint256 amountOut);

If execution would result in less than minAmountOut, the transaction reverts:

if (finalAmountOut < minAmountOut) {
    revert ThresholdViolation(finalAmountOut, minAmountOut);
}

Setting minAmountOut:

  • Tight tolerance (0.1-0.5%): Protects against MEV but may fail in volatile markets
  • Normal tolerance (0.5-1%): Balance of protection and success rate
  • Wide tolerance (1-3%): Higher success rate but more exposure to slippage

2. MEV-Protected RPCs

Hide transactions from public mempool to prevent front-running and sandwich attacks.

Free Public Endpoints (Ethereum L1)

Provider Endpoint Notes
MEV Blocker https://rpc.mevblocker.io CoW Protocol's protection
Flashbots Protect https://rpc.flashbots.net/fast Fast mode, may sacrifice some protection
Merkle https://eth.merkle.io Free tier available
Llama Nodes https://eth.llamarpc.com Free tier available
BlockRazor https://eth.blockrazor.xyz MEV protection on by default

Free Public Endpoints (BNB Chain)

Provider Endpoint
48 Club https://rpc.48.club
Merkle https://bsc.merkle.io
Llama Nodes https://binance.llamarpc.com
BlockRazor https://bsc.blockrazor.xyz

Free Public Endpoints (Base)

Provider Endpoint
Llama Nodes https://base.llamarpc.com

Private RPC Networks (Multi-Chain)

Provider Coverage MEV Protection
Alchemy Ethereum, Polygon, Arbitrum, Optimism, Base Always on
BlockPI Multi-chain Enable in dashboard
dRPC Multi-chain Enable in dashboard
Helius Solana Optional Jito integration

3. Timing Strategies

Strategy Description Trade-off
Low volatility periods Trade when markets are calm May miss opportunities
Order splitting Break large orders into smaller pieces Higher gas costs
Limit orders Set exact price (if supported) May not execute
Off-peak hours Reduced MEV competition Lower liquidity

Chain-Specific Considerations

Ethereum L1 (Public Mempool)

Ethereum's public mempool makes all pending transactions visible to anyone running a node. MEV searchers continuously monitor for profitable reordering opportunities.

Transaction ordering: Gas auction—highest priority fee wins position in block.

Protection: Use MEV-protected RPCs (listed above) to submit transactions directly to trusted block builders.

Arbitrum / OP Stack Rollups (Sequencer)

Transactions go directly to a centralized sequencer, which has full visibility of pending transactions but is expected to order fairly.

Original ordering: FCFS (First-Come-First-Served) Current (Arbitrum): Timeboost auction for priority lane Current (Base/OP): FCFS with priority fee escalation

Protection: Sequencer is trusted not to extract MEV directly. Third-party MEV is limited by sequencer control over ordering.

Solana (Gulf Stream)

No public mempool—transactions forwarded directly to slot leaders. The leader controls ordering.

MEV infrastructure: Jito provides bundle auctions at the validator level.

Protection: Helius RPC offers optional Jito integration for MEV protection.

Sui (Narwhal DAG)

DAG-based mempool with object-based execution model. MEV concentrated around "shared objects" (e.g., AMM pools).

Ordering: Parallel execution of independent transactions reduces ordering-based MEV for simple transfers.

Protection: Contention-based MEV still exists for AMM trades accessing shared pool state.

Practical Recommendations

For Retail Users

  1. Always set minAmountOut to at least 99% of quoted output
  2. Use MEV-protected RPCs on Ethereum and BNB Chain
  3. Check gas prices—high gas often correlates with MEV activity
  4. Split large trades if you're swapping more than 1% of pool depth

For Integrators

  1. Quote with fresh oracle prices before displaying to users
  2. Calculate realistic slippage bounds based on volatility
  3. Provide RPC configuration for MEV protection
  4. Show price impact clearly before execution

For Large Traders

  1. Use intent-based systems (CoW Protocol, UniswapX) for better execution
  2. Consider private mempools or direct builder connections
  3. Time-weight execution across multiple blocks
  4. Monitor markout to measure actual execution quality

Research & Further Reading

  • Private MEV Protection RPCs - Analysis of private RPC effectiveness
  • MEV on Polygon - Cross-chain MEV impact study

  • Flashbots Docs - MEV infrastructure
  • Jito Documentation - Solana MEV infrastructure

Related Documentation
