1.1.6-toxic-flow-mitigation.title: 1.1.6. Toxic Flow Mitigation
1.1.6-toxic-flow-mitigation.html:
Anti-Toxic Flow Protection

Mechanisms to mitigate adverse selection, stat-arb extraction, and JIT attacks

1. Overview

AIMM is arbitrage-friendly for rebalancing but anti-toxic for extractive flows. The protocol employs multiple defense mechanisms against common AMM attack vectors while maintaining capital efficiency.

Design Philosophy:

  • Arbitrageurs provide valuable price discovery → encouraged via fair spreads
  • Toxic flow extractors exploit information asymmetry → penalized via dynamic fees
  • Liquidity providers deserve protection from adverse selection
  • MEV searchers can be allies, not enemies → Cooperative MEV rebate program

2. Toxic Flow Vectors

2.1. Adverse Selection

Attack: Informed traders execute against stale prices before oracle updates.

Example:

  1. CEX price moves ETH from $2000 → $2050
  2. Trader front-runs oracle update
  3. Buys ETH at $2000 from pool
  4. Sells at $2050 on CEX
  5. Pool LPs lose $50/ETH

Impact: LPs systematically lose to informed traders.

2.2. Statistical Arbitrage vs CEXs

Attack: High-frequency traders exploit price lags between pool and centralized exchanges.

Characteristics:

  • Sub-second execution windows
  • Exploits oracle staleness
  • Unidirectional (always against LPs)
  • Risk-free profit extraction

Impact: Continuous drain on LP returns, especially during volatile periods.

2.3. Just-In-Time (JIT) Liquidity

Attack: Sophisticated actors add liquidity just before large swaps and remove immediately after, capturing fees without exposure to toxic flow.

Mechanism:

  1. Bot detects large pending swap in mempool
  2. Adds concentrated liquidity front-running the swap
  3. Captures disproportionate fee share
  4. Removes liquidity in same block
  5. Passive LPs bear inventory risk, JIT bot extracts fees

Status: ⚠️ Not yet mitigated (planned for next version)

3. AIMM Defense Mechanisms

3.1. Volatility-Based Fees

Dynamic fees that increase during high volatility periods when adverse selection risk is highest.

Formula:

ϕσ=ν⋅σ
WHERE
ϕσis the volatility fee component
σ=(σf+σs)2is the average volatility (fast + slow EMAs)
νis the volatility sensitivity parameter (vega)

How it protects:

  • Volatility spikes → fees increase automatically
  • Toxic flow becomes more expensive during attack windows
  • Arbitrageurs pay higher costs during uncertainty
  • LPs compensated for increased adverse selection risk

Implementation: See LibPricing.sol:584-624

Parameters:

  • vega: Controls fee sensitivity to volatility (default: 10000 = 1.0×)
  • Fast vol EMA: 5min window, 0.02% smoothing
  • Slow vol EMA: 1hr window, 0.18% smoothing

Example:

Normal conditions:  σ = 5%  → volatilityFee = 5 bps
High volatility:    σ = 50% → volatilityFee = 50 bps

3.2. Asymmetric Spread (Deviation-Based)

Prices lag true market value based on directional inventory imbalance. Higher fees charged on the imbalanced side.

Mechanism:

ϕψ=λ⋅|(ψ)|
WHERE
ϕψ= inventory fee component
ψ= inventory skew (deviation from target coverage)
λ= deviation sensitivity
Range:ψ ∈[−100,+100]

Asymmetry:

  • Pool overcollateralized (selling pressure) → higher fees on buys
  • Pool undercollateralized (buying pressure) → higher fees on sells
  • Fee increases proportional to imbalance severity

How it protects:

  • Toxic flow typically unidirectional (exploits price lag)
  • Imbalance indicates likely mispricing
  • Higher fees on imbalanced side = adverse selection protection
  • Rebalancing arbitrage encouraged (bringing pool back to equilibrium)

Implementation: See LibPricing.sol:85-144

Parameters:

  • lambda: Deviation sensitivity (default: 10000 = 1.0×)
  • gamma: Skew curve convexity (default: 10000 = linear)

Example:

Coverage = 100% (balanced):     skew = 0   → inventoryFee = 0
Coverage = 70% (imbalanced):    skew = +60 → inventoryFee = 60 × lambda
Coverage = 150% (imbalanced):   skew = -50 → inventoryFee = 50 × lambda

3.3. Dual-Window TWAP Oracle

Internal oracle resists manipulation via dual time windows and same-block rejection.

Windows:

  • Fast TWAP (5min): Responsive to real price movements
  • Slow TWAP (1hr): Stable reference, filters noise

Same-Block Rejection:

if (dt == 0) return;  // Skip if same block

How it protects:

  • Flash loan price manipulation → rejected (same block)
  • Multi-block manipulation → expensive (requires sustained capital)
  • Dual windows → harder to exploit both simultaneously
  • Volatility measured from TWAP deltas → smooths spikes

Attack cost:

1% price manipulation for 5 minutes:
  capital × time × opportunity_cost ≫ expected profit

See: InternalOracleV1

3.4. Market-Aware Bi-Factor Fee

Combines protections into single adaptive fee:

S={Sv+Uif worsening coverageSvif improving coverage
WHERE
Sv=100+(σ cν.)(100 c10000.)is the volatility band
U=(Δ cλ.)10000is the deviation surcharge
ϕp=S cρ.100is the protocol share
ϕ LP=S−ϕpis the LP fee

Note: Inventory skew affects mid-price (not fees). The fee model is bi-factor: volatility band Sv + deviation surcharge U.

Bounds:

  • minFeeBps: Floor fee (0.0001% units, e.g., 100 = 0.01%)
  • maxFeeBps: Ceiling fee (0.0001% units, e.g., 50000 = 5%)

Adaptive behavior:

  • Normal conditions: ~Sv (volatility band)
  • Oracle disagreement: +U (deviation surcharge)
  • Coverage-worsening trades: pay Sv+U
  • Coverage-improving trades: pay Sv only (arb-friendly)

See: Spread & Fees

3.5. Coverage-Aware Haircuts

Withdrawals during undercollateralization incur haircuts, discouraging bank runs and adverse selection exits.

Formula:

h=(1−c)2⋅η
y=x⋅(1−h)
WHERE
his the haircut percentage
cis the coverage ratio
ηis the haircut suppressor
xis the gross withdrawal amount
yis the final amount received

How it protects:

  • LPs can't exit at par during adverse selection events
  • Early exits subsidize remaining LPs
  • Prevents cascading withdrawals
  • Incentivizes staying during temporary imbalances

Example:

Coverage = 90%:  haircut = (0.1)² = 1%
Coverage = 80%:  haircut = (0.2)² = 4%
Coverage = 50%:  haircut = (0.5)² = 25%

See: LibPricing.sol:1006-1055

3.6. Cooperative Arbitrage

Rather than fighting arbitrageurs, AIMM collaborates with them through a whitelisted, reputation-based rebate program that aligns incentives.

The Problem with Traditional Arbitrage:

  • CEX-DEX arbitrageurs extract value from pools by exploiting oracle staleness
  • LPs bear the cost of price corrections (Loss-Versus-Rebalancing)
  • Adversarial relationship: arbitrageurs extract, LPs lose
  • No mechanism to reward arbitrageurs who help the pool

AIMM's Solution: Cooperative Arbitrage:

Not MEV, but Statistical Arbitrage: This mechanism targets cross-exchange (CEX-DEX) statistical arbitrage, not MEV in the formal sense (which manipulates block ordering). Cooperators are arbitrageurs—a broader category encompassing MEV searchers, HFT desks, and medium-frequency stat arb traders.

How Arbitrageurs Become Cooperators:

  1. Whitelist application: Arbitrageurs apply to the DAO for Cooperator status at btr.supply/coop
  2. Equal starting rebate: All approved cooperators start with the same rebate tier (e.g., 20%)
  3. Reputation tracking: Performance measured by reputation = total_donations / total_rebates
  4. Tiered rebates: Higher reputation → higher rebate percentage (up to parametric max, e.g., 80%)
  5. Revocation threshold: Low reputation (<0.9) leads to loss of Cooperator status
  6. Competitive dynamics: All cooperators compete on equal terms; best performers earn highest rebates

Parameters (pool-level governance):

  • maxCooperators: Maximum whitelisted cooperators (default: 10)
  • maxRebateBps: Maximum rebate percentage (default: 8000 = 80%)
  • minReputation: Minimum reputation to maintain status (default: 0.9)
  • rebateCooldown: Cooldown period for claiming rebates (default: 1 week)

How it works:

Standard arbitrage:
  Arbitrageur profit = CEX_price - pool_price - fees
  Pool gets = fees only
  LP cost = LVR (loss-versus-rebalancing)
 
Cooperative arbitrage:
  Arbitrageur profit = CEX_price - pool_price - fees + rebate
  Pool gets = fees + donations (from high-reputation cooperators)
  LP cost = Reduced LVR (faster price convergence)
 
Rebate accrual (per swap):
  accrued_rebate += spread_captured × cooperator_rebate_bps / 10000
 
Claimable after cooldown (prevents instant extraction)

Reputation-Based Rebate Tiers:

Example progression:
  Cooperator A: 1000 USDC donated / 500 USDC rebates = 2.0 reputation
  Cooperator B: 800 USDC donated / 1000 USDC rebates = 0.8 reputation
 
  → A qualifies for higher rebate tier (e.g., 40%)
  → B below threshold (0.9), faces revocation
 
Why donate?
  Higher donations → higher reputation → higher rebates
  → more profitable arbitrage (lower effective cost)
  → sustainable competitive advantage

The DAO's Natural Advantage (unstated but emergent): If the DAO operates its own arbitrage bot and donates 100% of proceeds back to the pool:

  • Reputation = total_donated / total_rebates → maximized
  • Qualifies for highest rebate tier automatically
  • Effectively front-runs adversarial arbitrageurs (lower profit threshold due to rebates)
  • Closes the LVR loop: arbitrage profits return to LPs who suffered the LVR

This creates a competitive but fair game where all cooperators have equal opportunity, but those who contribute most to the pool (whether DAO or external) earn the best terms.

Why this protects LPs:

Factor Without Cooperation With Cooperation
Arbitrage timing Extract after oracle lag Race to rebalance first (incentivized by rebates)
Inventory impact Extract then abandon Actively managed (donations improve coverage)
Price accuracy Exploits staleness Minimizes staleness (competitive delagging)
LP PnL Systematic LVR Drastically reduced LVR (donations offset losses)
Competition Adversarial extraction Cooperative improvement (reputation game)

Whitelist Rationale:

  • Quality control: Ensure cooperators don't expose LP deposits to excessive external CEX risk
  • Inventory management: DAO and trusted actors carry inventory risk (bounded to small fraction of pool TVL)
  • Active monitoring: Track cooperator behavior, donations, and reputation
  • Credit risk management: Prevent cooperators from using pool as leverage source

Important: This is not fully permissionless—it requires DAO curation and monitoring. However, it avoids:

  • Oracle centralization (UAMM, DODO, Swaap): No single point of failure or manipulation
  • Manager trust (am-AMM): No single entity controlling all fees and arb profits
  • Builder dependency (McAMM): No reliance on off-chain infrastructure or PBS
  • Complexity (McAMM on multi-asset pools): Simple per-swap rebate accrual, no auction mechanics

Rebate Accrual & Claiming:

// Per-cooperator accounting (in base tokens)
mapping(address => uint256) public accruedRebates;
mapping(address => uint256) public totalDonations;
mapping(address => uint256) public totalRebates;
mapping(address => uint256) public lastClaim;
mapping(address => uint16) public cooperatorRebateBps;  // Individual rebate tier
mapping(address => bool) public isCooperator;
 
// Reputation tracking
function getReputation(address cooperator) public view returns (uint256) {
    if (totalRebates[cooperator] == 0) return 1e18;  // Perfect reputation initially
    return (totalDonations[cooperator] * 1e18) / totalRebates[cooperator];
}
 
// On every swap by a cooperator:
if (isCooperator[msg.sender]) {
    uint256 rebateAmount = spreadPaid * cooperatorRebateBps[msg.sender] / 10000;
    accruedRebates[msg.sender] += rebateAmount;
    totalRebates[msg.sender] += rebateAmount;
}
 
// Cooperators can donate to improve reputation:
function donate(uint256 amount) external {
    baseToken.transferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amount);
    totalDonations[msg.sender] += amount;
    // DAO reviews reputation and may upgrade rebate tier
}
 
// Claim after cooldown:
function claimRebate() external {
    require(isCooperator[msg.sender], "Not a cooperator");
    require(block.timestamp >= lastClaim[msg.sender] + rebateCooldown, "Cooldown active");
 
    uint256 amount = accruedRebates[msg.sender];
    require(amount > 0, "Nothing to claim");
 
    accruedRebates[msg.sender] = 0;
    lastClaim[msg.sender] = block.timestamp;
 
    baseToken.transfer(msg.sender, amount);
}

The virtuous cycle:

  1. Cooperators compete to arbitrage first (rebates lower their profit threshold)
  2. Competition → faster price convergence → smaller LVR window
  3. High-reputation cooperators donate proceeds → LPs recover LVR losses
  4. Better LP returns → more liquidity → tighter spreads
  5. Tighter spreads → more arbitrage opportunities → more cooperation
  6. Low-reputation cooperators revoked → only aligned actors remain

We call these participants "Cooperators" or "Cooperative Arbitrageurs"—transforming adversarial extraction into collaborative market-making.

See: Manifesto - Cooperative Arbitrage

4. Comparison with Other AMMs

4.1. Uniswap V2/V3

Uniswap:

  • Static fees (0.05%, 0.3%, 1%)
  • No volatility adaptation
  • No inventory awareness
  • JIT vulnerable (V3 concentrated liquidity)

AIMM Advantage:

  • Dynamic fees respond to risk
  • Inventory skew protection
  • Dual TWAP manipulation resistance

4.2. Balancer V2

Balancer:

  • Static fees per pool
  • Oracle price feeds (external dependency)
  • No built-in JIT protection

AIMM Advantage:

  • Market-aware bi-factor dynamic fees
  • Internal + external oracle redundancy
  • Volatility-aware pricing

4.3. Curve V2 (LLAMMA)

Curve:

  • Dynamic fees via internal oracle
  • Inventory-based repricing
  • No explicit volatility component

AIMM Advantage:

  • Explicit volatility measurement and fees
  • Dual-window TWAP (more manipulation resistant)
  • Configurable sensitivity parameters

4.4. State-of-the-Art LVR Mitigation Comparison

AIMM's Cooperative Arbitrage fits within the landscape of LVR mitigation research as a rebate-style, whitelisted revenue redistribution mechanism that avoids the strong oracle and block-builder assumptions of competing designs.

4.4.1. McAMM (MEV-Capturing AMM)

What it is: McAMM auctions the right to be the first trader in each block. Arbitrageurs bid for this slot, and the winning bid goes to LPs, internalizing MEV that would otherwise be extracted.^1

How it fights LVR: When external price moves, the first-trade slot captures most arbitrage value. By auctioning it, LPs recapture what they'd lose to informed flow.^2

Pros:

  • Conceptually clean
  • Minimal AMM changes
  • Strongly LVR-reducing with competitive auctions

Cons:

  • Block-builder dependent: Requires PBS (proposer-builder separation) and builders who respect the auction—only realistic on Ethereum mainnet with MEV-boost^1
  • Anti-democratizing: Professional MEV shops integrated with builders dominate; retail arbitrage priced out
  • Portability issues: Thin auctions on chains without mature MEV infrastructure
  • Multi-asset complexity: "First trade of block" must translate to "first batch" across N tokens, complicating auction and MEV search

Why AIMM chose differently: Cross-chain deployment requires solutions that work without builder infrastructure. McAMM is Ethereum-specific.

4.4.2. am-AMM (Auction-Managed AMM)

What it is: Harberger-style auction for a pool manager lease. Winner pays continuous rent to LPs and in return controls fee schedules and captures all internal arbitrage profits.^7^9

How it fights LVR: Manager continuously arbs the pool vs. external markets, internalizing MEV while paying competitive rent upfront. LPs recover LVR via rent payments and optimized fees.^5

Pros:

  • Economically elegant
  • Unifies LVR reduction and fee optimization
  • Chain-agnostic (only needs on-chain auction)

Cons:

  • Centralizing: Single large manager controls all fees and trading revenue at any time^7
  • Manager trust: Malicious or absent manager creates governance risk
  • Oracle dependency in practice: Competitive managers need off-chain CEX feeds and HFT infrastructure
  • Anti-democratizing: Smaller players locked out until they can outbid incumbent

Why AIMM chose differently: Manager trust and centralization conflict with AIMM's permissionless design goals. We prefer distributed competition among multiple cooperators rather than winner-take-all auctions.

4.4.3. UAMM (Oracle-Driven AMM)

What it is: AMM that derives price from external oracles rather than pool balances, adding slippage only to manage inventory toward a target.^11

How it fights LVR: If oracles reflect true market price, UAMM quotes near-oracle prices, leaving essentially no arbitrage gap. Classical LVR from stale prices disappears.^10

Pros:

  • Strongest LVR solution theoretically (if oracle is perfect)
  • Eliminates arbitrage opportunities at the source

Cons:

  • Oracle-centric and fragile: Wrong, manipulated, or lagging oracle → unbounded LP losses^10
  • Single point of failure: AMM safety = oracle safety
  • Centralization: Oracle choice, update frequency, and failover are governance decisions
  • Lag still exists: Even fast oracles (Pyth, Chainlink) lag CEX prices by seconds; LVR reduced but not eliminated

Related designs: DODO, Swaap, and other oracle-first AMMs share these tradeoffs.

Why AIMM chose differently: Oracle-first designs trade decentralization for LVR reduction. AIMM's internal TWAP + optional external fallback provides redundancy without single-point dependency.

4.4.4. AIMM's Cooperative Arbitrage

What it is: Whitelisted arbitrageurs earn rebates proportional to their reputation (donations/rebates ratio), incentivizing them to donate arbitrage proceeds back to the pool.

How it fights LVR:

  • Rebates lower cooperators' profit threshold → they arbitrage faster → smaller LVR window
  • High-reputation cooperators donate proceeds → LPs recover LVR losses directly
  • DAO can run its own bot with 100% donation rate → maximal reputation → closes LVR loop entirely

Comparison:

Approach Portability Centralization Oracle Dependency LVR Reduction Permissionless?
McAMM Low (PBS only) Medium (pro MEV shops) None High Yes (auction open)
am-AMM High High (single manager) Practical (manager needs CEX) Very High Yes (auction open)
UAMM High Very High (oracle control) Total Highest (if oracle perfect) Yes (trading open)
AIMM Coop Arb High Medium (DAO whitelist) None (internal TWAP) High (via donations) No (whitelist)

Key differentiators:

  1. No builder dependency: Works on any EVM chain, not just Ethereum with PBS
  2. Distributed competition: Multiple cooperators (max 10) instead of single manager
  3. No oracle single-point-of-failure: Internal TWAP with optional external fallback
  4. Simple per-swap mechanics: No auctions, no manager leases—just rebate accrual
  5. Emergent DAO advantage: Any cooperator can compete, but 100% donation rate naturally dominates

Tradeoff: Not fully permissionless (requires DAO curation), but avoids strong trust assumptions of oracle-first or manager-controlled designs.

Why this works: AIMM's dynamic fee model already prices LVR risk via volatility and inventory components. Cooperative Arbitrage adds a revenue redistribution layer that returns extracted value to LPs without requiring perfect oracles or centralized managers.

5. Configuration

5.1. Asset-Level Parameters

struct Asset {
    uint16 gamma;              // Inventory sensitivity
    uint16 vega;               // Volatility sensitivity
    uint16 lambda;             // Deviation sensitivity
    uint16 haircutSuppressor;  // Withdrawal penalty dampener
    uint16 minFeeBps;          // Floor fee
    uint16 maxFeeBps;          // Ceiling fee
}

5.2. Recommended Ranges

Asset Class gamma vega lambda minFee maxFee
Stablecoins 5000-10000 5000-8000 8000-12000 1-3 bps 50-100 bps
Major pairs 10000-15000 10000-15000 10000-15000 5-10 bps 100-300 bps
Volatile alts 15000-25000 15000-25000 15000-25000 10-30 bps 300-1000 bps

5.3. Tuning Guidelines

Conservative (maximize LP protection):

  • Higher vega → stronger volatility penalties
  • Higher lambda → stronger inventory penalties
  • Higher minFee → baseline protection

Aggressive (maximize volume):

  • Lower sensitivity parameters
  • Lower minFee
  • Rely on haircuts for extreme events

Balanced (default):

  • Moderate parameters (10000 = 1.0× multiplier)
  • Caps at maxFee for tail events
  • Tested against historical data

6. Monitoring & Alerts

On-Chain Metrics:

  • Real-time coverage ratios
  • Fee tier distribution
  • Swap directionality (buy/sell pressure)
  • Volatility EMAs

Off-Chain Analytics:

  • LP vs arbitrageur PnL segregation
  • Adverse selection cost estimation
  • CEX-DEX price correlation
  • JIT detection (when implemented)

7. Related Documentation

  • Inventory Management - Coverage and skew formulas
  • Spread & Fees - Complete fee model
  • Internal Oracle - TWAP implementation
  • Security Overview - Broader security model

1.1.4-spread-fees.title: 1.1.4. Spread & Fees
1.1.4-spread-fees.html:
AIMM Spread & Fee Model

Asymmetric spread with symmetrical fee distribution

1. Overview

AIMM implements a sophisticated fee model that separates spread asymmetry (pricing) from fee distribution fairness (LP earnings):

1.1. Spread Asymmetry (Pricing)

  • Volatility Band Sv: Symmetric base spread around mid-price
  • Directional Surcharge U: Asymmetric penalty for coverage-worsening trades
  • Bid-Ask Spread: Different costs for coverage-improving vs coverage-worsening directions

1.2. Fee Distribution Symmetry (LP Fairness)

  • 50/50 Split: Half of fee taken from input token, half from output token
  • Fair LP Earnings: LPs earn fees in both tokens regardless of trade direction
  • No One-Sided Fee Problem: Unlike traditional AMMs where fees concentrate in one token

2. Unit System

2.1. BPS Precision

All fees and spreads use 0.0001% precision (not standard 0.01% bps):

B=1,000,000

where B = BPS_PRECISION. This means:

  • 1 unit = 0.0001%
  • 10,000 units = 1%
  • 100 units = 0.01% (1 standard bps)

2.2. Fee Bounds

Parameter Type Max Value Max Fee
minFeeBps uint16 65,535 ~6.5%
maxFeeBps uint16 65,535 ~6.5%

2.3. Volatility Units

Volatility σ uses 1e6 base:

  • 1,000,000 = 1%
  • 10,000,000 = 10%

3. Spread Calculation

3.1. Risk Signals

Per-Hop Volatility σ:

σi= σf,i+σs,i2

where:

  • σ_f = fast EMA volatility
  • σ_s = slow EMA volatility

Per-Hop Deviation:

Δi= max(|(of,i−os,i)|,|(of,i)|)

where:

  • o_{f,i} = fast TWAP offset at hop i
  • o_{s,i} = slow TWAP offset at hop i

Path-Level Aggregation:

σp= maxi(σi)
Δp= maxi(Δi)

3.2. Symmetric Volatility Band

Baseline spread, direction-agnostic:

Sv=100+ σp timesν100 timesM

where:

  • S_v = volatility band (basis points)
  • σ_p = path volatility
  • ν = max(ν_in, ν_out) (vega, endpoint-only)
  • M = MULT_BASE (10000)
  • Units: 0.0001% precision (B = 1,000,000)

3.3. Directional Deviation Surcharge

Asymmetric penalty for informed/toxic flow:

U= Δp timesλM

where:

  • U = deviation surcharge
  • Δ_p = path deviation
  • λ = max(λ_in, λ_out) (lambda, endpoint-only)
  • M = MULT_BASE (10000)

3.4. Coverage Classification

c= RL
I0=|(c ∈,0−1)|+|(c out,0−1)|
I1=|(c ∈,1−1)|+|(c out,1−1)|
 improves=(I1<I0)

where:

  • c = coverage ratio
  • R, L = reserves, liabilities
  • I = sum of coverage deviations
  • Subscripts 0, 1 = before and after trade

3.5. Final Spread

S= beg∈casesSv& ifimprovescoverage\Sv+U& otherwise endcases
S f∈al= clamp(S,f min,f max)

where:

  • S_final = final spread (basis points, clamped)
  • f_min, f_max = fee bounds

4. Fee Distribution: 50/50 Split

4.1. Motivation

Problem with Traditional AMMs:

  • Uniswap V2/V3: Fee taken 100% from input → LPs earn one-sided fees
  • Curve V1: Fee taken 100% from output → LPs earn one-sided fees
  • Issue: Fee concentration creates imbalanced LP earnings

AIMM Solution:

  • 50% from input token → LPs earn fees in token being sold
  • 50% from output token → LPs earn fees in token being bought
  • Result: Symmetrical fee distribution regardless of trade direction

4.2. Implementation

ϕ ∈= x timesS2B
ϕ out= y timesS2B

where:

  • φ_in, φ_out = fees from input and output
  • x = input amount
  • y = output amount
  • S = spread (basis points)
  • B = BPS_PRECISION (1,000,000)
x′=x−ϕ ∈
y′=y−ϕ out

where:

  • x', y' = net amounts after fee deduction

4.3. State Updates

Input Asset: Reserves increased by net amount (after fee), liabilities unchanged.

Output Asset: Reserves decreased by net amount (after fee), liabilities unchanged.

Fee Retention: Both fee_in and fee_out stay in reserves → increases coverage.

4.4. Example: ETH → USDC Swap

Setup:

  • Trader swaps 1 ETH for USDC
  • Mid-price: 1 ETH = 2000 USDC
  • Spread: 5000 (0.5% in 0.0001% units)

Traditional AMM (100% input fee):

Fee = 1 ETH × 0.50% = 0.005 ETH
LPs earn: 0.005 ETH only

AIMM (50/50 split):

fee_in = 1 ETH × 0.25% = 0.0025 ETH
fee_out = 2000 USDC × 0.25% = 5 USDC
LPs earn: 0.0025 ETH + 5 USDC (balanced!)

5. Bid-Ask Asymmetry

5.1. Two-Sided Market

At any instant, effective bid/ask around mid-price m:

  • Bid (coverage-improving): m⋅(1−SvB)
  • Ask (coverage-worsening): m⋅(1+(Sv+U)B)
  • Spread Width: 2Sv+U

5.2. Coverage-Dependent Asymmetry

When pool is over-collateralized (c>1):

  • Buying from pool (reduces reserves) → improves coverage → pays Sv only
  • Selling to pool (increases reserves) → worsens coverage → pays Sv+U

When pool is under-collateralized (c<1):

  • Buying from pool → worsens coverage → pays Sv+U
  • Selling to pool → improves coverage → pays Sv only

At equilibrium ($c ~~ 1$):

  • Both directions pay similar spreads unless deviation high

5.3. Economic Interpretation

Volatility Band Sv: Market maker spread covering:

  • Expected adverse selection
  • Inventory rebalancing costs
  • Option value of providing liquidity

Deviation Surcharge U: Informed flow penalty:

  • High Δ signals oracle disagreement
  • Coverage-worsening trades during uncertainty pay extra
  • Prevents exploitation during price manipulation

6. Protocol Fee Split

6.1. Revenue Sharing

After calculating total fees (50% from input + 50% from output):

ϕ proto=ϕ times r100
ϕ lp=ϕ−ϕ proto

where:

  • φ_proto = protocol fee portion
  • φ_lp = LP fee portion
  • φ = total fees
  • r = protocol share percentage (0-100)

6.2. Proto Share Parameter

Proto Share Type Distribution
0 uint8 100% to LPs
25 uint8 25% protocol, 75% LPs (default)
50 uint8 50/50 split

protoShare is a uint8 with base 100 (0-100 range representing 0%-100%).

7. Fee Bounds

7.1. Per-Asset Configuration

Each asset defines fee-related parameters:

  • minFeeBps, maxFeeBps: Floor/ceiling in 0.0001% units
  • vega: Volatility sensitivity (basis 10000)
  • lambda: Deviation sensitivity (basis 10000)

See: Parametrization

7.2. Path-Level Bounds

For multi-hop swaps:

f min,p= maxi(f min,i)
f max,p= maxi(f max,i)
S= clamp(S raw,f min,p,f max,p)

where:

  • f_min,p = path-level minimum fee
  • f_max,p = path-level maximum fee
  • S_raw = unclamped spread
  • i = index over all hops in path

8. Comparison with Other AMMs

8.1. Fee Token Location

Protocol Fee Taken In Distribution
Uniswap V2/V3 100% input One-sided LP earnings
Trader Joe V2 100% input One-sided LP earnings
Curve V1 100% output One-sided LP earnings
Wombat Input, redistributed Single-asset LP friendly
AIMM 50% input + 50% output Symmetrical LP earnings

8.2. Spread Characteristics

Aspect Uniswap V3 AIMM
Fee structure Fixed tiers (0.01-1%) Market-aware (bi-factor)
Volatility response None σ-scaled band
Inventory response None Skew + surcharge
Coverage awareness No Yes (directional)
LVR mitigation Via hooks only Built-in surcharge
Fee distribution One-sided (input) Symmetrical (50/50)

9. Parameter Guidelines

9.1. Vega (Volatility Sensitivity)

  • Basis: 10,000 = 1.0x sensitivity
  • Example: ν=10000, σ=1,000,000 (1%) → Sv≈200 units (0.02%)
  • Tuning: Higher vega → wider spreads for volatile assets

9.2. Lambda (Deviation Sensitivity)

  • Basis: 10,000 = 1.0x sensitivity
  • Example: λ=10000, Δ=500,000 → $U ~~ 50$ units (0.005%)
  • Tuning: Higher lambda → larger penalty during oracle disagreement

9.3. Fee Bounds

  • Units: 0.0001% precision (B=1,000,000)
  • Example: f(min)=100 (0.01%), f(max)=50000 (5%)
  • Purpose: Prevent extreme spreads (max) and free-option attacks (min)

10. Multi-Hop Fee Aggregation

10.1. Path Structure

For swap A → B through intermediate hops:

A -> X_1 -> X_2 -> ... -> B

10.2. Signal Aggregation

Signal Aggregation Rationale
σp max(σi) across legs Conservative uncertainty
Δp max(Δi) across legs Conservative deviation
$nu$ $max$ (endpoints only) Risk at edges
λ $max$ (endpoints only) Risk at edges
f(min) $max$ (all legs) Strictest floor
f(max) $max$ (all legs) Strictest ceiling

10.3. Edge vs Intermediate Pricing

  • Edge hops (first/last): Full price impact via spline traversal
  • Intermediate hops: Mid-price only (no impact accumulation)

11. Implementation Reference

Key functions in LibPricing.sol:

  • _calculatePathSpreadCached(): Spread calculation with caching
  • splitFee(): Protocol/LP fee division

12. Economic Benefits

12.1. For Liquidity Providers

Symmetrical Fee Earnings:

  • Earn fees in both tokens proportionally
  • No concentration risk from one-sided fees
  • Better portfolio balance maintenance

Coverage Protection:

  • Fees retained in reserves improve coverage
  • Higher coverage → better LP protection
  • Lower withdrawal haircuts

12.2. For Traders

Fair Pricing:

  • Spread reflects actual market conditions (volatility + deviation)
  • Coverage-improving trades get better prices (arb-friendly)
  • Coverage-worsening trades pay fair premium during uncertainty

Predictable Costs:

  • Bounded fees prevent extreme spreads
  • Transparent market-aware model
  • No hidden LVR extraction

13. Flash Loan Fees

13.1. Base Fee

Fixed percentage of borrowed amount:

ϕ(flash)=(x⋅f(flash))B

where f(flash) = flash fee in bps.

13.2. Parameters

Parameter Type Default Description
flashFeeBps uint16 90 0.009% flash loan fee

14. Related Documentation

  • Inventory Management — Coverage impact calculation
  • Internal Oracle — σ and Δ computation
  • Liquidity Shaping — Spline-based depth
  • Parametrization — Complete parameter reference

15. References

  • Empirical spread-volatility linearity: Relation between Bid-Ask Spread, Impact and Volatility
  • Multi-timeframe uncertainty: Volatility, Information Feedback and Market Microstructure Noise
  • Inventory-aware pricing: Inventory Risk and Market Making

1.1.8-invariants.title: 1.1.8. Invariants
1.1.8-invariants.html:
AIMM Invariants

System-wide constraints that must hold for pool safety and correctness

1. Overview

This document specifies the invariants that AIMM enforces. These constraints are critical for:

  • Testing: Fuzzing and formal verification
  • Auditing: Security review checkpoints
  • Monitoring: Runtime anomaly detection
  • Simulator alignment: Ensuring off-chain models match on-chain behavior

2. Core Accounting Invariants

2.1. Reserve-Liability Relationship

Invariant: Reserves and liabilities are non-negative and bounded.

Ri≥0∧Li≥0  ∀i∈assets

Invariant: Total reserves equal sum of individual reserves.

∑iRi=R(total)

2.2. LP Token Conservation

Invariant: LP tokens minted equal liabilities outstanding.

LPi(total)=Li  ∀i∈assets

Invariant: No LP tokens created without corresponding liability.

ΔLP>0⇒ΔL>0

2.3. Fee Conservation

Invariant: Fees are always non-negative.

ϕ(in)≥0∧ϕ(out)≥0

Invariant: Total fees never exceed trade amounts.

ϕ(in)≤x2∧ϕ(out)≤y2

3. Coverage Invariants

3.1. Coverage Definition

Invariant: Coverage is well-defined when liabilities are positive.

ci=RiLi  where  Li>0

3.2. Deposit Coverage Improvement

Invariant: Deposits always improve or maintain coverage.

For deposit of amount a:

c′=(R+a)(L+a)≥c=RL  when  c≤1

Proof:

(R+a)(L+a)≥RL
⇒(R+a)⋅L≥R⋅(L+a)
⇒aL≥aR
⇒L≥R  (c≤1)  □

3.3. Donation Coverage Improvement

Invariant: Donations strictly improve coverage.

c′=(R+a)L>RL=c

3.4. Withdrawal Coverage Impact

Invariant: Withdrawals at full coverage maintain coverage.

When c=1:

c′=(R−a)(L−a)=1=c

Invariant: Withdrawals below full coverage may worsen coverage (haircut applied).

4. Pricing Invariants

4.1. Mid-Price Bounds

Invariant: Mid-price is bounded by oracle price and skew limits.

pm=po⋅(1+ψ106)
WHERE
ψ ∈[−100 times104,+100 times104](i.e., -100% to +100%)

4.2. Spread Bounds

Invariant: Spread is always within configured bounds.

f(min)≤S≤f(max)

Invariant: Spread components are non-negative.

Sv≥100  ∧  U≥0

4.3. Price Impact Monotonicity

Invariant: Price impact is monotonic in trade size.

a1<a2⇒|(impact(a1))|≤|(impact(a2))|

Larger trades always have equal or greater price impact.

4.4. Reservation Price Floor

Invariant: Trade must not push price below reservation price.

For each asset i with reservation price p(res,i) (vs its anchor):

pi(after)≥p(res,i)

Implementation (CoreV1.sol:565-578):

function _checkReservationPrice(
    IPoolV1.PoolStorage storage $,
    address token,
    IPoolV1.Asset storage asset
) private {
    uint64 reservationPrice = asset.reservationPrice;
    if (reservationPrice == 0) return; // No floor configured
 
    IOracleV1.FeedData memory feed = _readOracle($, token);
    if (feed.lastPriceB64 < reservationPrice) {
        revert IErrors.PriceBelowReservation(feed.lastPriceB64, reservationPrice);
    }
}

Purpose:

  • Prevents flash crashes from large trades
  • Protects against oracle manipulation attacks
  • Ensures minimum liquidity depth at critical price levels
  • Acts as circuit breaker for extreme market conditions

Configuration: Each asset defines reservationPrice in B64 format (price vs anchor). Set to 0 to disable.

4.5. Minimum Liquidity Floor

Invariant: Reserves cannot fall below minimum liquidity.

Ri≥L(min,i)  ∀i∈assets

Implementation (CoreV1.sol:552-554, FlashV1.sol:43):

// In swap execution
if (assetOut.reserves < assetOut.minLiquidity) {
    revert IErrors.InsufficientAmount(assetOut.reserves, assetOut.minLiquidity);
}
 
// In flash loan
if (asset.reserves < amount || asset.reserves - amount < asset.minLiquidity) {
    revert IErrors.InsufficientAmount(asset.reserves, amount);
}

Purpose:

  • Prevents complete liquidity drain attacks
  • Ensures minimum depth for price discovery
  • Protects against dust attacks
  • Maintains market functionality during extreme events

Configuration: Each asset defines minLiquidity as uint128 in raw token units.

5. Anchor Tree Invariants

5.1. Tree Structure

Invariant: Anchor graph is a tree (connected, acyclic).

anchor[root]=0  ∧  ∀i≠root:anchor[i]≠0

Invariant: No cycles exist.

∀i:path(i→root) terminates

5.2. Depth Bounds

Invariant: Maximum tree depth is 4.

d(i)≤4  ∀i∈assets

5.3. Path Length Bounds

Invariant: Maximum path length between any two assets is 6.

ell(t(in),t(out))≤6

This follows from ell(max)=2⋅d(max)−2=6 for depth-4 tree.

5.4. LCA Correctness

Invariant: LCA exists for any two assets.

∀(i,j)∈assets:∃LCA(i,j)

6. Oracle Invariants

6.1. Price Non-Zero

Invariant: Oracle prices are strictly positive.

po>0  ∀ configured feeds

6.2. TWAP Window Ordering

Invariant: Fast window shorter than slow window.

Wf<Ws   (300<3600)

6.3. Volatility Bounds

Invariant: Volatility EMAs are bounded.

0≤σ≤σ(max)=100,000,000  (10,000%)

6.4. Same-Block Rejection

Invariant: Oracle updates rejected within same block.

t=t(last)⇒skip update

7. Flow Guard Invariants

7.1. Reentrancy Protection

Invariant: No recursive calls allowed.

g=1⇒revert

7.2. JIT Cooldown

Invariant: Operations require minimum time since last action.

t−t(last)[user][asset]≥τ

8. Spline Invariants

8.1. Knot Ordering

Invariant: Spline knots are strictly increasing.

x0<x1<x2<x3<x4<x5

8.2. Non-Negative Depth

Invariant: Liquidity depth is non-negative.

yi≥0  ∀i∈[0,5]

8.3. Normalized Utilization

Invariant: Utilization stays in [0, 1].

0 <= u <= 1

9. State Transition Invariants

9.1. Swap State Changes

Invariant: Swap only modifies edge asset reserves.

For swap through path [A, X_1, ..., X_n, B]:

ΔRA≠0∧ΔRB≠0∧ΔR(Xi)=0

Invariant: Swap conserves value (modulo fees).

R(in)⋅p(in)+ϕ≈R(out)⋅p(out)

9.2. Deposit State Changes

Invariant: Deposit increases both reserves and liabilities.

ΔR>0∧ΔL>0

9.3. Withdraw State Changes

Invariant: Withdraw decreases both reserves and liabilities.

ΔR<0∧ΔL<0

10. Economic Invariants

10.1. No Free Lunch

Invariant: Arbitrage-free within transaction (excluding external markets).

No sequence of swaps within AIMM yields profit without external price difference.

10.2. LP Solvency

Invariant: Total LP claims never exceed reserves at full coverage.

∑iLi⋅pi≤∑iRi⋅pi  when  c≥1

10.3. Haircut Effectiveness

Invariant: Haircut prevents coverage deterioration during bank runs.

If all LPs withdraw simultaneously:

Rf≥0  ∧  Lf=0

11. Parameter Invariants

11.1. Fee Parameter Bounds

Parameter Type Min Max
minFeeBps uint16 0 65,535
maxFeeBps uint16 0 65,535
vega uint16 0 65,535
lambda uint16 0 65,535
gamma uint16 0 65,535

Invariant: minFeeBps <= maxFeeBps

11.2. Liquidity & Coverage Parameter Bounds

Parameter Type Min Max Description
minLiquidity uint128 0 2^128-1 Minimum reserves floor (raw token units)
reservationPrice uint64 0 2^64-1 Price floor vs anchor (B64 format, 0=disabled)
haircutSuppressor uint16 0 65,535 Withdrawal haircut dampener
decayHalfLifeSeconds uint32 1 2^32-1 Liability decay period

11.3. Oracle Parameter Bounds

Parameter Type Min Max
ttl uint16 0 65,535
confidence uint8 0 100

12. Invariant Verification

12.1. Compile-Time

Solidity type bounds enforce parameter constraints.

12.2. Runtime Checks

// Price floor check
require(priceAfter >= asset.reservationPrice, "PriceBelowReservation");
 
// Spread bounds
spreadBps = clamp(rawSpread, minFeeBps, maxFeeBps);
 
// Coverage check
require(coverage > 0, "ZeroCoverage");

12.3. Fuzzing Targets

// Invariant: coverage monotonic on deposit
function invariant_depositImprovesCoverage() external {
    uint256 coverageBefore = getCoverage(token);
    deposit(token, amount);
    uint256 coverageAfter = getCoverage(token);
    assert(coverageAfter >= coverageBefore || coverageBefore > 1e18);
}
 
// Invariant: no LP token inflation
function invariant_lpConservation() external {
    uint256 totalLP = getTotalLP(token);
    uint256 liabilities = getLiabilities(token);
    assert(totalLP == liabilities);
}
 
// Invariant: price above reservation
function invariant_priceAboveReservation() external {
    uint256 price = getPrice(token);
    uint256 reservation = getReservationPrice(token);
    assert(price >= reservation);
}
 
// Invariant: reserves above minLiquidity
function invariant_reservesAboveMinLiquidity() external {
    uint256 reserves = getReserves(token);
    uint256 minLiq = getMinLiquidity(token);
    assert(reserves >= minLiq);
}
 
// Invariant: fee bounds respected
function invariant_feeBounds() external {
    (uint16 minFee, uint16 maxFee) = getFeeBounds(token);
    assert(minFee <= maxFee);
}

13. Related Documentation

  • Inventory Management — Coverage formulas
  • Liquidity Shaping — Spline constraints
  • Spread & Fees — Fee bounds
  • Parametrization — Parameter ranges
  • Flow Guards — Guard invariants

1.3.1-composability.title: 1.3.1. Composability
1.3.1-composability.html:
Composability

Standard interfaces and integration patterns for external protocols to interact with AIMM pools

1. Overview

Composability enables external protocols, applications, and users to seamlessly integrate with AIMM pools through standardized interfaces. Rather than forking code or maintaining custom adaptations, external developers use:

  • Public pool interfaces: Standardized function signatures for swaps, liquidity provision, staking
  • ERC standards: ERC-20 (tokens), ERC-3156 (flash loans), ERC-7201 (storage layout)
  • Modular architecture: Swap any combination of tokens, query prices, execute flash loans
  • SDK integration: TypeScript utilities for quote calculation, transaction building, reward tracking

Key principle: AIMM prioritizes open interfaces over walled-garden integrations.

2. Core Integration Patterns

2.1. Token Swaps

Interface: ICoreV1 (module selector 0xb4e0c84b)

Function:

function swap(
    address tokenIn,
    address tokenOut,
    uint256 amountIn,
    uint256 minAmountOut,
    address recipient
) external payable returns (uint256 amountOut);

Integration flow:

  1. Quote calculation:

    • Call getSwapQuote(tokenIn, tokenOut, amountIn) (read-only)
    • Returns spread, fees, oracle prices, skew impact
    • Calculate minAmountOut = quote.amountOut × (1 - slippageBps / 10000)

  2. Token approval:

    • If swapping non-native token: approve(pool, amountIn)
    • If swapping native (ETH): Send via msg.value

  3. Execute swap:

    • Call pool.swap() with recipient address
    • Pool route: Swap module → Oracle update → Fee distribution
    • Emits: SwapExecuted(tokenIn, tokenOut, amountIn, amountOut)

  4. Slippage protection:

    • Revert if amountOut < minAmountOut
    • Typical slippage: 0.1% - 1% depending on swap size

SDK helper (sdk/src/flows/swap.ts):

const quote = await pool.getSwapQuote(tokenIn, tokenOut, amountIn);
const minOut = quote.amountOut * BigInt(9999n) / BigInt(10000n);  // 0.01% slippage
const tx = await pool.swap(tokenIn, tokenOut, amountIn, minOut, recipient);

Common use cases:

  • DEX aggregators (1inch, 0x) routing through AIMM
  • Liquidation bots swapping collateral for repayment assets
  • Rebalancing protocols maintaining portfolio ratios
  • Bridge contracts (LayerZero) swapping received assets

2.2. Liquidity Provision

Interface: ICoreV1 (module selector 0xb4e0c84b)

Functions:

Deposit:

function deposit(
    address token,
    uint256 amount
) external payable returns (DepositResult memory);
 
struct DepositResult {
    uint256 lpAmount;      // LP tokens minted
    uint256 actualDeposit; // Amount actually deposited (post-slippage)
}

Withdrawal:

function withdraw(
    address token,
    uint256 lpAmount,
    uint256 minAmountOut
) external returns (WithdrawResult memory);
 
struct WithdrawResult {
    uint256 amountOut;     // Underlying tokens received
    uint256 lpBurned;      // LP tokens burned
}

Integration flow:

  1. Approve LP token (if withdrawing):

    • Not needed for deposit (tokens only)
    • For withdrawal: lpToken.approve(pool, lpAmount)

  2. Deposit flow:

    • Check coverage ratio before deposit (ALM constraint)
    • Approve token: token.approve(pool, amount)
    • Call pool.deposit(token, amount)
    • Receive LP tokens for deposited assets
    • Can immediately stake LP tokens for emissions

  3. Withdrawal flow:

    • Check if LP tokens exist: lpBalance = lpToken.balanceOf(user)
    • Call pool.withdraw(token, lpAmount, minAmountOut)
    • Receive underlying asset (may include haircut if coverage < 100%)

  4. Haircut mechanism:

    • Applied only when coverage ratio < 100%
    • Protects remaining LPs during undercollateralization
    • See Inventory Management §5 for formula and examples

SDK helper (sdk/src/flows/deposit.ts):

// Deposit
const result = await pool.deposit(token, amount);
console.log(`Received ${result.lpAmount} LP tokens`);
 
// Withdraw
const result = await pool.withdraw(token, lpAmount, minExpected);
console.log(`Withdrew ${result.amountOut} tokens`);

Common use cases:

  • Protocol-owned liquidity (treasury deploying LP positions)
  • Liquidity aggregators balancing across multiple pools
  • Yield farming protocols earning LP emissions
  • Market makers providing liquidity for trading incentives

2.3. Liquidity Staking (Emissions Eligibility)

Interface: IStakingV1 (standalone module)

Functions:

function stakeLP(
    address lpToken,
    uint256 amount
) external;
 
function unstakeLP(
    address lpToken,
    uint256 amount
) external;
 
function claimLiquidityTokenUnstaked(
    address lpToken
) external;

Integration flow:

  1. Obtain LP token:

    • Deposit into pool → receive LP token (1:1 per pool)
    • Can also acquire LP tokens from other sources (trades, transfers)

  2. Stake LP tokens:

    • Approve staking module: lpToken.approve(stakingModule, amount)
    • Call stakingModule.stakeLP(lpToken, amount)
    • Receive receipt token (sLP): sLP.balanceOf(user) increases
    • Voting power: sLP holdings contribute to governance voting power

  3. Earn emissions:

    • 90% of total emissions distributed pro-rata to LP stakers
    • Per-asset earnings depend on: (tvl_asset / total_tvl) × (coverage_weight) × (utilization_weight)
    • Claim rewards anytime via: distributor.claim()
    • Rewards accumulate using O(1) accumulator pattern

  4. Unstake flow:

    • Call stakingModule.unstakeLP(lpToken, amount)
    • Triggers 2-week cooldown (prevents flash-loan voting attacks)
    • After cooldown: claimLiquidityTokenUnstaked(lpToken) to withdraw LP tokens

Key constraints:

  • Minimum lock: 14 days before LP tokens can be fully withdrawn
  • Flow guard: Protection against Just-In-Time liquidity attacks
  • Voting snapshot: LP stake counted at governance snapshot block only

SDK helper (sdk/src/rewards/):

// Stake LP tokens
await stakingModule.stakeLP(lpToken, amount);
 
// Claim rewards
const earned = await distributor.claim();
 
// Unstake (2-week wait)
await stakingModule.unstakeLP(lpToken, amount);
// After 14 days...
await stakingModule.claimLiquidityTokenUnstaked(lpToken);

Common use cases:

  • LP incentive farming (earn BTR for providing liquidity)
  • Governance participation (sLP holders have voting power)
  • Liquidity mining campaigns (highest earning pool per period)
  • Strategic capital positioning (earn emissions while maintaining voting power)

2.4. Governance Token Staking

Interface: IStakingV1 (standalone module)

Functions:

function stakeGov(uint256 amount) external;
 
function unstakeGov(uint256 amount) external;
 
function delegateVoting(address to) external;

Integration flow:

  1. Stake BTR:

    • Approve treasury: btToken.approve(stakingModule, amount)
    • Call stakingModule.stakeGov(amount)
    • Receive sBTR (staked BTR) 1:1
    • Voting power = sBTR × btPrice / 1e18 (scaled by govMultiplier, subject to quadratic damping)

  2. Delegate voting power:

    • Call sBTR.delegate(delegatee) or stakingModule.delegateVoting(delegatee)
    • Voting power transfers to delegatee at next snapshot block
    • Revoke: delegatee.delegate(address(0)) to self-delegate

  3. Earn staking rewards:

    • 5% of total emissions allocated to BTR stakers
    • Pro-rata distribution: rewards = (sBTR_balance / total_sBTR) × annual_emissions
    • Claim: stakingModule.claim() or governance dashboard

  4. Unstake flow:

    • Call stakingModule.unstakeGov(amount)
    • Immediate withdrawal (no cooldown for governance token)
    • sBTR burned, BTR transferred to user

Key constraints:

  • Self-delegation required: Must call delegate(self) to enable voting power (ERC-20 Votes pattern)
  • Snapshot voting: Voting power calculated at snapshot block height
  • No unstake cooldown: Unlike LP staking, BTR unstaking immediate

SDK helper (sdk/src/rewards/voting-power.ts):

// Stake
await stakingModule.stakeGov(amount);
 
// Delegate
await sBTR.delegate(delegatee);
 
// Claim rewards
await stakingModule.claim();
 
// Voting power calculation (off-chain)
const votingPower = await computeVotingPower({
  sBTR: userBalance,
  sLP: userLPBalances,
  btPrice, lpPrices,
  applyDamping: true
});

Common use cases:

  • Governance participation (stake BTR, earn voting power)
  • Protocol alignment (stakers earn 5% of emissions)
  • Delegation to governance organizations (stake, delegate to council)
  • Multi-sig treasury management (treasury stakes BTR, delegates to Counsel)

2.5. Flash Loans

Standard: ERC-3156 (IERC3156FlashLender)

Interface: IFlashV1 (module selector 0xb6205b86)

Functions:

function flashLoan(
    IERC3156FlashBorrower receiver,
    address token,
    uint256 amount,
    bytes calldata data
) external returns (bytes32);
 
function maxFlashLoan(address token)
    external view returns (uint256);
 
function flashFee(address token, uint256 amount)
    external view returns (uint256);
 
// Receiver contract must implement:
interface IERC3156FlashBorrower {
    function onFlashLoan(
        address initiator,
        address token,
        uint256 amount,
        uint256 fee,
        bytes calldata data
    ) external returns (bytes32);
}

Integration flow:

  1. Create flash loan receiver:

    contract MyFlashReceiver is IERC3156FlashBorrower {
    IERC3156FlashLender pool = IERC3156FlashLender(...);
 
    function executeFlashLoan(address token, uint256 amount) external {
        bytes memory data = abi.encode(msg.sender, token, amount);
        pool.flashLoan(this, token, amount, data);
    }
 
    function onFlashLoan(
        address initiator,
        address token,
        uint256 amount,
        uint256 fee,
        bytes calldata data
    ) external override returns (bytes32) {
        // Now have 'amount' of 'token' in contract
        // Execute any logic (swap, arbitrage, liquidation, etc.)
 
        // Must repay: amount + fee
        IERC20(token).transfer(msg.sender, amount + fee);
 
        return keccak256("ERC3156FlashBorrower.onFlashLoan");
    }
}

  2. Query flash loan parameters:

    • maxFlashLoan(token) → Maximum amount available for borrowing
    • flashFee(token, amount) → Borrowing fee in basis points (90 bps = 0.09%)

  3. Execute flash loan:

    • Initiate via pool.flashLoan(receiver, token, amount, data)
    • Pool transfers tokens to receiver contract
    • Receiver executes arbitrary logic in onFlashLoan()
    • Must repay in same transaction: token.transfer(pool, amount + fee)
    • Transaction reverts if repayment fails

Fee calculation:

  • Flat fee: fee = amount × flashFeeBps / 10000
  • Current: 0.009% (90 basis points per year annualized)
  • Treasury receives 25%, LP emission pool receives 75%

Common use cases:

  • Arbitrage: Borrow assets, execute profitable trades, repay from profits
  • Liquidations: Liquidator borrows repayment token, pays penalty fee, retains spread
  • Collateral swaps: Swap collateral types without external capital
  • Yield farming: Borrow to temporarily increase LP position, repay from earned fees
  • Oracle manipulation tests: Security teams testing oracle resilience

SDK helper (sdk/src/flows/):

// Create receiver contract (Solidity)
const receiverAddress = await deployFlashLoanReceiver();
 
// Execute flash loan
const fee = await pool.flashFee(token, amount);
const tx = await pool.flashLoan(
    receiverAddress,
    token,
    amount,
    abi.encode({ arbitrageData })
);

3. Advanced Integration Patterns

3.1. Liability Swaps (Hedging)

Function: swapLiability(address tokenIn, address tokenOut, uint256 lpAmountIn, uint256 minLpAmountOut)

Use case: Liquidity providers hedging directional exposure while maintaining LP position.

Example:

  • LP has 100 LP-tokens for ETH/USDC pool (50 ETH equivalent, 50 USDC equivalent)
  • Expects ETH to fall, wants to reduce ETH exposure
  • Executes liability swap: Sell ETH liabilities, buy USDC liabilities
  • Result: LP position becomes more USDC-heavy (reduced ETH risk)

3.2. Protocol-Owned Liquidity (POL)

Pattern: Treasury deposits assets, receives LP tokens, stakes for emissions.

// Treasury flow
1. treasury.approve(pool, 1M_USDC);
2. (lpAmount,) = pool.deposit(USDC, 1M_USDC);
3. stakingModule.stakeLP(lpToken, lpAmount);
4. // Now earning 90% of pool emissions
5. // LP fees auto-compounded in treasury

Benefits:

  • Treasury earns trading fees
  • Provides baseline liquidity
  • Eligible for full emission rewards
  • Can be unwound if needed for operations

3.3. Cross-Pool Routing

Pattern: Swap routes through multiple pools if single pool lacks depth.

Example: ETH → DAI may route ETH → USDC (Pool A) → DAI (Pool B)

Implementation:

  • Quote system returns routeHops and hopAmounts
  • SDK aggregates best route
  • Pool interface handles multi-hop execution (via modules or caller orchestration)

3.4. Reward Distribution Integration

Contract: IDistributorV1

Campaign types:

  1. Points campaigns: Issue non-transferable SBT tokens (achievement tracking)
  2. Token campaigns: Distribute actual ERC-20 rewards

Integration pattern:

// Create campaign (governance-approved)
uint256 campaignId = distributor.createTokenCampaign(
    rewardToken, // e.g., BTR
    manager      // Who updates merkle roots
);
 
// Manager periodically updates reward snapshots
distributor.updateCampaignRoot(
    campaignId,
    merkleRoot,
    updatedAt,
    totalClaimable
);
 
// Users claim via merkle proof
distributor.claimCampaign(
    campaignId,
    index,
    address,
    totalEarned,
    merkleProof
);

Common use cases:

  • Incentive campaigns (e.g., "earn 1M BTR for $10M TVL")
  • Airdrop distribution (merkle tree of allocations)
  • Governance rewards (voting participation bonuses)

4. SDK Integration Examples

4.1. Complete Swap Example

import { Pool } from 'sdk/src/flows';
 
const pool = new Pool(poolAddress);
 
// Get quote
const quote = await pool.getSwapQuote(
    token(USDC),
    token(ETH),
    parseUnits('1000', 6)
);
 
console.log(`Spread: ${quote.spreadBps} bps`);
console.log(`Amount out: ${quote.amountOut}`);
 
// Calculate slippage
const slippage = 50; // 0.5%
const minOut = quote.amountOut * (10000n - BigInt(slippage)) / 10000n;
 
// Execute
const tx = await pool.swap(
    token(USDC),
    token(ETH),
    parseUnits('1000', 6),
    minOut,
    userAddress
);
 
const receipt = await tx.wait();
console.log(`Swapped successfully in block ${receipt.blockNumber}`);

4.2. Complete Deposit & Stake Example

import { Pool, Staking } from 'sdk/src/flows';
 
const pool = new Pool(poolAddress);
const staking = new Staking(stakingModuleAddress);
 
// Deposit
const depositTx = await pool.deposit(
    token(ETH),
    parseEther('10')
);
const depositReceipt = await depositTx.wait();
const lpTokens = await lpToken.balanceOf(userAddress);
 
// Stake LP for emissions
const stakeTx = await staking.stakeLP(
    lpToken.address,
    lpTokens
);
await stakeTx.wait();
 
// Now eligible to earn LP emissions
const earned = await staking.getPendingRewards(userAddress);
console.log(`Earning BTR: ${earned}`);

4.3. Flash Loan Example

import { FlashLoanReceiver } from 'sdk/src/flows';
 
const receiver = new FlashLoanReceiver(poolAddress);
 
// Execute arbitrage
const result = await receiver.executeFlashLoan({
    token: USDC,
    amount: parseUnits('100000', 6),
    arbData: {
        buyPool: poolA,
        sellPool: poolB,
    }
});
 
console.log(`Profit: ${result.profit} USDC`);

5. Safety & Best Practices

5.1. Slippage Protection

Always specify minimum output:

// ✅ Safe: Revert if output too low
swap(tokenIn, tokenOut, amountIn, minAmountOut, recipient);
 
// ❌ Unsafe: Accept any output
swap(tokenIn, tokenOut, amountIn, 0, recipient);

Recommended slippage bounds:

  • Small swaps (< $10k): 0.05% - 0.1%
  • Medium swaps ($10k - $100k): 0.1% - 0.5%
  • Large swaps (> $100k): 0.5% - 2%+

5.2. Flash Loan Safety

Always verify flash loan callback:

function onFlashLoan(
    address initiator,
    address token,
    uint256 amount,
    uint256 fee,
    bytes calldata data
) external override {
    require(msg.sender == address(pool), "Untrusted pool");
    // Execute logic
    require(
        IERC20(token).balanceOf(address(this)) >= amount + fee,
        "Insufficient repayment"
    );
    IERC20(token).transfer(msg.sender, amount + fee);
}

5.3. Staking Cooldowns

Respect 2-week LP unstaking delay:

// Day 1: Initiate unstake
stakingModule.unstakeLP(lpToken, amount);
 
// Day 15: Can now claim
stakingModule.claimLiquidityTokenUnstaked(lpToken);

Don't assume immediate liquidity.

5.4. Voting Power Snapshots

Voting power is frozen at snapshot block:

// Snapshot block set during proposal creation
// e.g., block 18500000
 
// These counts:
await sBTR.transfer(user, 100); // Before snapshot
 
// These don't:
await sBTR.transfer(user, 100); // After snapshot

Flash loans won't work for voting attacks due to snapshot finality.

6. Code References

6.1. Core Pool Interface

File: contracts/src/interfaces/IPoolV1.sol

Key structs:

  • Asset — Inventory, liabilities, pricing parameters
  • SwapQuote — Quote output with fees and impact
  • DepositResult / WithdrawResult — Transaction outcomes
  • RiskConfig — Per-asset risk parameters

6.2. Staking Interface

File: contracts/src/interfaces/modules/IStakingV1.sol

Functions:

  • stakeGov(amount) — Stake BTR
  • stakeLP(lpToken, amount) — Stake LP
  • unstakeGov(amount) / unstakeLP(lpToken, amount) — Initiate unstake
  • delegate(address) — Delegate voting power

6.3. Flash Loan Interface

File: contracts/src/interfaces/modules/IFlashV1.sol

ERC-3156 compliant:

  • flashLoan(receiver, token, amount, data)
  • maxFlashLoan(token)
  • flashFee(token, amount)

6.4. SDK

Location: sdk/src/

Key modules:

  • flows/swap.ts — Swap execution
  • flows/deposit.ts — Liquidity provision
  • flows/flash.ts — Flash loan receiver
  • rewards/voting-power.ts — Voting power calculation
  • oracles/base-oracle.ts — Price feed integration

7. Related Documentation

  • [Architecture Overview](../../1. AIMM/1.1. Architecture.md) — Pool structure and module design
  • [Swap & Fees](../../1. AIMM/1.2. Pricing/1.2.4. Spread & Fees.md) — Fee mechanics
  • [Emissions Control](../../2. Governance/2.6. Emission Control.md) — Reward distribution
  • [Liquid Staking](../../2. Governance/2.5. Liquid Staking.md) — Staking mechanics

References

  • ERC-20: Token Standard
  • ERC-7201: Namespaced Storage Layout

1.3.3-curation-white-labelling.title: 1.3.3. Curation & White Labelling
1.3.3-curation-white-labelling.html:
Curation & White Labelling

Custom pool deployment, token curation, and white-label integration for protocols and operators

1. Overview

Pool curation in AIMM enables any protocol, exchange, or operator to:

  • Deploy custom pools with their own token lists, pricing curves, and risk parameters
  • Manage pool ownership via timelock governance (protect against rash decisions)
  • Add/remove tokens dynamically using an asset request + execute pattern
  • Extend functionality by deploying custom hook contracts for specialized logic
  • Implement modules as diamond-pattern facets for unlimited extensibility
  • White-label the entire pool proxy as their own branded interface

Key principle: AIMM is fully permissionless — anyone can deploy, no central approval needed. We welcome interested teams to reach out for strategic partnerships.

2. Pool Ownership & Control

2.1. Pool Deployment

Any address can deploy a new PoolProxyV1 instance:

// Step 1: Deploy proxy (no initialization)
PoolProxyV1 pool = new PoolProxyV1();
// - Immutably sets msg.sender as DEPLOYER
// - Prevents initialization front-running
// - Each deployment is independent (no factory registry)
 
// Step 2: Initialize with base config
pool.initialize(
    owner,           // Who controls the pool
    baseToken,       // Anchor token (e.g., USDC, USDT)
    wnative,         // Wrapped native asset (WETH, WAVAX, etc.)
    FeeParams(...)   // Protocol fee configuration
);
// - Only DEPLOYER can call (prevents hijacking)
// - owner becomes the pool administrator

Access control:

  • Deployer: Can only initialize once
  • Owner: Controls all administrative functions (add assets, set hooks, freeze assets)
  • Timelock: Protects major changes (1-7 day delays)
  • Users: Can deposit, withdraw, swap freely (subject to pool settings)

2.2. Ownership Model

Action Authority Timelock Notes
Freeze/unfreeze asset Owner None Emergency powers, immediate effect
Set pricing anchor Owner None Adjust pricing tree topology
Set flow cooldown Owner None Configure JIT protection (0-256 sec)
Add asset Owner 1 day Request → wait → execute pattern
Update risk config Owner 1 day Change per-asset risk parameters
Register module Owner 3 days Add new functionality (swap, flash, etc.)
Transfer ownership Owner 3 days Handoff to new operator
Migrate base token Owner 7 days Change anchor (critical, rarely done)

3. Token Curation

3.1. Adding Tokens (Asset Manager Pattern)

Two-phase process (prevents configuration mistakes):

Phase 1: Request asset addition

pool.requestAddAsset(
    address token,                      // ERC-20 token address
    IPoolV1.OracleConfig calldata cfg,  // Price feed configuration
    IPoolV1.RiskConfig calldata risk,   // Risk parameters
    IPoolV1.LiquidityProfile calldata profile,  // Liquidity distribution
    uint16 minFeeBps,                   // Minimum swap fee (0.01% = 1 basis point)
    uint8 decimals,                     // Token decimals (6, 8, 18, etc.)
    uint64 initialPrice,                // Starting price in B64 format
    uint32 initialFastVolEMA,           // Fast volatility estimate
    uint32 initialSlowVolEMA            // Slow volatility estimate
);

Phase 2: Execute after 1-day timelock

vm.warp(block.timestamp + 1 days);  // Wait 1 day
pool.executeAddAsset(token);

3.2. Oracle Configuration

Three oracle modes:

Mode Primary Secondary Use Case
Internal Pool's TWAP None Stablecoins (USDC, USDT), most tokens
External Chainlink/Pyth Pool TWAP fallback Exotic assets, price feeds unavailable internally
Hybrid Fallback chain Pool TWAP Maximum safety for critical assets

Configuration struct:

struct OracleConfig {
    address primary;            // Primary feed (address(pool) = internal TWAP)
    address secondary;          // Fallback (address(0) = none)
    bytes32 feedId;            // Oracle identifier (Pyth feed ID, etc.)
    uint16 modeFlags;          // Oracle mode bits
    uint8 accDecimals;         // B64 accumulator precision (6-18)
}

Precision selection (accDecimals):

  • 6 decimals: Stablecoins (USDC, USDT, USDS) - price change: $0.000001
  • 8 decimals: Natural assets (LINK, UNI) - price change: $0.00000001
  • 12 decimals: ETH/major assets - price change: $0.000000000001
  • 18 decimals: Exotics with extreme volatility - maximum precision

3.3. Risk Configuration

struct RiskConfig {
    uint16 decayStartRatioBps;     // Coverage ratio to activate decay (e.g., 9800 = 98%)
    uint16 coverageFloor;          // Critical safety floor (e.g., 5000 = 50%)
    uint32 decaySlope;             // Liability decay rate per year (%)
    uint16 depthAmplifier;         // Depth curve sensitivity (higher = steeper)
    uint16 flags;                  // Feature enablement
}

Coverage-based logic:

  • 100%+ coverage: No penalties, optimal pricing
  • 98-100%: Decay activates, withdrawal haircuts begin (encourages rebalancing)
  • 50% floor: Critical; swaps may be disabled if breached

Flags:

SWAP_ENABLED          = 0x0002    // Allow swaps for this asset
LIABILITY_SWAP_ENABLED = 0x0004   // Allow liability swaps
FLASH_ENABLED         = 0x0010    // Include in flash loan pool
FROZEN                = 0x0001    // Emergency freeze (owner only)

3.4. Liquidity Profile (Distribution Curve)

Segment-based distribution for customizable price impact:

struct LiquidityProfile {
    uint8[16] weights;       // Relative depths per segment (sum = 200 = 100%)
    int8[17] knots;          // Price offset knots (weights.length + 1 points)
}
 
// Example: Concentrated (like Uniswap v4 concentrated liquidity)
weights = [100, 50, 20, 10, 0, ...];     // Front-loaded (4 segments)
knots = [-50, -25, 0, 25, 50, ...];      // 5 knots for 4 segments, narrow range
 
// Example: Uniform (like Uniswap v3 full range)
weights = [50, 50, 50, 50, 0, ...];      // Balanced (4 segments)
knots = [-50, -25, 0, 25, 50, ...];      // 5 knots for 4 segments, wide range

Impact on pricing:

  • Concentrated profiles: Lower slippage near mid-price, higher on extremes
  • Uniform profiles: Consistent slippage across range
  • Custom profiles: Tailor to expected trading patterns (stablecoin vs. exotic)

3.5. Token Removal (Freeze vs. Deletion)

Freeze token (temporary):

pool.freezeAsset(token);   // Disable swaps, deposits allowed for cleanup
pool.unfreezeAsset(token); // Re-enable

Permanent removal: Not supported (prevents liquidity loss). Instead:

  • Owner should freeze the asset
  • Allow users to withdraw LP positions over time
  • Migrate to new pool if needed

4. Custom Hooks

4.1. Hook Interfaces

Hook system enables per-asset, per-event callbacks similar to Uniswap v4 and Balancer V3's implementations.

interface IPoolHooks {
    // Lifecycle
    function preInitialize(address pool, address owner, address baseToken, address wnative) external;
    function postInitialize(address pool, address owner, address baseToken, address wnative) external;
 
    // Deposit/Withdrawal
    function preDeposit(address pool, address sender, address token, uint256 amountIn) external;
    function postDeposit(address pool, address sender, address token, uint256 amountIn, uint256 lpMinted)
        external returns (uint256 hookFeeOut, uint256 hookIncentiveOut);
 
    function preWithdraw(address pool, address sender, address token, uint256 lpAmount) external;
    function postWithdraw(address pool, address sender, address token, uint256 amountOutGross, uint256 lpBurned)
        external returns (uint256 exitFee, uint256 incentiveOut);
 
    // Swaps (called for both input and output asset)
    function preSwap(address pool, address sender, address tokenIn, address tokenOut,
                     uint256 amountIn, uint256 amountOutQuoted)
        external returns (uint256 extraFeeOut, uint16 newFeeBps);
    function postSwap(address pool, address sender, address tokenIn, address tokenOut,
                      uint256 amountIn, uint256 amountOutFinal)
        external returns (int256 hookDeltaOut);
 
    // Donations
    function preDonate(address pool, address sender, address token, uint256 amount) external;
    function postDonate(address pool, address sender, address token, uint256 amount) external;
 
    // Flash Loans
    function preFlashLoan(address pool, address initiator, address token, uint256 amount, uint256 fee, bytes calldata data) external;
    function postFlashLoan(address pool, address initiator, address token, uint256 amount, uint256 fee, bytes calldata data) external;
 
    // Flags indicating which hooks are implemented
    function hookFlags() external pure returns (uint32);
}

4.2. Hook Examples

Example 1: Fee Boost on Deposits

contract DepositBonusHook is IPoolHooks {
    function postDeposit(
        address pool, address sender, address token,
        uint256 amountIn, uint256 lpMinted
    ) external override returns (uint256 hookFeeOut, uint256 hookIncentiveOut) {
        // Give 1% bonus to depositors
        hookIncentiveOut = (lpMinted * 100) / 10000;
        return (0, hookIncentiveOut);
    }
 
    function hookFlags() external pure override returns (uint32) {
        return (1 << 3);  // HOOK_POST_DEPOSIT only
    }
}

Example 2: Withdrawal Tax

contract WithdrawalTaxHook is IPoolHooks {
    function postWithdraw(
        address pool, address sender, address token,
        uint256 amountOutGross, uint256 lpBurned
    ) external override returns (uint256 exitFee, uint256 incentiveOut) {
        // 2% withdrawal fee to treasury
        exitFee = (amountOutGross * 200) / 10000;
        return (exitFee, 0);
    }
 
    function hookFlags() external pure override returns (uint32) {
        return (1 << 5);  // HOOK_POST_WITHDRAW only
    }
}

Example 3: Dynamic Swap Fees Based on Volatility

contract DynamicFeeHook is IPoolHooks {
    function preSwap(
        address pool, address sender, address tokenIn, address tokenOut,
        uint256 amountIn, uint256 amountOutQuoted
    ) external override returns (uint256 extraFeeOut, uint16 newFeeBps) {
        // Get volatility, scale fee accordingly
        uint256 vol = IPoolV1(pool).getVolatility(tokenIn);
 
        if (vol > 10000) {  // High vol
            newFeeBps = 100;  // 1% fee
        } else {
            newFeeBps = 20;   // 0.2% fee
        }
        return (0, newFeeBps);
    }
 
    function hookFlags() external pure override returns (uint32) {
        return (1 << 6);  // HOOK_PRE_SWAP only
    }
}

4.3. Installing Hooks

// Owner sets custom hook for specific token
pool.setHook(token, address(customHookContract));
 
// Hook is called automatically on relevant events
// No additional integration needed from users

5. Custom Modules (Diamond-Lite Extensibility)

5.1. Module System Architecture

AIMM uses EIP-2535 Diamond pattern lite — a lightweight function selector registry:

// Each PoolProxyV1 has a module registry:
mapping(bytes4 selector => address implementation) modules;
 
// When any function is called:
fallback() external payable {
    address impl = modules[msg.sig];
    assembly {
        delegatecall(gas(), impl, ...)  // Delegate to module
    }
}

Benefits:

  • Modular code (each function family in separate contract)
  • Upgradeable (swap implementations without redeployment)
  • Composable (combine features freely)
  • Efficient (minimal proxy overhead)

5.2. Pre-Built Modules

Module Functions Status
CoreV1 swap(), deposit(), withdraw(), swapLiability(), donate() ✅ Core
AdminV1 Asset management, risk config, timelock ✅ Core
InternalOracleV1 TWAP tracking, price feeds ✅ Core
FlashV1 ERC-3156 flash loans ✅ Core
StakingV1 LP/Gov token staking ✅ Core
DistributorV1 Reward distribution ✅ Core
RescueV1 Emergency asset recovery ✅ Core
LendV1 Lending/borrowing 🔜 Future
AMMv2 Advanced AMM mechanics 🔜 Future

5.3. Implementing Custom Modules

Custom module example (MarketMaker incentives):

interface IMarketMakerV1 {
    function claimMakerRewards(address token) external returns (uint256 amount);
    function getMakerAPY(address token) external view returns (uint256);
}
 
contract MarketMakerV1 is IMarketMakerV1 {
    using LibStorage for LibStorage.Layout;
 
    function claimMakerRewards(address token) external override returns (uint256 amount) {
        LibStorage.Layout storage $ = LibStorage.load();
        // Custom logic: reward market makers for tighter spreads
        amount = $.makerRewards[msg.sender][token];
        $.makerRewards[msg.sender][token] = 0;
        IERC20(token).transfer(msg.sender, amount);
    }
 
    function getMakerAPY(address token) external view override returns (uint256) {
        // Return APY based on participation
    }
}

Registering custom module:

// Owner requests registration
pool.requestModuleUpdate(
    address(customModule),
    [IMarketMakerV1.claimMakerRewards.selector, IMarketMakerV1.getMakerAPY.selector],
    initData  // Optional initialization
);
 
// Wait 3 days
vm.warp(block.timestamp + 3 days);
 
// Execute
pool.executeModuleUpdate();
 
// Now available as:
IMarketMakerV1(address(pool)).claimMakerRewards(token);

6. White-Labelling

6.1. Pool as Branded Interface

No fork required. Simply:

  1. Deploy pool proxy with your configuration
  2. Add your tokens (proprietary or curated list)
  3. Install custom hooks for your branding (deposit bonuses, withdrawal taxes, etc.)
  4. Host your own UI connecting to the pool address
  5. Market as your own exchange (with BTR branding attribution)

6.2. Frontend Integration

// Your app's pool client (generic, works with any AIMM pool)
const pool = new PoolClient(poolAddress);
 
// Swap
const quote = await pool.getSwapQuote(tokenIn, tokenOut, amount);
const tx = await pool.swap(tokenIn, tokenOut, amount, minOut);
 
// Provide liquidity
const depositTx = await pool.deposit(token, amount);
const lpTokens = await pool.getLPBalance(token);
 
// Stake for emissions
const stakeModule = new StakingClient(stakingAddress);
const stakeTx = await stakeModule.stakeLP(lpToken, amount);

No backend complexity — all logic is on-chain and self-contained.

6.3. Branding & Attribution

When white-labelling, we ask that:

  • Credit AIMM: Mention "Powered by AIMM" or similar in UI/docs
  • Link to docs: Direct interested users to official documentation
  • Maintain security: Don't modify pool logic (use hooks/modules instead)
  • Keep open: Don't create artificial barriers to token lists

6.4. Strategic Partnerships

For major integrations (large exchanges, ecosystem plays), reach out to the team:

  • Custom oracle configurations for exotic assets
  • Dedicated module development (faster than DIY)
  • Multi-pool coordination across chains
  • Enhanced security audits for your instance

7. Complete Deployment Walkthrough

Example: Stablecoin Exchange Deployment

// 1. Deploy pool
PoolProxyV1 pool = new PoolProxyV1();
 
// 2. Initialize
pool.initialize(
    owner,  // My exchange address
    USDC,   // Anchor token
    WETH,   // Native wrapper
    FeeParams(25, 5, ...)  // 25% protocol fee, 0.005% flash fee
);
 
// 3. Register core modules (swap, deposit, oracle, etc.)
bytes4[] memory selectors = [
    0x1234abcd,  // swap selector
    0x5678efgh,  // deposit selector
    // ... etc
];
pool.requestModuleUpdate(address(coreModule), selectors, "");
vm.warp(block.timestamp + 3 days);
pool.executeModuleUpdate();
 
// 4. Add stablecoins
pool.requestAddAsset(
    USDC,
    OracleConfig(address(pool), address(0), 0, 0, 6),
    RiskConfig(9800, 5000, 31709791, 10000, SWAP_ENABLED),
    LiquidityProfile(...),  // Uniform distribution
    10,  // 0.1% min fee
    6,   // 6 decimals
    encodeB64(1e6),  // $1.00
    10000,  // volatility
    10000
);
vm.warp(block.timestamp + 1 days);
pool.executeAddAsset(USDC);
 
// Similar for USDT, USDS, etc.
 
// 5. Deploy custom hook: 0.5% deposit bonus
DepositBonusHook hook = new DepositBonusHook(500);  // 5 bps bonus
pool.setHook(USDC, address(hook));
 
// 6. Deploy your UI pointing to pool address
// Frontend is now fully operational!

8. Security Considerations

8.1. Timelock Protection

All major changes are timelocked to allow users to exit if governance is compromised:

  • 1-day delay (low risk): Asset additions, risk config updates
  • 3-day delay (medium risk): Module registration, ownership transfers
  • 7-day delay (critical): Base token migration

Example: If owner proposes adding a malicious token, users have 1 day to withdraw before it takes effect.

8.2. Access Control

  • Owner only: Freeze assets, add tokens, register modules
  • No owner transfer without notice: 3-day timelock prevents hijacking
  • No user impact: Users can always deposit/withdraw/swap (no owner powers here)

8.3. Hook Safety

  • Hooks can return arbitrary values, but cannot access other tokens (isolated execution)
  • Hook failures revert transactions (prevent orphaned rewards)
  • Owner can disable hooks anytime

9. Code References

9.1. Pool Proxy

File: contracts/src/PoolProxyV1.sol

Functions:

  • initialize(owner, baseToken, wnative, feeParams) — One-time setup
  • fallback() — Module selector routing

9.2. Asset Management

  • executeAddAsset() — Finalize token addition

9.3. Hook Interface

12 lifecycle hooks covering deposits, withdrawals, swaps, donations, flash loans.

9.4. Module Examples

  • StakingV1.sol — LP/Gov staking
  • FlashV1.sol — ERC-3156 flash loans
