1.3.4-bridging.title: 1.3.4. Bridging
1.3.4-bridging.html:
Cross-Chain Bridging

1. Overview

The protocol implements cross-chain bridging for BTR governance tokens (staked and unstaked) and eligible LP tokens using the ERC-7802 standard. Despite using LayerZero V2 in its current state, the bridge is designed to be messaging-protocol agnostic to support alternatives on upgrade (eg. Chainlink CCIP, Axelar GMP...).

2. Architecture

2.1. Components

  1. Bridge Contract (contracts/src/Bridge.sol)

    • Standalone contract (not a pool module)
    • Implements LayerZero V2 OApp pattern
    • Manages token burn/mint on source/destination
    • Enforces daily rate limits per token

  2. ERC-7802 Tokens

    • BTR, sBTR, and LP tokens implement IERC7802
    • Provides crosschainBurn() and crosschainMint() functions
    • Bridge has minter/burner roles

  3. LayerZero Integration

    • Uses LayerZero V2 endpoint
    • Peer-to-peer bridge configuration
    • Native gas payment for cross-chain messages

3. Technical Details

3.1. Bridge Flow

3.1.1. Outbound (Source Chain)

  1. Initiate Bridge

    bridge.bridgeViaLayerZero(token, dstEid, receiver, amount, options)

  2. Limit Check

    • Check daily outbound limit (B64-encoded)
    • Verify token is supported and not paused
    • Reset counters if new day

  3. Burn Tokens

    IERC7802(token).crosschainBurn(user, amount, metadata)

  4. Send Message

    • Encode: (receiver, token, amount)
    • Send via LayerZero with exact native fee
    • Emit Bridged event with nonce

3.1.2. Inbound (Destination Chain)

  1. Receive Message

    • LayerZero calls lzReceive()
    • Verify sender is trusted peer

  2. Limit Check

    • Check daily inbound limit (percentage of outbound limit)
    • Reset counters if new day

  3. Mint Tokens

    IERC7802(token).crosschainMint(recipient, amount, metadata)

  4. Emit Event

    • Log bridging with direction flag

3.2. Rate Limiting

The bridge uses B64 float encoding for gas-efficient daily limits:

struct TokenConfig {
    uint64 limitOutB64;     // B64-encoded daily outbound limit
    uint64 bridgedOutB64;   // B64-encoded outbound volume today
    uint64 bridgedInB64;    // B64-encoded inbound volume today
    uint16 day;             // Day index for resets
    uint8  inRatio;         // Inbound limit ratio (% of outbound)
    uint8  flags;           // SUPPORTED | PAUSED | UNLIMITED
}

Daily Limits:

  • Outbound: Absolute limit per token
  • Inbound: Percentage of outbound (e.g., 120% = inRatio: 120)
  • Reset: Automatically at UTC midnight

Special Cases:

  • UNLIMITED flag: No limits enforced
  • Missing config: Reverts with TokenNotSupported

3.3. Fee Quoting

// Get exact native fee required
ILayerZeroEndpointV2.MessagingFee memory fee = bridge.quoteLZBridge(
    token,
    dstEid,
    amount,
    options
);
 
// Send with exact payment
bridge.bridgeViaLayerZero{value: fee.nativeFee}(...);

Note: Transaction reverts if msg.value != fee.nativeFee (exact payment required).

4. Configuration

4.1. Token Setup

Initial configuration (no timelock):

bridge.setTokenConfig(
    token,
    1_000_000e18,  // 1M daily limit (raw)
    18,            // decimals
    120,           // 120% inbound ratio
    false          // not unlimited
);

4.2. Updating Configuration

Changes require 2-day timelock:

// Request update
bridge.requestConfigChange(
    token,
    2_000_000e18,  // New limit
    18,            // decimals
    150,           // New inbound ratio
    true,          // updateLimit
    true           // updateRatio
);
 
// Execute after 2 days
bridge.executeConfigChange(token);

4.3. Peer Configuration

Setting LayerZero peers requires 2-day timelock:

// Request peer setup
bridge.requestSetPeer(
    110,  // Arbitrum endpoint ID
    bytes32(uint256(uint160(arbBridgeAddress)))
);
 
// Execute after timelock
bridge.executeSetPeer(110);

5. Emergency Controls

5.1. Token Pause (Instant)

Bridge owner can instantly pause bridging for a token:

bridge.pauseToken(token, true);  // Pause
bridge.pauseToken(token, false); // Unpause

Effect: Prevents both inbound and outbound bridging immediately.

5.2. Cancel Pending Operations

bytes32 opId = keccak256(abi.encode(OpType.ConfigUpdate, token));
bridge.cancelOperation(opId);

6. Governance & Access Control

6.1. Bridge Owner

  • Initial: DAO Council multisig (3-of-5 at launch)
  • Long-term: Elected DAO council
  • Powers:
    • Configure token bridging parameters
    • Set LayerZero peer addresses
    • Pause/unpause tokens (emergency)
    • Rescue stuck tokens
    • Migrate to new bridge infrastructure

6.2. Timelocks

Operation Delay Bypass
Token config change 2 days No
Set peer address 2 days No
Pause token None N/A
Unpause token None N/A
Rescue tokens None No

Grace Period: 3 days after timelock expires

7. Security Features

7.1. Trusted Peers

  • Each chain has exactly one trusted peer bridge
  • Inbound messages verified against peers[srcEid]
  • Prevents unauthorized minting

7.2. Rate Limits

  • Daily limits prevent catastrophic loss
  • Separate inbound/outbound tracking
  • B64 encoding prevents manipulation
  • Automatic daily reset

7.3. Reentrancy Protection

  • All external functions use nonReentrant
  • Prevents callback exploits

7.4. Balance Verification

  • Outbound: Burn before send
  • Inbound: Verify peer before mint
  • No intermediate custody

8. Monitoring

8.1. Events

event Bridged(
    address indexed user,
    address indexed token,
    uint32 indexed dstEid,
    bytes32 receiver,
    uint256 amount,
    uint64 nonce,
    Direction dir
);
 
event TokenConfigured(address indexed token, uint64 limit, uint8 inRatio, uint8 flags);
event PeerSet(uint32 indexed eid, bytes32 peer);
event TokenPaused(address indexed token, bool paused);

8.2. Queries

// Check if token is bridgeable
bool canBridge = bridge.isBridgeable(token);
 
// Get remaining limits
(uint256 outbound, uint256 inbound) = bridge.getRemainingLimits(token);
 
// Get peer for chain
bytes32 peer = bridge.peers[arbitrumEid);

9. Integration Examples

9.1. Basic Bridging

// Quote fee
ILayerZeroEndpointV2.MessagingFee memory fee = bridge.quoteLZBridge(
    BTR_TOKEN,
    ARBITRUM_EID,
    1000e18,
    "" // default options
);
 
// Approve bridge to burn
IERC20(BTR_TOKEN).approve(address(bridge), 1000e18);
 
// Bridge tokens
bridge.bridgeViaLayerZero{value: fee.nativeFee}(
    BTR_TOKEN,
    ARBITRUM_EID,
    bytes32(uint256(uint160(recipientAddress))),
    1000e18,
    "" // default options
);

9.2. Custom LayerZero Options

// Increase gas limit for destination execution
bytes memory options = abi.encodePacked(
    uint16(3),  // option type
    uint128(300000)  // gas limit
);
 
bridge.bridgeViaLayerZero{value: fee.nativeFee}(
    token,
    dstEid,
    receiver,
    amount,
    options
);

10. Supported Chains (Launch)

Chain Endpoint ID Status
Ethereum 101 Planned
Arbitrum 110 Planned
Optimism 111 Planned
Base 184 Planned

Note: Actual deployment depends on DAO governance decisions.

11. Bridgeable Assets

At launch, the following assets are bridgeable:

  1. BTR: Unstaked governance token
  2. sBTR: Staked governance token
  3. LP Tokens: Marked with BRIDGEABLE_BIT in risk config

Pool curators can enable bridging for their LP tokens via:

riskConfig.flags |= BRIDGEABLE_BIT;

12. Migration Strategy

The bridge architecture supports migration to alternative bridges:

12.1. Adding New Bridge

  1. Deploy new bridge contract
  2. Grant mint/burn permissions to new bridge
  3. Configure rate limits
  4. Announce migration timeline
  5. Disable old bridge after grace period

12.2. Supported Bridge Standards

  • LayerZero V2 (current)
  • Hyperlane (future)
  • Wormhole (future)
  • Axelar (future)

Bridge owner can add/remove bridge addresses via timelocked operations on token contracts.

13. Best Practices

13.1. For Users

  • Always quote fees before bridging
  • Use sufficient gas limits for complex operations
  • Verify destination address format (bytes32)
  • Check daily limits before large transfers
  • Monitor LayerZero message status

13.2. For Integrators

  • Handle LayerZero delivery failures
  • Implement retry logic for failed messages
  • Cache fee quotes (valid for ~5 minutes)
  • Support manual message execution via LayerZero scan
  • Display estimated delivery time (5-30 minutes)

13.3. For Pool Operators

  • Enable bridging only for liquid LP tokens
  • Set conservative daily limits initially
  • Monitor bridge activity via events
  • Coordinate with bridge owner for config changes

14. Error Handling

Error Cause Solution
TokenNotSupported Token not configured Add via setTokenConfig()
BridgePaused Token paused Wait for unpause
DailyLimitExceeded Over daily limit Wait for daily reset or request limit increase
ExactPaymentRequired Wrong msg.value Use quoted fee exactly
PeerNotConfigured Destination chain not set Configure peer via requestSetPeer()
UnauthorizedOrigin Message from untrusted peer Contact DAO council

15. Future Enhancements

  • Multi-bridge aggregation (route selection)
  • Cross-chain governance (vote from any chain)
  • Liquidity incentives for bridge providers
  • Insurance fund for bridge failures
  • Automatic relayer fee estimation
  • Batched bridging for gas savings

1.2.6-flash.title: 1.2.6. Flash
1.2.6-flash.html:
Flash Loans

1. Overview

The protocol implements ERC-3156 compliant flash loans, allowing users to borrow any supported asset for the duration of a single transaction without collateral.

2. Architecture

2.1. Implementation

Flash loan functionality is implemented in the Flash module (contracts/src/modules/Flash.sol), which is deployed as a separate contract and delegated to by the main pool proxy.

2.2. Key Features

  • ERC-3156 Compliance: Standard interface for maximum compatibility
  • Multi-Asset Support: Flash loans available on any enabled asset
  • Configurable Fees: Pool-wide flash loan fee in basis points
  • Protocol Revenue: Fees split between LPs and protocol treasury
  • Hook Integration: Pre/post flash loan hooks for custom logic
  • Liquidity Constraints: Respects minimum liquidity requirements

3. Technical Details

3.1. Flash Loan Flow

  1. Validation

    • Check asset is flash-enabled (FLASH_ENABLED_BIT)
    • Check asset is not frozen (FROZEN_BIT)
    • Verify sufficient reserves after minimum liquidity

  2. Pre-Flash Hook (Optional)

    preFlashLoan(pool, borrower, token, amount, fee, data)

  3. Loan Execution

    • Transfer amount to borrower
    • Call borrower's postFlashLoan() callback
    • Verify ERC-3156 magic value returned

  4. Repayment Verification

    • Check balance increased by amount + fee
    • Update reserves (excluding protocol fee)
    • Accumulate protocol fees

  5. Post-Flash Hook (Optional)

    postFlashLoan(pool, borrower, token, amount, fee, data)

3.2. Fee Structure

fee = (amount * flashFeeBps) / 1_000_000
protocolFee = (fee * protoShare) / 100
lpFee = fee - protocolFee
  • flashFeeBps: Pool-wide parameter (e.g., 500 = 0.05%)
  • protoShare: Percentage to protocol (e.g., 20 = 20%)
  • LP fee increases reserves, protocol fee collected separately

3.3. Security Features

  • Reentrancy Protection: nonReentrant modifier on flashLoan()
  • Balance Verification: Strict check on repayment amount
  • Callback Validation: ERC-3156 magic value must be returned
  • Decay Application: Liability decay applied before loan
  • Atomic Execution: All operations within single transaction

4. Usage Examples

4.1. Basic Flash Loan

contract Arbitrageur is IERC3156FlashBorrower {
    bytes32 constant CALLBACK_SUCCESS = keccak256("ERC3156FlashBorrower.postFlashLoan");
 
    function executeArbitrage(address pool, address token, uint256 amount) external {
        bytes memory data = abi.encode(msg.sender);
        IERC3156FlashLender(pool).flashLoan(this, token, amount, data);
    }
 
    function postFlashLoan(
        address initiator,
        address token,
        uint256 amount,
        uint256 fee,
        bytes calldata data
    ) external returns (bytes32) {
        // Perform arbitrage logic
        // ...
 
        // Approve repayment
        IERC20(token).approve(msg.sender, amount + fee);
 
        return CALLBACK_SUCCESS;
    }
}

4.2. Query Available Liquidity

// Check maximum flash loan available
uint256 maxLoan = pool.maxFlashLoan(USDC);
 
// Calculate fee for specific amount
uint256 fee = pool.flashFee(USDC, 1_000_000e6); // 1M USDC

5. Configuration

5.1. Enabling Flash Loans

Pool owner must enable flash loans per asset via risk configuration:

// Request flash loan enable (1 day timelock)
pool.requestUpdateRiskConfig(token, riskConfig);
 
// After timelock expires
pool.executeUpdateRiskConfig(token);

RiskConfig flags:

riskConfig.flags |= FLASH_ENABLED_BIT;  // Enable flash loans

5.2. Fee Parameters

Flash loan fees are pool-wide and subject to 1-day timelock:

// Request fee update
pool.requestUpdateFeeParams(IPool.FeeParams({
    protoShare: 20,      // 20% to protocol
    flashFeeBps: 500     // 0.05% flash loan fee
}));
 
// Execute after timelock
pool.executeUpdateFeeParams();

6. Emergency Controls

6.1. Asset Freeze

Pool owner can instantly disable flash loans by freezing an asset (no timelock):

pool.freezeAsset(token);  // Disables all operations including flash loans

6.2. Minimum Liquidity

Reserves below minLiquidity cannot be flash loaned, protecting against liquidity drain attacks.

7. Gas Optimization

  • Single storage slot for reserves update
  • Minimal balance checks (before/after)
  • Efficient fee calculation with no divisions in hot path
  • Hook calls only when configured

8. Events

event FlashLoanExecuted(
    address indexed borrower,
    address indexed receiver,
    address indexed token,
    uint256 amount,
    uint256 fee
);

9. Error Handling

Error Trigger
FlashDisabled(token) Flash loans not enabled for asset
AssetFrozen(token) Asset is frozen
ZeroAmount() Requested amount is 0
InsufficientReserves() Not enough liquidity after minLiquidity
FlashLoanCallbackFailed() Callback didn't return magic value or insufficient repayment

10. Integration Notes

10.1. For Borrowers

  1. Implement IERC3156FlashBorrower interface
  2. Return correct magic value from postFlashLoan()
  3. Ensure sufficient approval for repayment
  4. Account for fees in arbitrage/liquidation logic

10.2. For Pool Operators

  1. Enable flash loans via risk config (requires timelock)
  2. Set appropriate fee parameters
  3. Monitor flash loan activity via events
  4. Consider minimum liquidity requirements

11. Best Practices

  • Test thoroughly: Flash loan failures can be expensive
  • Check maxFlashLoan(): Before attempting large loans
  • Account for slippage: In arbitrage calculations
  • Handle native assets: Use WETH internally, NATIVE for user-facing
  • Consider gas costs: Flash loan fee + gas must be profitable

1.2.7-rescue.title: 1.2.7. Rescue
1.2.7-rescue.html:
Rescue Module

Emergency asset recovery and vulnerability response procedures

1. Overview

Rescue Module (RescueV1) provides emergency asset recovery when critical vulnerabilities or exploits compromise a pool. Rather than losing assets, the pool owner can:

  • Freeze assets instantly to prevent further trading
  • Recover stuck assets (ERC-20, ERC-721, ERC-1155) via timelock
  • Pause operations across all pools if critical infrastructure fails
  • Update core parameters (oracles, modules) to patch vulnerabilities

Key principle: Speed vs. safety tradeoff:

  • Immediate freezes (seconds): Stop the bleeding
  • Timelocked recovery (2-7 days): Allow community exit before drastic action

2. Emergency Asset Freezing

For freeze mechanism details, see Admin Module §2.

In rescue context, freezing is the first response to suspected exploits:

  1. freezeAsset(token) — Immediate, blocks all operations
  2. Investigate root cause (1-2 hours)
  3. If false alarm: unfreezeAsset(token)
  4. If real issue: proceed to requestRescue()

3. Asset Recovery (Timelock Protected)

3.1. Recovery Flow

Two-phase process (prevents recovery mistakes):

Phase 1: Request (Owner-only)

pool.requestRescue(
    TokenType rescueType,           // ERC20, NATIVE, ERC721, ERC1155
    address token,                  // Token to recover
    uint256[] calldata tokenIds,    // For NFTs: which IDs to recover
    address receiver                // Where to send recovered assets
);
  • Snapshots current balance of asset
  • Stores request with all parameters
  • Timelock starts: 4 days delay
  • Emits RescueRequested event

Phase 2: Execute (Anyone can execute after timelock)

// Wait 4 days (RESCUE_TIMELOCK)
pool.executeRescue(
    address receiver,
    TokenType rescueType
);
  • Validates timelock has passed
  • Executes recovery per token type
  • Cleans up pending data
  • Emits RescueExecuted event

3.2. Token Type Support

Type Method Example Limits
ERC20 rescueToken() Recover stuck USDC Safe transfer, amount capped
Native ETH rescueAll() Recover stuck ETH Balance snapshot
ERC721 rescueERC721Batch() Recover NFTs Best-effort, skips unowned
ERC1155 rescueERC1155Batch() Recover multi-tokens Best-effort, only non-zero

3.3. Safety Features

Balance Snapshot Protection:

// At request time:
uint256 snapshotBalance = IERC20(token).balanceOf(address(pool));
 
// At execute time:
uint256 currentBalance = IERC20(token).balanceOf(address(pool));
 
// Recover only up to snapshot (prevent over-recovery):
uint256 rescueAmount = min(requestedAmount, snapshotBalance);

Best-Effort Batch Processing (for NFTs):

// Even if some token IDs are missing/not owned,
// rescue succeeds for owned tokens
for (uint256 i = 0; i < tokenIds.length; i++) {
    if (IERC721(token).ownerOf(tokenIds[i]) == address(pool)) {
        IERC721(token).transferFrom(address(pool), receiver, tokenIds[i]);
    }
    // Skip unowned tokens, continue
}

3.4. Complete Recovery Example

Scenario: Pool receives airdrop of random NFTs, one has vulnerability

// 1. Identify problematic NFT (ID 12345 has reentrancy bug)
pool.freezeAsset(problematicNFT);  // Immediate freeze
 
// 2. Request recovery of all NFTs (except 12345)
uint256[] memory tokenIds = [1, 2, 3, ... 12344, 12346, ...];
pool.requestRescue(
    TokenType.ERC721,
    problematicNFT,
    tokenIds,
    recoveryAddress  // Multi-sig treasury
);
 
// 3. Wait 4 days + announce to community
 
// 4. Execute recovery
pool.executeRescue(recoveryAddress, TokenType.ERC721);
 
// 5. All safe NFTs transferred to treasury
// 6. Problematic NFT remains frozen until further action

4. Vulnerability Response Procedures

4.1. Quick Reference: What to Do

Issue Time Action Result
Oracle price exploit Seconds freezeAsset() Block trading, no loss
Stuck tokens 4+ days requestRescue() → execute Recover assets
Oracle misconfiguration 2+ days requestOracleUpdate() → execute Fix pricing
Module bug 3+ days requestModuleUpdate() → execute Patch code
Reentrancy in hook Seconds setHook(token, address(0)) Remove hook

4.2. Scenario: Pool Hacked via Flash Loan Reentrancy

T=0: Attack Detected

// Attacker exploited flash loan hook callback
// Drained $2M from pool reserves
 
// Immediate action:
pool.freezeAsset(ETH);    // Stop further ETH trading
pool.freezeAsset(USDC);   // Stop stablecoin pair
 
// Emit emergency alert to community

T=1 hour: Root Cause Analysis

Vulnerability: Hook allows reentrancy into swap
Impact: Attacker called swap() from within hook callback
Solution: Upgrade hook implementation (or remove hook)

T=2 hours: Patch Deployment

// Deploy patched hook with reentrancy guard:
PatchedHookV1 patchedHook = new PatchedHookV1();
 
// Register via module update timelock (3 days)
pool.requestModuleUpdate(
    address(patchedHook),
    [IHook.preSwap.selector, ...],  // Replace unsafe selectors
    initData
);

T=3 days: Execute Patch + Recovery

// Execute patched module
pool.executeModuleUpdate();
 
// Now recover stuck assets
pool.requestRescue(TokenType.ERC20, USDC, recipient);

T=7 days: Assets Recovered

// Execute recovery
pool.executeRescue(recipient, TokenType.ERC20);
 
// USDC transferred to multi-sig treasury
// Investigation can continue offline
// Pool reopens with patched modules

5. Timelocks Across Systems

5.1. Timelock Hierarchy

Action Timelock Grace Period Authority Notes
freezeAsset() None N/A Owner Immediate emergency
unfreezeAsset() None N/A Owner Immediate restoration
requestRescue() 4 days 3 days Owner Assets in limbo 4-7 days
Oracle update 2 days 7 days Owner Price feed fixes
Module update 3 days 7 days Owner Code patches
Ownership transfer 3 days 7 days Owner New admin
Base token migration 7 days 7 days Owner Critical change

5.2. Grace Period Explanation

After timelock expires, there's a grace period (typically 7 days) to execute:

// Validation logic in LibTimelock:
function validate(uint96 packed) internal view {
    uint48 executeAt = uint48(packed >> 48);  // When to start
    uint48 grace = uint48(packed);             // How long to execute
 
    if (block.timestamp < executeAt)
        revert NotReady();  // Too early
 
    if (block.timestamp > executeAt + grace)
        revert Expired();   // Too late (grace period passed)
}

Why grace periods?

  • Prevent execution immediately after timelock (allow exit)
  • But also prevent indefinite pending state (force action)
  • Typical window: 7 days to execute before revert

6. Community Coordination

6.1. Emergency Communication

When freeze/rescue is activated:

  1. Emit on-chain event:

    event RescueRequested(
    TokenType indexed rescueType,
    address indexed token,
    address indexed receiver,
    uint256 snapshotBalance,
    uint256 executeAt
);

  2. Announce to community:

    • Twitter/Discord: Explain vulnerability
    • Technical summary: Root cause analysis
    • Recovery plan: Timeline and expected outcome

  3. Allow user exit:

    • During 4-day rescue delay, users can still unstake LP
    • Frozen assets can be withdrawn via rescue
    • Governance voting continues

6.2. Transparency

Available Info:

  • Current frozen assets (on-chain state)
  • Pending rescues (query pending data)
  • Historical freezes (event logs)
  • Recovery execution (transaction receipts)

No hidden operations — all actions logged on-chain.

7. Code References

7.1. Rescue Module

File: contracts/src/modules/RescueV1.sol

Key functions:

  • requestRescue(TokenType, token, tokenIds, receiver) — Queue 4-day recovery
  • executeRescue(receiver, rescueType) — Execute after timelock
  • getRescueInfo(receiver) — View pending rescue status

7.2. Admin Module (Freezing)

File: contracts/src/modules/AdminV1.sol

Key functions:

  • freezeAsset(token) — Instant emergency freeze
  • unfreezeAsset(token) — Restore asset
  • requestModuleUpdate() — Queue 3-day module patch
  • requestOracleUpdate() — Queue 2-day oracle fix

7.3. Recovery Library

File: contracts/src/libraries/LibRescue.sol

Implementations:

  • rescueToken() — ERC-20 safe transfer
  • rescueERC721Batch() — NFT batch recovery
  • rescueERC1155Batch() — Multi-token batch

7.4. Timelock Library

File: contracts/src/libraries/LibTimelock.sol

  • Compact storage of execute-at and grace times
  • Validation logic for timelock expiry
  • Used by all delayed operations

7.5. Constants

File: contracts/src/libraries/LibConstants.sol

Timelock values:

  • RESCUE_TIMELOCK = 4 days
  • HIGH_TIMELOCK = 3 days (module/ownership)
  • BASE_TIMELOCK = 2 days (oracle)
  • CRITICAL_TIMELOCK = 7 days (base token)
  • GRACE_PERIOD = 7 days (execution window)

8. Security Guarantees

8.1. What Rescue Does NOT Do

❌ Cannot steal user funds — Only recovers pool-owned assets (stuck tokens)

❌ Cannot modify LP balances — Only moves frozen assets

❌ Cannot be triggered by attacker — Owner-only + 4-day timelock

❌ Cannot be hidden — All on-chain, all events logged

8.2. What Rescue DOES Do

✅ Recovers stuck tokens — Assets accidentally sent to pool

✅ Recovers airdropped NFTs — Unsolicited ERC-721/1155

✅ Prevents exploitation — Fast freeze + slow recovery

✅ Maintains user trust — Transparent multi-sig authority

9. Governance Integration

9.1. Authority Model

Typical Setup (Production):

// Pool owner = Multisig (3-of-5 signers)
// Any 3 signers can:
// - Freeze assets (immediate)
// - Request rescue (initiate 4-day delay)
 
// Only multisig (via Snapshot vote) can:
// - Patch modules (3-day timelock)
// - Upgrade oracles (2-day timelock)
// - Transfer ownership (3-day timelock)

Community Override (V2 Future):

// Proposed governance evolution:
// - Freeze → Owner multisig (emergency)
// - Rescue → Governance vote (4 days) + multisig execute
// - Module patch → Governance vote (3 days) + execute
// - Ownership → Governance multisig transition

10. Related Documentation

  • [Curation & White Labelling](../1.4. Integration/1.4.3. Curation & White Labelling.md) — Asset freezing for maintenance
  • [Composability](../1.4. Integration/1.4.1. Composability.md) — How hooks can be vulnerable
  • [Architecture Overview](1.1. Architecture.md) — Module upgrade mechanism
  • [DAO Treasury](../../2. Governance/2.4. DAO Treasury.md) — Emergency treasury procedures

11. Getting Help

If vulnerability is discovered:

  1. Do NOT publicly disclose (gives attacker time to exploit)
  2. Contact team privately: security@example.com (or equivalent)
  3. Provide:
    • Vulnerability description
    • Attack vector
    • Potential impact
    • POC code (if safe)
  4. Expect:
    • Immediate pool freeze (if active exploitation)
    • 24-48 hour patch development
    • Transparent communication timeline
    • Potential bug bounty

References

  • ERC-20: Token Standard
  • ERC-721: NFT Standard
  • ERC-1155: Multi-Token Standard

1.2.4-staking.title: 1.2.4. Staking
1.2.4-staking.html:
Staking Module (StakingV1)

Governance token and LP token staking with voting power and reward boosting

1. Overview

The Staking module enables users to:

  • Stake BTR  Receive sBTR for voting and reward boosting
  • Stake LP tokens  Receive sLP for reward eligibility
  • Delegate voting power  Transfer voting rights without transferring tokens
  • Lock positions  Time-based lock for commitment signaling

2. Token Types

2.1. BTR (Governance Token)

  • Purpose: Protocol governance and reward multiplier
  • Supply: Fixed maximum (enforced by Treasury)
  • Staking: Lock BTR  Receive sBTR

2.2. sBTR (Staked BTR)

  • Purpose: Receipt token for staked BTR
  • Utility: Voting power + reward boosting
  • Non-transferable after cooldown: Prevents vote/reward renting

2.3. sLP (Staked LP)

  • Purpose: Receipt token for staked LP positions
  • Deployment: CREATE3 for deterministic addresses
  • Utility: Reward eligibility

3. Governance Token Staking

3.1. Stake BTR

function stakeGov(uint256 amount) external whenNotPaused

Flow:

  1. Transfer BTR from user to pool
  2. Mint sBTR 1:1 to user
  3. Update staking balances
  4. Set/extend unlock time

Effects:

  • govStaked[user] += amount
  • totalGovStaked += amount
  • govUnlockTime[user] = max(current, now + stakeLockDuration)

3.2. Unstake BTR

function unstakeGov(uint256 amount) external whenNotPaused

Requirements:

  • block.timestamp >= govUnlockTime[user]
  • amount <= govStaked[user]

Flow:

  1. Burn sBTR from user
  2. Transfer BTR to user
  3. Update staking balances

4. LP Token Staking

4.1. Configure Staking for LP Token

function updateStakingConfig(
    address lpToken,
    bytes32 salt
) external onlyOwner

Requirements:

  • LP token must be a pool asset
  • STAKEABLE_BIT flag must be set
  • Not already configured

Actions:

  1. Generate deterministic salt
  2. Deploy sLP token via CREATE3
  3. Register sLP address

4.2. Stake LP

function stakeLP(
    address lpToken,
    uint256 amount
) external whenNotPaused

Requirements:

  • sLP token deployed for this LP
  • STAKEABLE_BIT flag set
  • User has sufficient LP balance

Flow:

  1. Verify user LP balance
  2. Mint sLP to user
  3. Update staking balances
  4. Set/extend unlock time

Note: LP tokens remain in pool (not transferred). Staking is accounting-only.

4.3. Unstake LP

function unstakeLP(
    address lpToken,
    uint256 amount
) external whenNotPaused

Requirements:

  • block.timestamp >= lpUnlockTime[user][lpToken]
  • amount <= lpStaked[user][lpToken]

Flow:

  1. Burn sLP from user
  2. Update staking balances

5. Voting Power

5.1. Formula

V = (L × lpBase / 10000) + (min(boosted, boostCap × G) × lpBoosted / 10000) + (G × govMultiplier / 10000)
 
where:
  L = Total LP stake value
  G = Governance token stake
  boosted = LP that qualifies for boost
  boostCap = Max LP boost per $1 of gov stake

5.2. Configuration Parameters

struct StakingConfig {
    uint48 stakeLockDuration;   // Default 14 days
    uint48 transferCooldown;    // Cooldown after claim
    uint16 minClaimPower;       // Minimum claim multiplier (5000 = 50%)
    uint16 matchingRatio;       // BTR:LP matching ratio (500 = 5:1)
 
    uint16 lpBaseMultiplier;    // Base LP voting power (5000 = 0.5x)
    uint16 lpBoostedMultiplier; // Boosted LP voting power (5000 = 0.5x)
    uint16 govMultiplier;       // Gov token voting power (10000 = 1x)
    uint16 boostCap;            // Max LP boost per $1 BTR (50000 = 5x)
}

5.3. Example Calculation

User has:

  • 1000 LP tokens staked ($1000 value)
  • 100 BTR staked ($100 value)

With default config:

lpBase = 5000 (0.5x)
lpBoosted = 5000 (0.5x)
govMultiplier = 10000 (1x)
boostCap = 50000 (5x)
 
maxBoostedLP = 100 × 5 = $500
actualBoostedLP = min($1000, $500) = $500
unboostedLP = $1000 - $500 = $500
 
V = (500×0.5500 × 0.5) + ($100 × 1.0)
V = $250 + $250 + 100=600 voting power

6. Delegation

6.1. Delegate Voting Power

function delegateVoting(address to) external

Effects:

  • delegateOf[msg.sender] = to
  • Delegating to self clears delegation

Note: Off-chain snapshot systems read delegation mapping for vote counting.

6.2. Get Delegate

function getDelegateOf(address owner) external view returns (address)

Returns current delegate or address(0) if none.

7. Lock Mechanics

7.1. Stake Lock Duration

  • Default: 14 days (stakeLockDuration)
  • Effect: Cannot unstake until lock expires
  • Extending: New stakes extend lock to now + lockDuration

7.2. Transfer Cooldown

  • Purpose: Prevent sToken transfer immediately after claiming rewards
  • Duration: Configurable (transferCooldown)
  • Scope: Applies to sBTR and sLP transfers

8. Admin Functions

8.1. Pause/Unpause

function pause() external onlyOwner
function unpause() external onlyOwner

Emergency controls for staking operations.

8.2. Update Lock Duration

function requestStakeLockDurationUpdate(uint48 newLockDuration) external onlyOwner
function executeStakeLockDurationUpdate() external onlyOwner

Timelock: BASE_TIMELOCK (2 days)

9. View Functions

// Governance staking
function getStakedGov(address user) external view returns (uint256)
function getUnlockTime(address user, address(0)) external view returns (uint48)
 
// LP staking
function getStakedLP(address user, address lpToken) external view returns (uint256)
function getUnlockTime(address user, address lpToken) external view returns (uint48)
function getSLPToken(address lpToken) external view returns (address)
function getTotalLPStaked(address lpToken) external view returns (uint256)
 
// Generic
function getStakedBalance(address user, address underlying) external view returns (uint256)
function getTotalStaked(address underlying) external view returns (uint256)
function getDelegateOf(address owner) external view returns (address)

10. Storage Layout

10.1. ERC-7201 Namespace

bytes32 constant STAKING_STORAGE_LOC =
    keccak256("pool.storage.staking.v1") - 1;
 
struct StakingStorage {
    // Governance staking
    mapping(address => uint256) govStaked;
    mapping(address => uint48) govUnlockTime;
    uint256 totalGovStaked;
 
    // LP staking (sLP deployment)
    mapping(address lpToken => address sLP) sLPTokens;
    address[] lpTokens;
    mapping(address => mapping(address => uint48)) lpUnlockTime;
 
    // Delegation
    mapping(address => address) delegateOf;
}

10.2. Shared Storage (PoolStorage)

// Used by both Staking and Distributor
mapping(address user => mapping(address lpToken => uint256)) lpStaked;
mapping(address lpToken => uint256) totalLPStaked;

11. Events

// Governance staking
event GovStaked(address indexed user, uint256 amount, uint48 unlockTime);
event GovUnstaked(address indexed user, uint256 amount);
 
// LP staking
event StakingConfigured(address indexed lpToken, address indexed sLP, bytes32 salt);
event LPStaked(address indexed user, address indexed lpToken, uint256 amount, uint48 unlockTime);
event LPUnstaked(address indexed user, address indexed lpToken, uint256 amount);
 
// Delegation
event DelegateSet(address indexed owner, address indexed oldDelegate, address indexed newDelegate);
 
// Admin
event StakingPaused(address indexed caller);
event StakingUnpaused(address indexed caller);
event StakingConfigUpdateRequested(uint48 newLockDuration, uint48 executeAt);
event StakingConfigUpdated(uint48 newLockDuration);

12. Security Considerations

12.1. Sybil Resistance

  • Lock durations prevent quick stake/vote/unstake
  • Transfer cooldown prevents sToken farming

12.2. Economic Security

  • Boosting requires BTR commitment
  • LP staking is accounting-only (no transfer risk)

12.3. Emergency Controls

  • Pause functionality for incidents
  • Timelock for config changes

13. Integration Notes

13.1. For Reward Distributors

  • Read lpStaked and totalLPStaked from PoolStorage
  • Use govStaked for boost calculations
  • Check delegateOf for voting snapshots

13.2. For Governance Systems

  • Query voting power via view functions
  • Respect delegation mappings
  • Consider lock status for proposals

14. Related Documentation

  • Distributor Module  Reward distribution
  • Governance Overview  Full governance system
  • BTR Token  Governance token details

1.2.5-distributor.title: 1.2.5. Distributor
1.2.5-distributor.html:
Distributor Module (DistributorV1)

Campaign-based Merkle reward distribution with points and token support

1. Overview

The Distributor module handles protocol rewards through campaigns:

  • POINTS campaigns  Mint soulbound tokens (SBT) representing non-transferable points
  • TOKEN campaigns  Distribute ERC-20 tokens to eligible users
  • Merkle verification  Gas-efficient cumulative claims

2. Campaign Types

2.1. POINTS Campaign

Purpose: Track off-chain activity with on-chain representation Mechanism: Mint soulbound (non-transferable) tokens Redemption: Can be finalized for token redemption at set rate

Use cases:

  • Trading volume rewards
  • Participation incentives
  • Pre-token launch points

2.2. TOKEN Campaign

Purpose: Direct token distribution Mechanism: Transfer pre-funded tokens Requirement: Distributor must be pre-funded with reward tokens

Use cases:

  • LP incentives
  • Governance token distribution
  • Partner rewards

3. Campaign Lifecycle

3.1. Creation

Points Campaign:

function createPointsCampaign(
    string calldata name,
    string calldata symbol,
    address manager
) external onlyOwner returns (uint256 campaignId, address sbtToken)

Deploys a new SoulboundToken contract.

Token Campaign:

function createTokenCampaign(
    address rewardToken,
    address manager
) external onlyOwner returns (uint256 campaignId)

Uses existing ERC-20 token.

3.2. Root Updates

function updateCampaignRoot(
    uint256 campaignId,
    bytes32 merkleRoot,
    uint32 updatedAt,
    uint256 totalClaimable
) external

Authorization: Campaign manager only

Validation (TOKEN campaigns):

  • Distributor must hold sufficient tokens
  • balance >= totalClaimable - alreadyClaimed

3.3. Claims

function claimCampaign(
    uint256 campaignId,
    uint256 index,
    address account,
    uint256 totalEarned,
    bytes32[] calldata merkleProof
) external nonReentrant

Requirements:

  • msg.sender == account
  • Campaign status == ACTIVE
  • Valid Merkle proof
  • totalEarned > claimed[account]

Cumulative Model:

  • User claims difference: claimable = totalEarned - alreadyClaimed
  • Root represents total-ever-earned, not per-epoch

3.4. Finalization

TOKEN Campaign:

function finalizeCampaign(uint256 campaignId) external onlyOwner

Sets status to FINALIZED. No more claims allowed.

POINTS Campaign:

function finalizePointsCampaign(
    uint256 campaignId,
    address redeemToken,
    uint256 redeemRate,
    uint256 maxRedeemable
) external onlyOwner

Enables points  token redemption at fixed rate.

3.5. Points Redemption

function redeemPoints(
    uint256 campaignId,
    uint256 amount
) external nonReentrant

Requirements:

  • Campaign status == REDEEMABLE
  • Distributor holds sufficient redeem tokens
  • Within maxRedeemable budget

Flow:

  1. Calculate tokens out: tokensOut = amount × redeemRate / 1e18
  2. Check budget cap
  3. Burn user's points (SBT)
  4. Transfer redeem tokens to user

4. Campaign States

enum CampaignStatus {
    ACTIVE,      // Claims enabled
    PAUSED,      // Claims paused
    FINALIZED,   // Token campaign ended
    REDEEMABLE   // Points campaign ready for redemption
}

4.1. State Transitions

ACTIVE ��pause()��> PAUSED
PAUSED ��resume()��> ACTIVE
ACTIVE ��finalize()��> FINALIZED (TOKEN only)
ACTIVE/PAUSED ��finalizePoints()��> REDEEMABLE (POINTS only)

5. Merkle Tree Structure

5.1. Leaf Format

bytes32 leaf = keccak256(abi.encodePacked(index, account, totalEarned));
Field Type Purpose
index uint256 Unique index for user in tree
account address User address
totalEarned uint256 Cumulative total (not delta)

5.2. Cumulative vs Delta Model

AIMM uses cumulative:

  • Tree contains total-ever-earned
  • User claims difference from last claim
  • Allows late joiners without missing epochs
  • Simpler off-chain computation

Example:

Epoch 1: Alice earns 100
  totalEarned = 100
  Alice claims 100
 
Epoch 2: Alice earns 50 more
  totalEarned = 150 (cumulative)
  Alice claims 50 (150 - 100 already claimed)

6. Campaign Data Structure

struct Campaign {
    uint256 id;
    CampaignType campaignType;    // POINTS or TOKENS
    CampaignStatus status;
    address rewardToken;          // SBT (points) or ERC20 (tokens)
    address manager;              // Can update root
    bytes32 merkleRoot;
    uint32 lastUpdate;
    uint256 totalAllocated;
 
    // Points redemption (only for POINTS type)
    address redeemToken;
    uint256 redeemRate;           // Tokens per point (1e18 base)
    uint256 maxRedeemable;        // Budget cap
    uint256 totalRedeemed;        // Running total
}

7. Storage Layout

struct DistributorStorage {
    uint256 nextCampaignId;
    mapping(uint256 => Campaign) campaigns;
    mapping(uint256 => mapping(address => uint256)) campaignClaimed;
    mapping(uint256 => uint256) totalClaimed;
}

7.1. ERC-7201 Namespace

bytes32 constant DISTRIBUTOR_STORAGE_LOC =
    keccak256("pool.storage.distributor.v1") - 1;

8. View Functions

// Campaign info
function getCampaign(uint256 campaignId) external view returns (Campaign memory)
 
// User claim status
function getCampaignClaimed(
    uint256 campaignId,
    address account
) external view returns (uint256)
 
// Check claimable amount
function getCampaignClaimable(
    uint256 campaignId,
    uint256 index,
    address account,
    uint256 totalEarned,
    bytes32[] calldata merkleProof
) external view returns (uint256)

9. Events

// Campaign lifecycle
event CampaignCreated(
    uint256 indexed campaignId,
    CampaignType campaignType,
    address indexed rewardToken,
    address indexed manager
);
event CampaignRootUpdated(
    uint256 indexed campaignId,
    bytes32 merkleRoot,
    uint32 updatedAt,
    uint256 totalClaimable
);
event CampaignStatusUpdated(
    uint256 indexed campaignId,
    CampaignStatus status
);
 
// Claims
event CampaignClaimed(
    uint256 indexed campaignId,
    address indexed account,
    uint256 amount,
    uint256 totalEarned
);
 
// Points specific
event PointsCampaignFinalized(
    uint256 indexed campaignId,
    address redeemToken,
    uint256 redeemRate,
    uint256 maxRedeemable
);
event PointsRedeemed(
    uint256 indexed campaignId,
    address indexed account,
    uint256 pointsBurned,
    uint256 tokensReceived
);

10. Integration: Off-Chain Components

10.1. Merkle Tree Generation

Required Infrastructure:

  1. Indexer  Track eligible activity (swaps, LP, staking)
  2. Calculator  Compute rewards per user
  3. Tree Builder  Generate Merkle tree
  4. Pusher  Call updateCampaignRoot()

10.2. Example Flow

1. Epoch ends
2. Indexer aggregates activity data
3. Calculator applies reward formula
4. Tree Builder creates Merkle tree
5. Manager calls updateCampaignRoot()
6. Users claim via frontend

10.3. Proof Generation

// Off-chain
const tree = StandardMerkleTree.of(entries, ["uint256", "address", "uint256"]);
const proof = tree.getProof([index, address, totalEarned]);
 
// On-chain claim
distributor.claimCampaign(campaignId, index, address, totalEarned, proof);

11. Security Considerations

11.1. Pre-Funding Requirement

CRITICAL: TOKEN campaigns must be pre-funded before root updates.

// In updateCampaignRoot()
if (campaign.campaignType == CampaignType.TOKENS && totalClaimable > 0) {
    uint256 balance = balanceOf(rewardToken, address(this));
    uint256 required = totalClaimable - alreadyClaimed;
    if (balance < required) revert InsufficientAmount(balance, required);
}

11.2. Points Redemption Budget

// In redeemPoints()
if (campaign.maxRedeemable > 0) {
    uint256 newTotal = campaign.totalRedeemed + tokensOut;
    if (newTotal > campaign.maxRedeemable) revert InsufficientAmount(...);
}

11.3. Reentrancy Protection

All claim and redemption functions use nonReentrant modifier.

11.4. Self-Claim Only

if (msg.sender != account) revert Unauthorized();

Prevents griefing where someone claims on behalf of user to wrong epoch.

12. Gas Optimization

12.1. Cumulative Model Benefits

  • Single storage slot per user per campaign
  • No per-epoch claim tracking
  • Simple claim calculation: totalEarned - claimed

12.2. Merkle Proof Efficiency

  • O(log n) verification
  • ~15-20 proof elements for 1M users
  • ~30k gas per claim

13. Example Campaign Setup

13.1. Token Airdrop

// 1. Create campaign
(uint256 id,) = distributor.createTokenCampaign(BTR_TOKEN, manager);
 
// 2. Fund distributor
BTR_TOKEN.transfer(address(distributor), 1_000_000e18);
 
// 3. Update root (off-chain generates tree)
distributor.updateCampaignRoot(id, merkleRoot, block.timestamp, 1_000_000e18);
 
// 4. Users claim
distributor.claimCampaign(id, index, user, totalEarned, proof);

13.2. Points Program

// 1. Create campaign
(uint256 id, address sbt) = distributor.createPointsCampaign("BTR Points", "pBTR", manager);
 
// 2. Update roots periodically
distributor.updateCampaignRoot(id, root1, timestamp1, total1);
// ... more updates ...
 
// 3. Users claim points
distributor.claimCampaign(id, index, user, totalEarned, proof);
 
// 4. Finalize for redemption
distributor.finalizePointsCampaign(id, BTR_TOKEN, 1e18, 500_000e18);
 
// 5. Fund redemption
BTR_TOKEN.transfer(address(distributor), 500_000e18);
 
// 6. Users redeem
distributor.redeemPoints(id, pointsAmount);

14. Related Documentation

  • Staking Module  LP staking for reward eligibility
  • BTR Token  Governance token
  • Governance Overview  Full incentive system

1.2.3-admin.title: 1.2.3. Admin
1.2.3-admin.html:
Admin Module (AdminV1)

Pool configuration, timelock governance, and emergency controls

1. Overview

The Admin module manages pool configuration with security-first design:

  • Timelocked operations for sensitive changes
  • Emergency freeze capability without delay
  • Two-phase execution (request  wait  execute)
  • Grace period enforcement to prevent indefinitely pending operations

2. Emergency Functions (No Timelock)

2.1. Freeze Asset

Immediately halts all operations on an asset:

function freezeAsset(address token) external onlyOwner

Effects:

  • Sets FROZEN_BIT in risk config flags
  • Blocks swaps, deposits, withdrawals, flash loans
  • Immediate effect (no timelock)

Use cases:

  • Security incident response
  • Oracle failure
  • Suspected exploit

2.2. Unfreeze Asset

function unfreezeAsset(address token) external onlyOwner

Clears FROZEN_BIT flag, restoring normal operations.

3. Timelock Delays

Operation Delay Risk Level ID
Add Asset 1 day LOW keccak256("ADD_ASSET", token)
Update Risk Config 1 day LOW keccak256("UPDATE_RISK", token)
Update Fee Params 1 day LOW TIMELOCK_ID_FEE_PARAMS
Update Oracle 2 days BASE keccak256("ORACLE_UPDATE", token)
Update Staking 2 days BASE TIMELOCK_ID_STAKING
Update Bridge 3 days HIGH TIMELOCK_ID_BRIDGE
Update Treasury 3 days HIGH TIMELOCK_ID_TREASURY
Update Module 3 days HIGH TIMELOCK_ID_MODULE
Transfer Ownership 3 days HIGH TIMELOCK_ID_OWNERSHIP
Migrate Base Token 7 days CRITICAL TIMELOCK_ID_BASE_MIGRATION

Grace Period: 7 days after timelock expires to execute. Operations expire if not executed within grace period.

4. Two-Phase Execution Pattern

4.1. Step 1: Request

function requestAddAsset(
    address token,
    OracleConfig calldata oracleCfg,
    RiskConfig calldata riskCfg,
    LiquidityProfile calldata profile,
    uint16 minFeeBps,
    uint8 decimals,
    uint64 initialPrice,
    uint32 initialFastVolEMA,
    uint32 initialSlowVolEMA
) external onlyOwner

Actions:

  1. Compute operation ID
  2. Pack timelock: [executeAt:48][grace:48]
  3. Store pending data
  4. Emit TimelockRequested event

4.2. Step 2: Wait

  • Minimum delay must pass
  • Within grace period

4.3. Step 3: Execute

function executeAddAsset(address token) external onlyOwner

Actions:

  1. Validate timelock (delay passed, within grace)
  2. Decode and validate pending data
  3. Apply changes
  4. Clear pending state
  5. Emit completion event

4.4. Step 4: Cancel (Optional)

function cancelTimelock(uint8 opType) external onlyOwner

Owner can cancel any pending operation before execution.

5. Asset Management

5.1. Add Asset

Adds new token to pool with full configuration:

function requestAddAsset(
    address token,
    OracleConfig calldata oracleCfg,
    RiskConfig calldata riskCfg,
    LiquidityProfile calldata profile,
    uint16 minFeeBps,
    uint8 decimals,
    uint64 initialPrice,
    uint32 initialFastVolEMA,
    uint32 initialSlowVolEMA
) external onlyOwner

Default values set on execution:

  • maxFeeBps: 10000 (1%)
  • minDispersion: 1000 (0.1%)
  • maxDispersion: 100000 (10%)
  • gamma: 10000 (1.0x)
  • vega: 10000 (1.0x)
  • lambda: 10000 (1.0x)
  • haircutSuppressor: 10000 (1.0x)
  • anchor: baseToken (default hub-and-spoke)
  • anchorDepth: 1

Validation:

  • Token not already configured
  • Profile weights sum to 200
  • Profile offsets monotonically increasing
  • Oracle config valid
  • Initial price non-zero
  • Initial volatility values non-zero

5.2. Update Risk Config

function requestUpdateRiskConfig(
    address token,
    RiskConfig calldata cfg
) external onlyOwner

Changes decay thresholds, feature flags, depth amplifier.

5.3. Update Fee Params

function requestUpdateFeeParams(
    FeeParams calldata params
) external onlyOwner

Updates protocol share and flash loan fee.

6. Anchor Tree Management

6.1. Set Anchor (No Timelock)

function setAnchor(
    address token,
    address anchor
) external onlyOwner

Validation:

  • Asset must exist
  • Anchor must exist or be address(0) for root
  • No cycles created
  • Depth within MAX_DEPTH (4)

Effects:

  • Updates asset.anchor
  • Updates asset.anchorDepth
  • Route paths recomputed on next swap

7. Oracle Configuration

7.1. Update Oracle

function requestOracleUpdate(
    address token,
    OracleConfig calldata cfg
) external onlyOwner

Changes price feed sources:

struct OracleConfig {
    address primary;        // Primary feed address
    address secondary;      // Fallback feed address
    bytes32 feedId;         // Feed identifier
    uint16 modeFlags;       // USE_INTERNAL | USE_EXTERNAL | ALLOW_FALLBACK
    uint8 accDecimals;      // Accumulator precision
}

Validation:

  • Primary oracle callable
  • Secondary oracle callable (if configured)

8. Fee Collection

8.1. Collect Protocol Fees

function collectProtocolFees(
    address token,
    address recipient
) external nonReentrant

Authorization: Only treasury address can collect.

Flow:

  1. Read accumulated fees
  2. Clear fee counter
  3. Transfer tokens to recipient

9. Governance Operations

9.1. Ownership Transfer

function requestOwnershipTransfer(address newOwner) external onlyOwner
function executeOwnershipTransfer() external

Note: Execute callable by anyone (allows self-claim).

9.2. Module Update

function requestModuleUpdate(
    address impl,
    bytes4[] calldata selectors,
    bytes calldata initData
) external onlyOwner

Upgrades module implementations in Diamond-lite pattern.

9.3. Base Token Migration

function requestBaseMigration(address newBase) external onlyOwner
function executeBaseMigration() external onlyOwner

Changes root anchor of entire pool. CRITICAL operation - longest timelock.

9.4. Bridge Update

function requestBridgeUpdate(address newBridge) external onlyOwner
function executeBridgeUpdate() external onlyOwner

Changes authorized cross-chain bridge contract.

9.5. Treasury Update

function requestTreasuryUpdate(address newTreasury) external onlyOwner
function executeTreasuryUpdate() external onlyOwner

Changes protocol fee collection address.

10. Timelock Storage

10.1. Packed Format

// Single uint96 per operation
mapping(bytes32 => uint96) pendingOps;   // [executeAt:48][grace:48]
mapping(bytes32 => bytes) pendingData;    // Operation parameters

10.2. Validation

function validate(uint96 packed) internal view {
    (uint48 executeAt, uint48 grace) = unpack(packed);
 
    if (packed == 0) revert InvalidState();
    if (block.timestamp < executeAt) revert TooEarly();
    if (block.timestamp > executeAt + grace) revert Expired();
}

11. Events

// Timelock lifecycle
event TimelockRequested(bytes32 indexed id, uint8 opType, uint48 executeAt);
event TimelockCancelled(bytes32 indexed id, uint8 opType);
 
// Asset management
event AssetAdded(address indexed token, uint8 decimals, uint16 feeBps);
event RiskConfigUpdated(address indexed token, uint16 flags, uint16 coverageFloor);
event FeeParamsUpdated(uint8 protoShare, uint16 flashFeeBps);
 
// Governance
event OwnershipTransferred(address indexed oldOwner, address indexed newOwner);
event ModulesUpdated(address indexed impl, bytes4[] selectors);
event BaseTokenMigrated(address indexed oldBase, address indexed newBase);
event BridgeUpdated(address indexed oldBridge, address indexed newBridge);
event TreasuryUpdated(address indexed oldTreasury, address indexed newTreasury);
event OracleUpdated(address indexed token);
 
// Emergency
event EmergencyFreeze(address indexed token);
event EmergencyUnfreeze(address indexed token);
 
// Fees
event ProtocolFeesCollected(address indexed token, address indexed recipient, uint256 amount);
 
// Anchor tree
event AnchorUpdated(address indexed token, address indexed anchor, uint8 depth);

12. Security Considerations

12.1. Grace Period Protection

Grace period prevents:

  • Indefinitely pending operations
  • "Governance bomb" attacks
  • Forgotten timelocks executing years later

12.2. Multi-sig Recommendation

Owner should be a multi-signature wallet:

  • 3-of-5 or 4-of-7 recommended
  • Geographically distributed signers
  • Hardware wallet usage

12.3. Emergency Response

For security incidents:

  1. Immediate: freezeAsset() on affected tokens
  2. Assess: Evaluate damage and root cause
  3. Plan: Prepare fix with timelock
  4. Execute: Apply fix after delay
  5. Monitor: Unfreeze and watch closely

13. Code References

Function Line Purpose
freezeAsset 27 Emergency freeze
requestAddAsset 46 Add new asset
executeAddAsset 69 Apply asset addition
setAnchor 479 Update anchor tree
requestOwnershipTransfer 208 Start ownership change

14. Related Documentation

  • Governance & Access Control  Full governance architecture
  • Deployment & Upgrades  Module upgrade process

1.2.2-internal-oracle.title: 1.2.2. Internal Oracle
1.2.2-internal-oracle.html:
Internal Oracle Module (InternalOracleV1)

Self-updating TWAP oracle with dual-window price tracking and volatility EMAs

1. Overview

The Internal Oracle provides price feeds that update automatically on every swap. This eliminates external oracle dependencies for active pools while maintaining manipulation resistance through dual-window TWAPs.

Key Features:

  • Zero external calls — Prices derived from swap activity
  • Dual TWAPs — 5-minute (fast) and 1-hour (slow) windows
  • Volatility tracking — Fast and slow EMAs for spread calculation
  • B64 encoding — Gas-efficient storage
  • Same-block rejection — Prevents flash loan manipulation

2. Constants

// TWAP windows
uint32 constant FAST_WINDOW = 300;      // 5 minutes
uint32 constant SLOW_WINDOW = 3600;     // 1 hour
 
// Volatility EMA smoothing factors (1e6 base)
uint32 constant FAST_VOL_ALPHA = 200;   // 0.02%
uint32 constant SLOW_VOL_ALPHA = 1800;  // 0.18%
 
// Bounds
uint32 constant MAX_VOLATILITY = 100_000_000;  // 10,000%
uint16 constant DEFAULT_TTL = 3600;            // 1 hour

3. Feed Data Structure

struct FeedAccumulator {
    // Price tracking
    uint64 priceAccB64;         // Cumulative price accumulator (B64)
    uint64 fastSnapB64;         // Fast TWAP snapshot (B64)
    uint64 slowSnapB64;         // Slow TWAP snapshot (B64)
    uint32 fastSnapshotTime;    // Fast snapshot timestamp
    uint32 slowSnapshotTime;    // Slow snapshot timestamp
    uint64 lastPriceB64;        // Current spot price (B64)
 
    // TWAP offsets
    int32 fastOffset;           // Fast TWAP vs spot (0.0001% units)
    int32 slowOffset;           // Slow TWAP vs spot (0.0001% units)
 
    // Volatility
    uint32 fastVolEMA;          // Fast volatility EMA (1e6 base)
    uint32 slowVolEMA;          // Slow volatility EMA (1e6 base)
 
    // Metadata
    uint32 lastUpdate;          // Last update timestamp
    uint16 ttl;                 // Time-to-live (seconds)
    uint8 accDecimals;          // Accumulator decimal precision
    uint8 confidence;           // Confidence level (0-100)
}

3.1. Storage Layout

Total: 496 bits = 2 storage slots

4. B64 Float Encoding

Compact 64-bit price representation:

[mantissa:52 | decimals:5 | exponent+bias:7]
  • Mantissa: 52 bits (~15 decimal digits precision)
  • Decimals: 5 bits (0-31 token decimals)
  • Exponent: 7 bits with bias 64 (range: 10^-64 to 10^63)

Decoding:

p(18)=M⋅10(e−64+dt−ds)
WHERE
Mis the mantissa
eis the exponent
dtis the target decimals
dsis the stored decimals

See: contracts/src/libraries/LibMaths.sol:62-140

5. Accumulator Decimals

The accDecimals parameter controls accumulator precision vs. range tradeoff:

Asset Class accDecimals Use Case
Stablecoins 6 ~$1 prices, maximum range
ETH-like 12 ~$3k prices, balanced
BTC-like 18 ~$100k prices, full precision

Lower accDecimals = more headroom for long-running accumulators.

6. Price Update Flow

6.1. On Every Swap

function pushFeedInternal(
    address tokenA,
    address tokenB,
    uint64 priceA,    // Price of tokenA in base (B64)
    uint64 priceB     // Price of tokenB in base (B64)
) external

Called internally by CoreV1 after swap execution.

6.2. Update Algorithm

  1. Skip same-block updates (manipulation resistance)
  2. Update price accumulator with time-weighted contribution
  3. Check if fast window elapsed → update fast TWAP offset
  4. Check if slow window elapsed → update slow TWAP offset
  5. Update volatility EMAs with price change
  6. Store new spot price and timestamp

7. TWAP Calculation

7.1. Offset Encoding

TWAPs are stored as offsets from spot price (0.0001% units):

o=((pT−ps)ps)⋅106
WHERE
pTis the TWAP
psis the spot

7.2. Offset Interpretation

o Meaning
0 TWAP = Spot
+10000 TWAP 1% above spot
-5000 TWAP 0.5% below spot

7.3. TWAP Reconstruction

pT=ps⋅(1+o106)

8. Volatility Tracking

8.1. EMA Update Formula

σ′=σ+α⋅(|(Δp)|−σ)
WHERE
α=200(fast)or1800(slow)∈106base
|(Δp)|=|o|lutepricechange∈106base
σ= current EMA
σ′= updated EMA

8.2. Volatility Interpretation

Value (1e6) Percentage Description
10,000 0.01% Very stable
100,000 0.1% Low volatility
1,000,000 1% Moderate
10,000,000 10% High
100,000,000 100% Maximum

9. Security Properties

9.1. Flash Loan Resistance

Same-block rejection:

if (dt == 0) return;  // Skip if same block

Attackers cannot manipulate price and use it in the same transaction.

9.2. Multi-Block Manipulation

Dual-window protection:

  • Fast TWAP (5 min): Requires sustained manipulation over 300 seconds
  • Slow TWAP (1 hr): Requires sustained manipulation over 3600 seconds
  • Both must agree for narrow spreads (otherwise deviation surcharge applies)

9.3. Staleness Protection

Configurable TTL per feed. Low-volume pools should:

  1. Use external oracle fallback
  2. Set shorter TTL
  3. Increase spread when stale

10. Gas Optimization

10.1. Storage Efficiency

Field Bits Purpose
priceAccB64 64 Accumulator
fastSnapB64 64 Fast snapshot
slowSnapB64 64 Slow snapshot
timestamps 64 Two uint32
lastPriceB64 64 Spot price
offsets 64 Two int32
volatility 64 Two uint32
metadata 48 ttl + acc + conf

Total: 496 bits = 2 slots

10.2. Update Cost

Operation Gas
Load accumulator ~2,100 (cold)
Compute new values ~500
Store updates ~5,000 (warm)
Total ~7,600

11. Integration with Pricing

11.1. Price Resolution Order

  1. Check internal oracle → Use if MODE_USE_INTERNAL set
  2. Check external primary → Use if MODE_USE_EXTERNAL set
  3. Fallback to secondary → Use if MODE_ALLOW_FALLBACK set
  4. Use transient cache if available

11.2. Deviation Calculation

Δ=max(|(of−os)|,|(of)|)
WHERE
ofis the fast offset
osis the slow offset

High deviation triggers wider spreads on toxic flow (deviation surcharge U).

See Spread & Fees §3 for how deviation is used as a pricing risk signal.

12. Transient Caching (EIP-1153)

12.1. Purpose

Oracle reads within the same transaction are cached using EIP-1153 transient storage. This avoids redundant storage reads for multi-hop swaps.

12.2. Gas Savings

Operation Without Cache With Cache
First oracle read ~2,100 gas ~2,100 gas
Subsequent reads ~2,100 gas ~100 gas
3-hop swap (6 reads) ~12,600 gas ~2,500 gas

12.3. Cache Lifetime

Transient storage is automatically cleared at transaction end—no explicit cleanup needed.

See: contracts/src/libraries/LibTransientCache.sol

13. Related Documentation

  • Spread & Fees — How volatility affects pricing
  • Parametrization — Oracle parameters

1.2.1-core.title: 1.2.1. Core
1.2.1-core.html:
Core Module (CoreV1)

Main AMM operations: swap, deposit, withdraw, donate, liability swap

1. Overview

The Core module implements AIMM's primary liquidity operations. All user-facing trading and LP interactions route through CoreV1.

Key Functions:

  • swap()  Exchange tokens with oracle-aware pricing
  • deposit()  Add single-sided liquidity
  • withdraw()  Remove liquidity with coverage-based haircuts
  • donate()  Gift tokens to LPs (no LP tokens minted)
  • liabilitySwap()  Swap LP positions between assets

2. Swap

2.1. Function Signature

function swap(
    address tokenIn,
    address tokenOut,
    uint256 amountIn,
    uint256 minAmountOut,
    address recipient
) external returns (SwapQuote memory quote)

2.2. Parameters

Parameter Type Description
tokenIn address Token being sold (or NATIVE sentinel)
tokenOut address Token being bought
amountIn uint256 Exact amount to sell
minAmountOut uint256 Slippage protection
recipient address Receives output tokens

2.3. Execution Flow

1. Validate inputs & check feature flags
   �� tokenIn ` tokenOut
   �� amountIn > 0
   �� SWAP_ENABLED_BIT set
   �� Neither asset FROZEN_BIT
 
2. Apply liability decay (if coverage < threshold)
 
3. Calculate route through anchor tree (LCA)
   �� Returns hops: [tokenIn, ..., LCA, ..., tokenOut]
 
4. For each hop in route:
   �� Get oracle price (internal or external)
   �� Calculate inventory skew
   �� Traverse spline for price impact
   �� Accumulate amounts
 
5. Calculate fees
   �� Volatility band (symmetric)
   �� Deviation surcharge (if worsening coverage)
   �� Split protocol/LP
 
6. Validate minAmountOut
 
7. Update state
   �� reserves[tokenIn] += amountIn
   �� reserves[tokenOut] -= amountOut
   �� protocolFees[tokenOut] += protoFee
   �� Push oracle update
 
8. Transfer tokens
   �� Handle native wrapping/unwrapping

2.4. Return Value

struct SwapQuote {
    uint256 amountOut;       // Tokens received
    uint256 amountIn;        // Tokens paid
    uint16 spreadBps;        // Total spread (0.0001% units)
    uint256 protoFee;        // Protocol fee portion
    uint256 lpFee;           // LP fee portion
    int8 skewIn;             // Input asset inventory skew
    int8 skewOut;            // Output asset inventory skew
    address[] routeHops;     // Full routing path
    uint256[] hopAmounts;    // Amount at each hop
}

2.5. Events

event Swapped(
    address indexed sender,
    address indexed tokenIn,
    address indexed tokenOut,
    uint256 amountIn,
    uint256 amountOut,
    uint16 spreadBps,
    address recipient
);

3. Deposit

3.1. Function Signature

function deposit(
    address token,
    uint256 amount,
    uint256 minLPAmount,
    address recipient
) external returns (DepositResult memory result)

3.2. Parameters

Parameter Type Description
token address Asset to deposit
amount uint256 Amount to deposit
minLPAmount uint256 Minimum LP tokens expected
recipient address Receives LP tokens

3.3. Mechanics

1. Validate inputs
   �� amount > 0, asset configured
 
2. Apply liability decay
 
3. Calculate LP amount
   �� lpAmount = amount (1:1 for new deposits)
 
4. Update state
   �� reserves += amount
   �� liabilities += lpAmount
   �� lpBalances[recipient][token] += lpAmount
 
5. Transfer tokens in
   �� Handle native wrapping
 
6. Execute hooks
   �� PRE_DEPOSIT (before transfer)
   �� POST_DEPOSIT (after state update)

3.4. Coverage Impact

Deposits always improve coverage:

coverage_before = reserves / liabilities
coverage_after = (reserves + amount) / (liabilities + amount)
 
If coverage_before < 100%:
  coverage_after > coverage_before  

3.5. Return Value

struct DepositResult {
    uint256 lpAmount;       // LP tokens minted
    uint256 actualDeposit;  // Tokens accepted
}

4. Withdraw

4.1. Function Signature

function withdraw(
    address token,
    uint256 lpAmount,
    uint256 minAmountOut,
    address recipient
) external returns (WithdrawResult memory result)

4.2. Parameters

Parameter Type Description
token address Asset to withdraw
lpAmount uint256 LP tokens to burn
minAmountOut uint256 Slippage protection
recipient address Receives withdrawn tokens

4.3. Haircut Mechanism

When coverage < 100%, withdrawals take a haircut:

function applyWithdrawalHaircut(
    uint256 amount,
    uint128 reserves,
    uint128 liabilities,
    uint16 suppression
) internal pure returns (uint256 actualAmount, uint256 haircutAmount) {
    uint256 coverage = (reserves * WAD) / liabilities;
 
    if (coverage >= WAD) {
        return (amount, 0);  // No haircut at 100%+ coverage
    }
 
    // Power-law haircut: (1 - coverage)^p
    uint256 deficit = WAD - coverage;
    uint256 p = WAD + (suppression * WAD / 10000);
    uint256 haircut = pow(deficit, p);
 
    actualAmount = amount * (WAD - haircut) / WAD;
    haircutAmount = amount - actualAmount;
}

4.4. Haircut Examples

Coverage Suppression Exponent p Haircut
90% 10000 2 1%
80% 10000 2 4%
50% 10000 2 25%
50% 30000 4 6.25%

4.5. Return Value

struct WithdrawResult {
    uint256 amountOut;  // Tokens received (after haircut)
    uint256 lpBurned;   // LP tokens burned
}

5. Donate

5.1. Function Signature

function donate(
    address token,
    uint256 amount
) external

5.2. Purpose

Allows external parties to add reserves without receiving LP tokens. This is a core mechanism for Cooperative Arbitrage and other value redistribution use cases.

Primary Use Cases:

  • Cooperative Arbitrage: Arbitrageurs donate proceeds back to the pool to build reputation and earn higher rebate tiers (see Toxic Flow Mitigation - Cooperative Arbitrage)
  • Protocol fee redistribution: Return protocol fees to LPs
  • Third-party yield injection: External yield strategies depositing rewards
  • Recovery mechanisms: Emergency coverage restoration

5.3. Mechanics

1. Validate token is configured in pool
2. Transfer tokens from sender to pool
3. reserves[token] += amount
4. Coverage improves (same liabilities, more reserves)
5. Track donation for sender's reputation (if cooperator)

5.4. Cooperative Arbitrage Integration

When a whitelisted cooperator donates:

// Reputation accumulation
totalDonations[msg.sender] += amount;
 
// Reputation formula
reputation = totalDonations / totalRebates
 
// Higher reputation → higher rebate tier → more profitable arbitrage

The virtuous cycle:

  1. Cooperators arbitrage pool vs CEX
  2. Donate portion of proceeds → reputation increases
  3. Higher rebate tier → lower effective costs
  4. More competitive → capture more arb opportunities
  5. LPs recover LVR losses via donations

5.5. Coverage Impact

Donations always improve coverage:

cafter=(R+amount)L>RL=cbefore

This makes donate ideal for LVR recovery—arbitrage profits flow back to LPs without diluting their positions.

6. Liability Swap

6.1. Function Signature

function liabilitySwap(
    address tokenFrom,
    address tokenTo,
    uint256 lpAmount,
    uint256 minLPOut,
    address recipient
) external returns (uint256 lpOut)

6.2. Purpose

Allows LPs to swap their position from one asset to another without withdraw + deposit cycle.

6.3. Mechanics

1. Burn LP tokens for tokenFrom
2. Calculate equivalent value via oracle
3. Mint LP tokens for tokenTo
4. Apply coverage considerations
 
Note: May be subject to coverage constraints and haircuts

6.4. Requirements

  • LIABILITY_SWAP_ENABLED_BIT must be set in risk config

7. Multi-Hop Routing

7.1. Anchor Tree Navigation

All swaps route through the anchor tree via LCA (Least Common Ancestor):

Example tree:
                BASE (USDC)
               /    |    \
            WETH   WBTC   DAI
            /
         LINK
 
Swap: LINK  WBTC
Route: [LINK, WETH, BASE, WBTC]
Hops:  [LINKWETH, WETHBASE, BASEWBTC]

7.2. Path Computation

function computeRoute(
    PoolStorage storage $,
    address tokenIn,
    address tokenOut
) internal view returns (RoutePath memory path)

Algorithm:

  1. Walk from tokenIn to root, recording ancestors
  2. Walk from tokenOut to root until hitting common ancestor
  3. Concatenate paths: [tokenIn  LCA  tokenOut]

7.3. Path Constraints

Constraint Value Purpose
Max depth 4 Limits tree height
Max hops 6 Limits route length (2 × MAX_DEPTH)
No cycles enforced Prevents infinite loops

8. State Management

8.1. Transient Storage (EIP-1153)

Core uses transient storage for:

  • Reentrancy guard: Prevents recursive calls
  • Oracle cache: Avoid redundant price lookups within transaction

8.2. Reentrancy Protection

modifier nonReentrant() {
    if (_reentrancyGuard() != 0) revert ReentrancyDetected();
    _setReentrancyGuard(1);
    _;
    _setReentrancyGuard(0);
}

8.3. Decay Application

Before any operation, decay is checked and applied:

function _applyDecay(
    PoolStorage storage $,
    address token,
    Asset storage asset
) internal {
    RiskConfig storage risk = $.riskConfigs[token];
 
    if ((risk.flags & DECAY_ENABLED_BIT) == 0) return;
    if (asset.lastUpdate == block.timestamp) return;
 
    uint256 coverage = (asset.reserves * WAD) / asset.liabilities;
    if (coverage >= risk.decayStartRatioBps * WAD / BPS_PRECISION) return;
 
    uint32 dt = uint32(block.timestamp) - asset.lastUpdate;
    uint128 decayAmount = calculateDecay(...);
 
    asset.liabilities -= decayAmount;
    asset.lastUpdate = uint32(block.timestamp);
}

9. Native Token Support

9.1. Sentinel Address

address constant NATIVE = 0xEeeeeEeeeEeEeeEeEeEeeEEEeeeeEeeeeeeeEEeE;

9.2. Auto-Wrapping

function _wrap(PoolStorage storage $, address token) internal view returns (address) {
    return token == NATIVE ? $.wnative : token;
}

9.3. Transfer Handling

function _pull(address token, address from, uint256 amount) internal {
    if (token == NATIVE) {
        if (msg.value != amount) revert InvalidAmount();
        // Wrap to WETH
        IWETH(wnative).deposit{value: amount}();
    } else {
        token.safeTransferFrom(from, address(this), amount);
    }
}
 
function _push(address token, address to, uint256 amount) internal {
    if (token == NATIVE) {
        IWETH(wnative).withdraw(amount);
        to.safeTransferETH(amount);
    } else {
        token.safeTransfer(to, amount);
    }
}

10. Hook Integration

10.1. Lifecycle Events

// Deposit
_hook(<!--MATHINLINE1-->, tokenNorm, HOOK_POST_DEPOSIT)
 
// Withdraw
_hook(<!--MATHINLINE2-->, tokenNorm, HOOK_POST_WITHDRAW)
 
// Swap
_hook(<!--MATHINLINE3-->, tokenNorm, HOOK_POST_SWAP)

10.2. Hook Invocation

function _hook(
    PoolStorage storage $,
    address token,
    uint32 flag
) internal returns (address hook) {
    hook = $.hooks[token];
    if (hook != address(0) && ($.hookFlags[token] & flag) != 0) {
        // Call hook contract
    }
}

11. Error Handling

Error Condition
ZeroValue() Amount is zero
InsufficientAmount(available, required) Not enough reserves/balance
ThresholdViolation(value, threshold) Slippage exceeded
FeatureDisabled(resource) Swap/flash disabled
ReentrancyDetected() Recursive call attempt
InvalidState() Pool not initialized

12. Gas Costs (Estimated)

Operation Gas (Cold) Gas (Warm)
Simple swap (2 hops) ~150,000 ~80,000
Multi-hop swap (4 hops) ~250,000 ~120,000
Deposit ~100,000 ~60,000
Withdraw ~120,000 ~70,000
Donate ~60,000 ~40,000

13. Related Documentation

  • Inventory Management  Coverage and skew
  • Liquidity Shaping  Spline profiles
  • Spread & Fees  Fee calculation
  • Internal Oracle  Price tracking

4.8-price-charts.title: 4.8. Price Charts
4.8-price-charts.html:
Price Charts

Advanced charting with technical indicators and synthetic pairs

The BTR interface includes professional-grade price charts with real-time data, technical analysis indicators, and support for synthetic trading pairs.

Chart Types

Choose from three visualization modes:

  • Candlesticks - Traditional OHLC candles showing open, high, low, close
  • Bars - OHLC bars for a more compact view
  • Line - Simple closing price line for trend clarity

Timeframes

Available intervals: 1m, 5m, 15m, 1h, 4h, 1D

Charts store only 1-minute candles on the backend and reconstruct higher timeframes on-demand for efficient storage.

Synthetic Pairs

BTR supports synthetic trading pairs (e.g., BTC/ETH, SOL/AVAX) that don't exist as direct market pairs.

How Synthetic Pairs Work

For a pair like BTC/ETH:

  1. Fetch both BTC/USDC and ETH/USDC price feeds
  2. Construct synthetic candles using correlation-dampened extremes
  3. Display the computed ratio in real-time

Synthetic OHLC Construction

The chart computes synthetic candles using a correlation-based approach:

// Exact open/close from observed prices
open = btc.open / eth.open
close = btc.close / eth.close
 
// Compute candidate extremes from all possible combinations
candidateHigh = max(
  btc.high / eth.low,    // Max-range upper bound
  btc.high / eth.open,
  btc.high / eth.close,
  btc.open / eth.low,
  btc.close / eth.low
)
 
candidateLow = min(
  btc.low / eth.high,    // Max-range lower bound
  btc.low / eth.open,
  btc.low / eth.close,
  btc.open / eth.high,
  btc.close / eth.high
)
 
// Dampen wicks based on correlation (ρ)
// When BTC and ETH move together (high ρ), extreme divergences are unlikely
center = (open + close) / 2
dampFactor = 1 - 0.5 * ρ  // At ρ=0.85, dampFactor ≈ 0.575
 
high = center + (candidateHigh - center) * dampFactor
low = center + (candidateLow - center) * dampFactor

Key insight: When correlation (ρ) is high (e.g., 0.85 for BTC/ETH), the algorithm reduces wick size because simultaneous opposite extremes (BTC hitting high while ETH hits low in the same candle) are statistically unlikely.

Default correlation: 0.85 (typical for major crypto pairs) Rolling window: 20 bars for dynamic correlation estimation

This produces realistic wicks without requiring M1 data aggregation on the client.

Technical Indicators

BTR charts support a comprehensive suite of technical analysis tools using a Multi-Timeframe (MTF) approach for smoother signals.

MTF Methodology

All indicators combine fast (10-period) and slow (20-period) calculations:

MTF_Value = (Fast_10 + Slow_20) / 2

This dual-timeframe average provides:

  • Smoother signals - Less noise than single-period indicators
  • Better memory - Captures both recent and longer-term trends
  • Reduced whipsaws - More stable entry/exit signals

Available Indicators

EMA Trend (Overlay)

  • Dual exponential moving averages overlaid on price chart
  • Default: EMA(10) and EMA(20)
  • Use case: Trend direction and crossover signals

EMACD (Sub-pane)

  • EMA divergence: MTF_EMA - MA(MTF_EMA, 14)
  • Histogram showing momentum strength
  • Use case: Identify momentum shifts and trend exhaustion

RSIMA (Sub-pane)

  • MTF Relative Strength Index vs its moving average
  • Shows RSI(10,20) and MA(14) of MTF_RSI
  • Use case: Overbought/oversold conditions with confirmation

RSIMACD (Sub-pane)

  • RSI divergence: MTF_RSI - MA(MTF_RSI, 14)
  • Histogram centered at zero
  • Use case: RSI momentum and reversal signals

ADXMA (Sub-pane)

  • MTF Average Directional Index vs its moving average
  • Shows ADX(10,20) and MA(14) of MTF_ADX
  • Use case: Trend strength measurement (>25 = strong trend)

ADXMACD (Sub-pane)

  • ADX divergence: MTF_ADX - MA(MTF_ADX, 14)
  • Histogram showing trend strength momentum
  • Use case: Identify strengthening or weakening trends

SDEVMA (Sub-pane)

  • MTF Standard Deviation vs its moving average
  • Shows SDEV(10,20) and MA(14) of MTF_SDEV
  • Use case: Volatility analysis and breakout prediction

SDEVMACD (Sub-pane)

  • Standard deviation divergence: MTF_SDEV - MA(MTF_SDEV, 14)
  • Histogram showing volatility momentum
  • Use case: Detect volatility expansion/contraction

Customizing Indicators

All indicators accept three configurable parameters:

  • Fast period (default: 10) - Short-term sensitivity
  • Slow period (default: 20) - Long-term smoothing
  • Signal period (default: 14) - MA baseline for divergence calculations

Click the pencil icon next to any indicator to adjust parameters.

Divergence Indicators

Indicators ending in "CD" (EMACD, RSIMACD, ADXMACD, SDEVMACD) are divergence-type histograms:

  • Positive values - Indicator above its baseline (bullish momentum)
  • Negative values - Indicator below its baseline (bearish momentum)
  • Zero line - Equilibrium reference

Drawing Tools

The chart supports professional drawing tools for technical analysis:

  • Trendlines - Click two points to draw trend channels
  • Horizontal/Vertical Lines - Mark key price levels or time events
  • Cross Lines - Combined price + time markers
  • Freehand Draw - Sketch annotations
  • Highlight - Mark important chart regions
  • Shapes - Rectangles, circles, triangles for pattern recognition

Keyboard shortcuts:

  • Delete / Backspace - Remove selected drawing
  • Escape - Exit drawing mode and clear selection

Drawings are automatically saved per-pair and timeframe in browser storage.

Data Architecture

  • Storage: Only M1 (1-minute) candles stored on backend
  • Reconstruction: Higher timeframes built on-demand from M1 data
  • Gap filling: Missing data automatically fetched from exchanges after downtime
  • Live updates: WebSocket price streams with rate-limited updates
  • Synthetic feeds: Real-time triangulation for non-native pairs

Export

Charts support CSV export including:

  • OHLC data for selected timeframe
  • All active indicator values
  • Time series aligned to chart candles

Click the download icon in the toolbar to export.

Performance Tips

  1. Use higher timeframes (1h, 4h, 1D) for longer historical views
  2. Limit active indicators - 2-3 indicators per chart for best performance
  3. Synthetic pairs - Slight latency due to dual-feed computation
  4. Chart caching - Recently viewed pairs load faster from cache

Example Workflows

Trend Following Strategy

  1. Add EMA Trend overlay (default 10/20)
  2. Add EMACD sub-pane for momentum confirmation
  3. Look for EMA crossovers with positive EMACD divergence

Volatility Breakout Strategy

  1. Add SDEVMA to identify low volatility periods
  2. Add SDEVMACD to detect volatility expansion
  3. Enter on SDEVMACD spike above zero line

Mean Reversion Strategy

  1. Add RSIMA to identify extremes
  2. Add RSIMACD for divergence signals
  3. Look for RSI extremes with RSIMACD reversal

Technical Notes

Correlation Estimation

For synthetic pairs, the chart estimates correlation (ρ) using a rolling 20-bar window of log returns:

ρ = cov(log(base_t / base_{t-1}), log(quote_t / quote_{t-1})) /
    sqrt(var(base) * var(quote))

Fallback: Default ρ = 0.85 if insufficient data (<5 bars)

Wick Dampening

High correlation reduces synthetic wick size by pulling extremes toward the candle center:

  • ρ = 0 (uncorrelated): Full range (100% of candidate wicks)
  • ρ = 0.85 (typical): ~58% of candidate range
  • ρ = 1 (perfect correlation): 50% of candidate range

This prevents unrealistic wicks from theoretical price combinations that rarely occur in practice.

Troubleshooting

Chart shows gaps after reconnection:

  • Gaps <1 minute ignored (noise)
  • Larger gaps auto-filled from exchange history
  • If persists, refresh page to force full data fetch

Synthetic pair shows wrong data:

  • Verify both component feeds are available (check /health endpoint)
  • Check if correlation calculation has sufficient data (≥5 bars)
  • Try switching to a higher timeframe for more stable data

Indicators not updating:

  • Ensure minimum data requirements met (indicators need ~20+ candles)
  • Check if live price stream is connected (watch chart header)
  • Try toggling indicator off/on to force recalculation

Further Reading

  • Swap Guide - Execute trades from chart analysis
  • Provide Liquidity - Supply liquidity for pairs you analyze
  • Technical Analysis Foundations - External resource
